en: *Jinjiang Chan Deng* (The Lamp of Chan from the Jin River), Volume One.
Compiled by Zhaojue Zhangxue Tongzui;
Revised by Huan’an Hu Shengyou of Shaoxing.
The Sixth Generation under the Fourth Patriarch (a collateral line):
Chan Master Chonghui of Mount Tianzhu in Shuzhou, a dharma heir of Zhwei of Niuhead Mountain in Jinling.
Born into the Chen family of Pengzhou, he traveled to Shuzhou at the beginning of the Qianyuan era of the Tang dynasty.
He founded a temple on Mount Tianzhu in the prefecture. In the first year of the Yongtai era, it was granted an official plaque. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Mount Tianzhu?
The Master said, "The heights of Mount Zhububu make the sun difficult to see; before the Jade Mirror Peak, people are easily enlightened.

The monk asked, "Before Bodhidharma came to this land, did the Buddha-dharma exist or not? The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment whether it existed before he came, let us speak of the matter as it is right now."
"How is it? the monk asked. "I do not understand," he said. "I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "Ten thousand ages of eternal sky;
a single day of wind and moon. The monk was speechless. The Master spoke again, "Do you understand, *ācārya*? "I do not understand," he replied. The Master said, "What is it on your own account?
What does it have to do with whether Bodhidharma has come or not yet come? His coming here is very much like practicing divination."

Han said, "I see that you do not understand. For your sake, I shall pierce the lines of the divination with my awl. As soon as signs of good or ill fortune arise, they will all fall within your own sphere;
you must observe them for yourself. The monk asked, "What is one who understands divination? The Master said, "The moment you step out the door."
"That would not be hitting the mark. Question: "What is the 'house style' of Tianzhu? The Master said:
"At times white clouds come to close the door; there is no more wind or moon, yet the four mountains flow on. Question: "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? The Master said:

"The peaks of Mount Shuan are high and ever-accumulating with green; the bright moonlight of the Shu River shines with radiance. Question: "What is the Great [Way]? The Master said: [He remained silent.]
[The student] asked about the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. The Master said, "Throughout vast kalpas, he has never been obstructed. If he were not the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, what would he be?
[The student] asked, "Why then does the Buddha-dharma not manifest before me? The Master said, "It is precisely because you do not understand."
"Therefore, it is not manifested before you. If you were to go and understand it, there would likewise be no Buddha to be realized.
Question: "What is the Way? The Master said: "White clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies cling to the flowers in the courtyard.

Question: "What have the sages of the past ever said? The Master said: "What words do you see me uttering right now? Question: "I pray that the Master will proclaim the matters of the School. The Master said: [As above].
The Master said: "The stone ox bellows beyond the void; when the wooden horse neighs, the moon hides behind the mountains.
A questioner asked: "What is the Master’s way of benefiting others? The Master said: "A single rain nourishes all; the thousand peaks display their exquisite beauty. A questioner asked:

"What is it like to be among the people of Tianzhu Mountain? The Master said: "Walking alone atop a thousand peaks; strolling leisurely by the nine-fold spring. A questioner asked: "What is it like to be... [The text ends here.]

Regarding the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, the Master said: "A white monkey carries its offspring across the green cliffs; bees and butterflies carry blossoms amidst the green medicinal herbs.
He entered nirvana in the fourteenth year of the Dali era and was interred in a stupa to the north of the mountain.
The Fourth Generation under the Fifth Patriarch:
Chan Master Wuzhu of Baotang Monastery in Yizhou, a Dharma heir of Master Wuxiang of Yizhou. Having first received the Dharma from Master Wuxiang, he then resided in the south.

Yang Bai resided at Yaishan, devoting himself exclusively to the tranquility of meditative stillness. After several years had passed, students gradually began to arrive; as their earnest requests did not cease, he thereafter began to bestow his instructions.
Although he extensively expounded upon the verbal teachings, he took "non-thought" (*amanasikāra*) alone as his fundamental principle.

When Du Hongjian, the State Councilor of the Tang dynasty, went out to govern the region of Shu (Kunwei), he heard of the Master’s reputation and desired to pay him homage. He dispatched an envoy to the mountain to extend an invitation during that season.
The Regional Inspector Cui Ning also ordered the monastics of various temples to come out from afar to welcome and escort [the Master].

Upon arriving at Konghui Temple, Du Gong and the military commander summoned eminent masters of the Three Studies to assemble within the temple. After the formal greetings were concluded, Du Gong asked, "I, your disciple, have heard that you, O Master, speak of the Dharma-gate of the three phrases:
'no recollection,' 'no thought,' and 'do not delude. Is this so? The Master replied, "It is so."
The Duke said, "Are these three phrases one or three? The Master replied, "'No recollection' is called precept; 'no thought' is called concentration; 'do not delude' is called wisdom.
When the single mind does not arise, one possesses precept, concentration, and wisdom; it is neither one nor three.

The Duke asked, "In the last phrase, is the character for 'delusion' (妄) the same as the 'forgetting' (忘) that is written with the 'heart' radical (心)? The Master said, "It is the one written with the 'woman' radical (女). The Duke asked, "Is there a scriptural authority for this?"
The Master said, "The *Dharmapada* states: 'If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence. If one can ensure the mind is not deluded, diligence will be boundless.
Upon hearing this, the official’s doubts were completely dispelled. The official asked again, 'Does the Master still instruct people using the three phrases?
The Master replied, 'For a beginner practitioner, I first require them to cease their discursive thoughts and settle the waves of consciousness; when the water is clear, the reflection appears.'"

Manifesting, he realized the essence of non-thought; quiescent extinction was present before him, and even "non-thought" could no longer be established. At that time, a crow cawed in a tree in the courtyard.
The Master asked, "Did you hear it? The Master replied, "I heard it. After the crow had flown away, he asked again, "Did you hear it? The Master replied, "I heard it."
The Duke said, "The crows have departed without a sound; how can you say that you heard them? The Master then addressed the assembly at large:
"A Buddha’s world is difficult to encounter, and the True Dharma is difficult to hear. Each of you listen attentively! To hear is to have no hearing;

this is not a matter of the nature of hearing. It is originally unarisen—how could it ever cease? When there is sound, it is the sense-object of sound that arises of itself; when there is no sound, it is the [nature of] sound..."
The dust of sound naturally ceases, yet this nature of hearing does not arise with the sound, nor does it cease with the sound.
To awaken to this nature of hearing is to escape being turned by the sensory object of sound. You should know that hearing is without arising or ceasing; hearing is without coming or going.

The official, together with his subordinates and the great assembly, bowed their heads and asked again: "What is called the 'Primary Meaning' (paramārtha)? From what sequence is this Primary Meaning attained?"

[The Master] entered. The Master said, "The primary truth (paramārtha-satya) has no sequence; it neither enters nor exits. In the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), everything exists; in the primary truth, there is nothing.
That all phenomena (dharmas) are without intrinsic nature—that very nature is what is called the primary truth. The Buddha said, "That which has existence is named the conventional truth;
that which is without intrinsic nature is the primary truth. The Duke said, "As the Master has explained, this is truly inconceivable. The Duke spoke again:
"Your disciple’s nature and understanding are shallow and limited. Previously, during my leisure time, I composed two fascicles of commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith*.
May these be considered [in accord with] the Buddha-dharma? The Master said: "In composing commentaries, one invariably employs the consciousness and mind to deliberate and discriminate;

it is through conditioned activity and effort, by stirring the mind and giving rise to thoughts, that such works can be produced. According to the text of the treatise itself, it says: 'One should know that all dharmas...'"
From the very beginning, it is free from the marks of verbal expression, free from the marks of names and words, and free from the marks of mental objects. It is ultimately equal and without change;

there is only the one mind, and for this reason it is called True Suchness (*tathatā*). Now, you, sir, are attached to the marks of verbal expression, attached to the marks of names and words, and attached to the marks of mental objects.
Since you are attached to such various marks, how can this be the Buddha-dharma? Sir, please stand up!
The *Rites* say: "A disciple once asked various venerable monks (mahā-satpuruṣa), and they all praised the disciple as being inconceivable (*acintya*).
You should know that they were merely following worldly sentiment. Now, Master, you shall explain it from the perspective of understanding, in accordance with the Dharma of the mind-ground;
this is indeed the truth that is inconceivable. The Master further asked: "How is there no arising? How is there no ceasing? How can one attain [this]?"
"Liberation. The Master said: "When the mind does not arise upon encountering objects, this is called 'non-arising. That which does not arise is also non-extinguished.
Since there is neither arising nor extinguishing, one is not bound by external conditions; one is liberated in that very place. Non-arising is called 'no-thought' (amanasikāra).
Where there is no thought, there is no extinction. No-thought is no bondage; no-thought is no liberation. To state the essential point: when you recognize the mind, you are immediately free."
"Contemplate this: seeing one's nature is itself liberation. Apart from the mind that perceives through consciousness, there is no other dharma-gate for realizing unsurpassed bodhi;
such a thing is impossible. The official asked, "What is meant by 'perceiving one's nature through the mind of consciousness'?

The Master replied, "All practitioners of the Way drift along with their thoughts because they do not recognize the true mind. As for the true mind, even when thoughts arise, it does not follow them into birth."
Mindfulness of cessation does not rely on stillness; it neither comes nor goes, is neither fixed nor distracted, neither grasps nor abandons, and neither sinks nor floats.
It is unconditioned and signless, lively and agile, ordinary and sovereign. This essence of mind is ultimately ungraspable;

there is nothing to be known or perceived. Everything encountered by the eye is suchness; there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the nature. [The Master] and the assembly prostrated themselves.
He praised him and departed with great joy. Later, the Master resided at Baotang Monastery and passed away there.

The First Generation under Dajian [Huineng] was Chan Master Huairang of Nanyue, whose secular surname was Du and who hailed from Jinzhou. He was born on the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yifeng era of the Tang Dynasty.
On the day of his birth, a white vapor appeared as a response to the celestial signs in the region of Ankang. The Grand Astrologer observed it and reported it to Emperor Gaozong.
The Emperor then asked, "What auspicious omen is this? The Grand Astrologer replied, "It is a vessel of the state's Dharma."
Unstained by worldly glory, the Emperor issued an edict to Han Jie, the Governor of Jinzhou, ordering him to personally go and offer condolences to the family.

The family had three sons, of whom the Master was the youngest; he was exceptionally brilliant and his nature was solely characterized by kindness and deference. His father consequently named him Huairang.
At the age of ten, he took pleasure only in Buddhist scriptures. At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanjing visited their home and spoke to his parents.
He said, "If this youth leaves the household life, he will surely attain the Supreme Vehicle and extensively deliver sentient beings.

In the third year of the Chuigong era, when he was fifteen years old, he took leave of his parents and went to Yuquan Temple in Jingzhou, where he received the precepts under the Vinaya Master Hongjing.

In the second year of the Tongtian era, he received full ordination. Thereafter, he studied the Vinaya Piṭaka. One day, he sighed to himself, saying, "Now, one who leaves the household life does so for the sake of [the Dharma]..."
He practiced the Dharma; among gods and humans, there was none who surpassed him.

At that time, his fellow student Tantan, knowing that his teacher’s spirit and resolve were lofty and far-reaching, urged him to visit Master An of Mount Song. Master An inspired him, whereupon he went directly to Caoxi to attend upon the Sixth Patriarch.
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch said, "What thing comes in such a manner?"
The Master remained silent. Thus eight years passed until, suddenly, he attained realization. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached an understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so?
The Master replied, "To describe it as a single thing is not to hit the mark. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still need for cultivation and realization?
The Master replied, "There is no lack of cultivation and realization; it is simply that one must not be defiled. The Patriarch said, "Precisely this non-defilement—"
"Stained. You are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas; since you are thus, I am also thus. The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied of you:
'From beneath your feet shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world to death. The illness lies within your own mind; there is no need to speak of it hastily.
The Master attended him at his side for fifteen years. In the second year of the Xiāntián era, he resided at Mount Heng.

At a monastery during the Kaiyuan era, there was a śramaṇa named Daoyi who resided at Mount Heng and constantly practiced seated meditation. The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, went to him and asked, "Virtuous One, what do you hope to achieve by practicing seated meditation? Daoyi replied, "I hope to become a Buddha. The Master then took a brick and began to polish it on a stone slab in front of the hermitage. Daoyi asked, "What are you polishing that for? The Master said, "I am polishing it into a mirror. Daoyi said, "How long will it take to polish a brick into a mirror? The Master said, "If you cannot polish a brick into a mirror, how can you become a Buddha through sitting meditation? Daoyi was greatly enlightened by these words. He then prostrated himself before the Master and became his disciple. Subsequently, he established a monastery at Jiangxi and was known as Mazu Daoyi. His disciples numbered over a thousand, and they were all great masters of the Way. They propagated the teachings throughout the world, and their influence lasted for generations. This is called the Hongzhou School. It is the source of the Linji, Yunmen, Caodong, and Fayan schools. All four lineages are derived from this one school. Therefore, it is said: "The Dharma-gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs is not something that can be grasped by the mind or intellect; it is only transmitted from heart-mind to heart-mind. This is why it is called the "Direct Pointing" (Zhizhi) school. It is also called the "Southern School," for it was in the south that the Dharma flourished. It is also called the "Zen" (Chan) school, for it takes seated meditation as its primary practice. It is also called the "Sudden Enlightenment" (Dunwu) school, for it does not rely on gradual cultivation. It is also called the "Mind-Only" (Weixin) school, for it takes the mind as the fundamental principle. It is also called the "No-Mind" (Wuxin) school, for it is free from all conceptual attachments. It is also called the "Non-Abiding" (Wuzhu) school, for it has no fixed location. It is also called the "Unobtainable" (Buke-de) school, for it cannot be grasped. It is also called the "No-Form" (Wuxiang) school, for it is devoid of characteristics. It is also called the "No-Name" (Wuming) school, for it is beyond names and titles. It is also called the "No-Birth" (Wusheng) school, for it is originally unborn. It is also called the "No-Destroyed" (Wumie) school, for it is originally indestructible. It is also called the "No-Self" (Wuwo) school, for it is free from the self. It is also called the "No-Other" (Wuyi) school, for it is free from others. It is also called the "No-Coming" (Wulai) school, for it has no place of origin. It is also called the "No-Going" (Wuliang) school, for it has no destination. It is also called the "No-Attainment" (Wude) school, for there is nothing to be attained. It is also called the "No-Loss" (Wusui) school, for there is nothing to be lost. It is also called the "No-Gain" (Wude) school, for there is nothing to be gained. It is also called the "No-Loss" (Wusui) school, for there is nothing to be lost. It is also called the "No-Defilement" (Wuran) school, for it is free from defilement. It is also called the "No-Purity" (Wujing) school, for it is free from purity. It is also called the "No-Right" (Wushi) school, for it is free from correctness. It is also called the "No-Wrong" (Wuwang) school, for it is free from error. It is also called the "No-True" (Wuzhen) school, for it is free from truth. It is also called the "No-False" (Wuxie) school, for it is free from falsehood. It is also called the "No-Existence" (Wuyu) school, for it is free from existence. It is also called the "No-Non-existence" (Wuwu) school, for it is free from non-existence. It is also called the "No-Being" (Wuyu) school, for it is free from being. It is also called the "No-Non-being" (Wuwu) school, for it is free from non-being. It is also called the "No-Form" (Wuxiang) school, for it is free from form. It is also called the "No-Emptiness" (Wukong) school, for it is free from emptiness. It is also called the "No-View" (Wujian) school, for it is free from views. It is also called the "No-Obstruction" (Wuzhang) school, for it is free from obstructions. It is also called the "No-Barrier" (Wuqian) school, for it is free from barriers. It is also called the "No-Entrance" (Wurru) school, for it is free from entrances. It is also called the "No-Exit" (Wuchu) school, for it is free from exits. It is also called the "No-Path" (Wudao) school, for it is free from paths. It is also called the "No-Practice" (Wuxing) school, for it is free from practice. It is also called the "No-Realization" (Wuzheng) school, for it is free from realization. It is also called the "No-Enlightenment" (Wujue) school, for it is free from enlightenment. It is also called the "No-Buddha" (Wofojia) school, for it is free from the Buddha. It is also called the "No-Dharma" (Wofajia) school, for it is free from the Dharma. It is also called the "No-Sangha" (Wosengjia) school, for it is free from the Sangha. It is also called the "No-World" (Woshijian) school, for it is free from the world. It is also called the "No-Heaven" (Wutian) school, for it is free from heaven. It is also called the "No-Hell" (Wudiyu) school, for it is free from hell. It is also called the "No-Desire" (Wuyu) school, for it is free from desire. It is also called the "No-Anger" (Wunchen) school, for it is free from anger. It is also called the "No-Stupidity" (Wuchi) school, for it is free from stupidity. It is also called the "No-Greed" (Wu tan) school, for it is free from greed. It is also called the "No-Hatred" (Wu fen) school, for it is free from hatred. It is also called the "No-Delusion" (Wu wang) school, for it is free from delusion. It is also called the "No-Attachment" (Wu zhu) school, for it is free from attachment. It is also called the "No-Repulsion" (Wu fan) school, for it is free from repulsion. It is also called the "No-Love" (Wu ai) school, for it is free from love. It is also called the "No-Hate" (Wu ji) school, for it is free from hate. It is also called the "No-Respect" (Wu jing) school, for it is free from respect. It is also called the "No-Disrespect" (Wu bujing) school, for it is free from disrespect. It is also called the "No-Virtue" (Wu de) school, for it is free from virtue. It is also called the "No-Evil" (Wu xie) school, for it is free from evil. It is also called the "No-Good" (Wu shan) school, for it is free from good. It is also called the "No-Bad" (Wu e) school, for it is free from bad. It is also called the "No-Cause" (Wu yin) school, for it is free from causes. It is also called the "No-Effect" (Wu guo) school, for it is free from effects. It is also called the "No-Condition" (Wu yuan) school, for it is free from conditions. It is also called the "No-Dependence" (Wu yi) school, for it is free from dependence. It is also called the "No-Reliance" (Wu zhi) school, for it is free from reliance. It is also called the "No-Seeking" (Wu qiu) school, for it is
Jing said, "How can one ever produce a mirror by polishing a brick? The Master said, "Since polishing a brick cannot produce a mirror, how can sitting in meditation produce a Buddha?
Jing said, "What then is the way? The Master said, "It is like a cow pulling a cart; if the cart does not move,"
"Striking the cart is [striking it]; striking the ox is [striking it]. There is no counterpart. The Master spoke again:

"Do you study sitting meditation, or do you study sitting as a Buddha? If you study sitting meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If you study sitting as a Buddha, the Buddha has no fixed form.
Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you sit as a Buddha, that is to kill the Buddha. If you cling to the form of sitting, you have not attained realization."

As for its principle: upon hearing the instruction but once, it was like drinking *amṛta* (clarified butter). He prostrated and asked, "How should I apply my mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?
The Master said, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like sowing seeds below; I shall now explain the essentials of the Dharma."
"It is like the rain from heaven; because the conditions have converged, you shall see the Way. He asked again, "The Way has no form or characteristics; how can it be seen?
The Master said, "The Dharma-eye of the mind-ground can see the Way; so too is it with the signless samādhi."
The first asked, "Is there formation and destruction? The Master said, "If one perceives the Way through formation and destruction, gathering and dispersing, that is not seeing the Way.
Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; when meeting with moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless; what is destroyed, and what is formed?
At once he was enlightened, and his mind became transcendent. He served [the Master] for ten years, and his progress increased daily."
Profound and mysterious. His入室 disciples (入室弟子) numbered six in total. The Master individually certified them, saying:
"You six have collectively realized my person; each of you has attained one aspect. One has attained my eyebrows—he excels in dignified demeanor. One has attained my eyes."
One who is skilled in observing receives my ears; one who is skilled in listening to principles receives my nose; one who is skilled in knowing the vital breaths receives my tongue;
one who is skilled in discourse receives my mind; and one who is skilled in the past and present says: "All phenomena arise from the mind.
The mind has no place of arising, and phenomena have no place of abiding. If one penetrates the ground of the mind, all actions will be unimpeded. This is not...
Encountering those of superior faculties, one must be cautious in speech. On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the third year of the Tiānbǎo era, he entered parinirvāṇa at Mount Héng.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Dàhuì, and his stupa was named Zuìshènglún (The Most Victorious Wheel).
The Second Generation under the Great Mirror (Dajian Huineng):
Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi, the Dharma Heir of Nanyue Huairang.
He was the son of the Ma family from Zhangfang County in Hanzhou; he originally resided at Luohan Monastery in his native district.

His family name was Jia. His appearance was extraordinary: he walked like an ox and gazed like a tiger; his tongue could extend past his nose, and beneath each of his feet were the marks of two wheels.
In his youth, he received the tonsure under Venerable Tang of Zizhou and received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Yuzhou.

During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) on Mount Heng. There he met Venerable Rang, with whom six others studied together; among them, the Master alone attained the secret [teachings].
He received the Mind Seal (Citta-mudrā). Beginning at Mount Foji (Buddha-Trace) in Jianyang, he moved to Linchuan, and subsequently to Gonggong Mountain in Nankang.
During the Dali era, he registered his name at Kaiyuan Temple in Zhongling. At that time, Lu Sigong, the Regional Commander, heard of his reputation and admired him;
he personally received the core teachings from him. Consequently, scholars from the four quarters gathered under his seat like clouds. One day, he addressed the assembly:
He said: "All of you, believe that each of your own minds is the Buddha; this mind is itself the Buddha-mind.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle’s single mind, so as to cause you all to attain awakening.
Furthermore, he cited the texts of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to seal the ground of the minds of sentient beings, fearing that you might fall into delusion and fail to recognize it yourselves."

Faith. This Dharma of the one mind exists within each and every person. Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its core principle and the gateless as its Dharma-gate.
Now, those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek. Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha;
outside the Buddha there is no separate mind. Do not grasp at good, do not abandon evil; rely neither upon the two extremes of purity nor impurity. Realize the nature of sin...
Emptiness cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment, for it lacks intrinsic nature. Therefore, the triple world is mind-only.

The myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by this single Dharma. Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind; the mind does not exist as a self-sufficient entity, but exists only in dependence upon form.
You need only speak according to the occasion; whether in terms of phenomena or principle, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
It is the same with the fruit of the path to Bodhi: that which arises within the mind is immediately termed "form. Because one knows that form is empty, arising is non-arising.
If you understand this meaning, you may then dress and eat at the appropriate times, nourishing the holy embryo and passing through time spontaneously. Furthermore...
"What matters? You have received my instruction; listen to this verse of mine: 'The mind-ground is explained according to the occasion; Bodhi is likewise merely peace.
When phenomena and principle are both unimpeded, that which arises is immediately non-arising. A monk asked, "Why did the Master say 'this very mind is Buddha'?
The Master said, "To stop the crying of a small child. The monk asked, "What is it like when the crying has stopped? The Master said, "'Neither mind nor Buddha.'"
The Buddha said, "Setting aside these two kinds of people, how would you instruct them? The Master said, "I would tell them it is not a thing.
[The Buddha] asked, "If one of those people in the middle were to come, what then? The Master said, "First, have him realize the Great Way.
[Mañjuśrī] asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? The Master said, "Right now, what is this meaning? Pang Jushi asked, "Unobscured..."
"The original person—please, Master, cast your eyes high. The Master looked straight down. The layman said, "This is a single-stringed lute;
only you, Master, can play it wondrously. The Master looked straight up. The layman bowed. The Master returned to his quarters, and the layman followed after him, saying:
Just now, you were trying to be clever and ended up being clumsy. He asked again, "Water has no sinews or bones, yet it can support a ten-thousand-hu vessel;
what is the principle behind this? The Master said, "In this place there is neither water nor boat; why speak of sinews and bones?
One night, while Xitang, Baizhang, and Nanquan were attending him as they gazed at the moon, the Master asked, "At this very moment, how is it? Xitang said, "Right."
Baizhang said, "It is precisely for this that one should practice cultivation. Baizhang shook his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "The Sutras have entered the Canon;
Chan has returned to the sea. Only Puyuan alone transcends the mundane world. Baizhang asked, "What is the essential purport of the Buddha-dharma?"

The Master said, "This is precisely where you let go of body and life. The Master asked Baizhang, "With what Dharma do you instruct people? Baizhang held up his whisk. The Master said, "Is it only this, or is there something else? Baizhang threw down the whisk. A monk asked: [the Master said: "This is precisely where you let go of body and life. The Master asked Baizhang, "With what Dharma do you instruct people? Baizhang held up his whisk. The Master said, "Is it only this, or is there something else? Baizhang threw down the whisk. "How can one be in accord with the Way? The Master said, "I was already not in accord with the Way long ago. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Westward Journey?
The Master struck him and said, "If I had not struck you, the practitioners of all quarters would have laughed at me.
A junior disciple, Danyuan, returned from his travels and drew a circle before the Master. He then prostrated himself upon it and stood up. The Master said, "Do you wish to become a Buddha?"
“No. [The student] said, “I do not understand how to rub one’s eyes. The Master said, “I am not as good as you. The junior monk did not reply.
Deng Yinfeng took his leave of the Master. The Master asked, “Where are you going? He replied, “To Shitou. The Master said, “The path at Shitou is slippery.
He replied, “Carrying my staff and wood with me, I shall perform my play upon meeting the stage,” and he departed. As soon as he arrived at Shitou, he circumambulated the meditation seat once.
As he shook his mendicant’s staff once, he asked, "What is the essential principle? Shitou replied, "Heaven! Heaven! Feng remained silent.
He returned and reported this to the Master. The Master said, "Go back and ask him again; when he gives an answer, you should simply let out two sighs.
Feng went back and asked as before, whereupon Shitou let out two sighs. Feng again remained silent. He returned and reported this to the Master. The Master—
[The Master] said, "I told you before that the path at Shitou is slippery.

A monk drew four lines before the Master—the top line long and the bottom three lines short—and said, "Do not say that one line is long and three lines are short. Apart from these four words, I ask the Master to answer.
The Master then drew a line on the ground and said, "Do not speak of long or short; my answer to you is finished. There was [a monk present].
A lecturer-monk came and asked, "I do not know for certain what dharma the Chan school transmits and maintains. The Master instead asked, "What dharma do you, O Lecturer, transmit and maintain?
The monk replied, "I am fortunate enough to have lectured upon more than twenty treatises and scriptures. The Master said, "Are you not a 'lion cub'? The monk replied, "I dare not say so.
The Master made a sound like a sigh (*xū xū*). The monk said, "This is the Dharma. The Master asked, "What is it?"
"What dharma is this? The Master said, "The dharma of the lion emerging from its cave. The Master remained silent. The Master said, "This too is a dharma.
The Master asked, "What dharma is that? The Master said, "The dharma of the lion being in its cave. The Master said, "Neither emerging nor entering—what dharma is that?
The Master had no reply. He then took his leave and went out the door. The Master called out, "Dharma Master! The Master turned his head. The Master said, "It is this."
"What is it? The Master remained silent. The teacher said, "This dull-witted monk. The Provincial Inspector of Hongzhou asked, "Is it right to eat meat and drink wine, or is it not?
The Master replied, "If you eat, it is the inspector’s salary; if you do not eat, it is the inspector’s merit.
The Master had one hundred and thirty-nine入室 disciples (入室弟子), each of whom became a patriarch in their own region and spread [the teachings].
His transformations were inexhaustible. In the first month of the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, the Master ascended Mount Shimen in Jianchang.
While walking in meditation amidst the forest, he saw that the caves and ravines were level and said to his attendant, "This decaying body of mine shall return to this place next month.
Having finished speaking, he turned back. Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness. The head of the monastery asked, "Master, how have you been feeling lately?"
The Master asked, "How is it? The Master replied, "Sun-Face Buddha, Moon-Face Buddha. On the first day of the second month, he bathed, sat in the lotus posture, and entered nirvana.
During the Yuanhe era, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Daji, and his stupa was named Dazhuangyan (Great Adornment).
Chan Master Jinping of Xiyin was a dharma successor of Heze Shenhui and a native of the Wu clan of Jingzhao. He left the household life at Mingfu Monastery on Mount Yong’an.

His demeanor was upright and elegant; he had thoroughly investigated all the Mahayana sutras and great treatises. His exegesis and commentaries were so refined that they brought joy to those who heard them.
He did not contemplate meditative visualization. While in Luoyang, he encountered Master Heze Shenhui and attained full awakening.
He remarked, "How profound it is! For one who does not know from within, how difficult is that which is known! Later, he went to Tangzhou and resided at Mount Xiyin.
The Regional Inspector Zheng Wenjian invited him into the city to propagate the fundamental tenets of his school. He passed away at the age of eighty-one in the fourteenth year of the Dali era.

Master Liang of Xishan was a native of Shu. He had lectured extensively on the sūtras and śāstras. Upon visiting Mazu, Mazu asked him, "I have heard it said that you, Master, lecture extensively on the sūtras and śāstras;
is this true? The Master replied, "I dare not say so. Mazu asked, "With what do you lecture? The Master replied, "I lecture with my mind.
Mazu said, "The mind is like a skilled performer, and the intellect is like the conductor. How could such things ever understand how to lecture?"
The Master raised his voice and said, "If you cannot lecture on the mind, can you lecture on empty space? The Patriarch replied, "In fact, it is empty space that can lecture.
The Master, dissatisfied, was about to leave when he descended the steps; the Patriarch called out, "Seat-Master! The Master turned his head, and the Patriarch asked, "What is this?
At these words, the Master attained a sudden and great awakening and prostrated himself. The Patriarch said, "This dull-witted monk! Prostrate yourself!"
“Why do you bow? The Master said, “I thought that no one could equal me in the sutras and treatises I have studied.

Today, having been questioned by the Great Master, all the achievements of my life have been washed away at once like melting ice. He then paid his respects and withdrew, subsequently hiding in the Western Mountains of Hongzhou, where no further news of him was heard.

Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng on Mount Zhongnan, the dharma heir of Yuan of Suizhou, was a native of the He family from Xichong, Guozhou. His family was originally of great wealth and prominence.

At the age of five, he mastered the Confucian classics; at the age of twenty, he explored the Buddhist scriptures. In the second year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, while preparing to take the imperial examinations, he happened upon the Dharma seat of Master Yuan.
Finding a joyful resonance with him, he subsequently requested ordination and received full precepts that same year.

One day, following the assembly of monks to a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a local official, he was seated in a lower position. As he received the scriptures in order, he obtained the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Upon reaching the chapter on Perfect Enlightenment (*Yuanjue*), he attained profound realization.

The work consists of twelve chapters. Before he had even finished unrolling the scroll, he was moved to tears by his realization. Upon returning, he related the essence of what he had realized to Yuan.
Yuan patted him on the back and said, "You shall greatly propagate the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden; this is the ear-whispered transmission from all the Buddhas to you. Go forth!"
"One must not remain stagnant in a single corner. The Master wept as he accepted this command, paid his respects, and departed.

He then went to visit Chan Master Zhong of Jingnan. Zhong said, "This is a man of the Dharma transmission; he shall propagate the teachings in the imperial capital. He subsequently met Chan Master Zhao of Luoyang.
Zhao said, "This is a Bodhisattva; who could possibly recognize him? He soon arrived at Xianghan, where a sick monk entrusted him with...

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra* was composed by the Great Master Chengguan of the Capital. Although the Master had never previously studied or practiced [this text], he lectured upon it after reading it only once.
Delighted by what he had encountered, he said: "Regarding the commentaries and works produced by previous masters, few have exhausted its ultimate meaning;

none compare to this śāstra, whose fountain of words flows with such clarity and whose profound mysteries are so brilliantly illuminated. In meditation, I have met the Southern School; in the teachings, I have encountered the Perfect Enlightenment. One...

Upon finishing these words, my mind and spirit were opened and enlightened. Within this single scroll, the sky of meaning shone brightly. Now, having fortunately reached the end of the brush, I have exhausted the depths of my heart.
When the lectures concluded, I wished to meet the author of the commentary; it was at that time that his disciple, Taigong, severed his arm as an act of gratitude.

The Master first sent a letter to the author of the commentary to recount their teacher-disciple relationship from afar, exchanging greetings of mutual joy and consolation. He then sought out Taigong.
Upon his recovery, he accompanied [Hui]guan to the capital, where he observed the etiquette of a disciple.

Guan said, "As for one who can follow me on a journey through the Vairocana Flower Treasury (Vairocanābhisambodhi-kṣetra), it must be you. The Master entered Guan’s chamber and, day by day, renewed his virtue;

thus, the affliction of clinging to the means [of expression] as the truth or fixating on the image was forever eliminated. He traveled north to Mount Qingliang and resided four times at Caotang Monastery in Huxian. Not long after...
He entered the Guifeng Hermitage in Zhongnan Mountain several times again. During the Dazhong era, he was summoned to the imperial court and granted purple robes.

The Emperor repeatedly inquired about the essentials of the Dharma, and court officials looked up to him with devotion; however, it was only the Chancellor, Lord Pei Xu, who penetrated deeply into the inner sanctum of his teachings and received instruction as an external protector.

Because practitioners of Chan and the doctrinal schools were mutually disparaging one another, the Master subsequently composed the *Chan Yuan Zhi Quan* (Records of the Various Explanations of the Source of Chan) to serve as a compendium.

The various accounts compiled by different masters, which explain the fundamental principles of the Chan gate through words, phrases, and verses, have been gathered into a single canon to be bequeathed to future generations.
Its general preface states briefly: "Chan" is a term from India; in its full form, it is *dhyāna*.

This is translated here as "contemplative cultivation" (*sīwéi xiū*) or "meditative concentration" (*jìnglù*); these are all general designations for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). As for its source, it is all..."
The fundamental awakening of the true nature of sentient beings is also called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and also called the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).

Awakening to it is called wisdom (*prajñā*); cultivating it is called concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration and wisdom together are termed Chan (*dhyāna*). This nature is the original source of Chan; therefore, it is called the "Source of Chan" (*chanyuan*).
It is also called *dhyāna*. Regarding principle and practice: this original source is the principle of Chan; forgetting emotions and harmonizing with it is the practice of Chan.

Therefore, it is said that there are both principle (*li*) and practice (*xing*). However, among the various works collected here, most discuss the principle of Chan while saying little about the practice of Chan;
thus, I have provisionally titled this "The Source of Chan" (*Chan-yuan*). Nowadays, there are those who identify true nature alone as "Chan";

this shows they do not comprehend the intent of principle and practice, nor do they distinguish between the terminology of China and India. Nevertheless, it is not the case that something exists apart from true nature.

As for the essence of *dhyāna*: when sentient beings are deluded regarding the Truth and unite with the sensory dust, it is called "distraction. When they turn their backs on the dust and unite with the Truth, it is then called "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*).
If one discusses the fundamental nature directly, it is neither true nor false; there is no turning away and no uniting, no concentration and no distraction. Who then would speak of "dhyāna"?
Furthermore, this True Nature is not only the source of the gate of *dhyāna*, but is also the source of all phenomena.
Therefore, it is called the *dharmatā*. It is also the source of sentient beings' delusion and awakening; therefore, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and the *ālayavijñāna*.

It is also the source of the myriad virtues of all Buddhas; therefore, it is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). It is also the source of the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is called the "ground of the mind.
The myriad practices do not transcend the six *pāramitās*, and meditation (*dhyāna*) is merely one among these six. When...
How could the fifth [patriarch] possibly have intended for the ultimate true nature itself to be designated as a single practice of dhyāna?
Changqing An was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Dasui Fazhen of Yizhou; he was born into the Wang family of Zizhou and attained awakening at a young age, thereafter resolving to seek [the truth].
The Master left home at Huiyi Temple. After receiving full ordination, he traveled south. Initially, he visited Yaoshan, Daowu, Yunyan, and Dongshan;
subsequently, he went beyond the ridges to the assembly of Dayu Baizhang, where he remained for several years. His food did not reach satiety, and he sought no warmth while lying down.
He refined his practice through pure austerity, and his conduct was beyond the common. Master Mian of Shishuang held him in high esteem.
One day, Mian asked him, "Since you have been here with this old monk, you have never asked a single turning word. The Master replied, "Where would you have me begin?"
Miaoyan said, "Why do you not say, 'What is the Buddha? The Master then made a gesture with his hand to cover Miaoyan’s mouth.
Miaoyan sighed and said, "You have truly attained the marrow. From then on, his fame spread throughout the four seas.

Later, he returned to Shu and stayed at Longhuai Temple on Mount Pengkou in Tianpeng, where he brewed tea by the roadside and offered it freely for three years. While wandering toward the rear mountains, he saw one...
The ancient monastery was named Dasui. There, clusters of peaks rose in majestic beauty and the mountain streams were clear and cool.
In its midst stood a tree over forty feet in circumference with a single opening facing south; its interior was hollow and unobstructed, a natural hermitage formed without the use of axes or tools.

The Master called it "Wooden Chan" and took up residence there. For more than ten years he did not venture beyond the mountains, yet his reputation spread abroad, reaching the seekers of the profound Way from all quarters.

From a thousand li away, they rushed toward his reputation like the wind. The Ruler of Shu held him in high esteem and repeatedly dispatched envoys to summon him; each time, the Master declined on the grounds of old age and illness.
He was appointed as the Great Master Shenzhao. Entering the hall, he said: "This nature is originally pure and replete with myriad virtues.

It is only due to the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise. Therefore, the sages awaken to it and, through exclusively pure application, achieve the Way of Enlightenment. As for ordinary people..."
They are deluded; they are unilaterally immersed in the cycle of saṃsāra through defiled activity. Yet their essence is non-dual. Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā says:
"There is no duality, no division, no distinction, and no interruption. A monk asked, "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder:
does this [essence] perish or not? The Master said, "It perishes. The monk said, "If that is so, then it follows along with it. The Master said, "It follows along with it."

He departed. The monk was unwilling to go. Later, he arrived at Touzi and recounted the previous conversation. Touzi then prepared incense and prostrated from afar, saying, "An ancient Buddha has appeared in Western Sichuan.
He said to the monk, "Return quickly and repent. When the monk returned to Daguī, the Master had already passed away.
The monk went back to Touzi again, but Touzi had also passed away. [The monk] asked, "What is the mark of a great man? The Master replied, "The belly."
The Master did not post a notice. He asked a monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to live in a hut on West Mountain.
The Master said, "If I call for you from the top of East Mountain, will you come immediately? The monk said, "No. The Master said, "Then you have not yet attained the ability to dwell in a hut.

He asked, "When the time of birth and death arrives, what then? The Master said, "When you meet tea, drink the tea; when you meet rice, eat the rice. The monk asked, "Who receives [the karmic retribution]?"
He made an offering. The Master said, "Close your alms bowl. Beside the hut was a tortoise. The monk asked, "All sentient beings have skin wrapping their bones;
why does this sentient being have bones wrapping its skin? The Master picked up his straw sandals and covered them over the tortoise's back.
The monk was speechless. The monk asked, "What is the essential dharma of all Buddhas? The Master raised his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand."
The Master said, "A fly-whisk. [The student] asked, "What is the student's own self? The Master said, "It is my own self.
[The student] said, "Why is it, then, that it is the Master's own self? The Master said, "It is your own self. [The student] asked, "What is the singular reality of Daisui?
The Master said, "East, west, south, and north. [The student] asked, "The Buddha-dharma pervades all places; what is the teaching..."
The student asked, "Where does one find a place to stand? The Master said, "In the great ocean, the fish leap; in the vast sky, the birds fly.
The student asked, "When father and son are most intimate, yet part ways at a fork in the road—what then? The Master said, "Precisely because there are father and son.
The student asked, "What is the seamless stupa? The Master said, "Five feet high. The student said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "A solid brick."
A monk asked, "After you, Master, have passed away for a hundred years, to whom shall the Dharma be entrusted? The Master said, "The pillar and the brazier. The monk asked, "Will they receive it?
The Master said, "The brazier and the pillar. He then questioned another monk, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to Mount Emei to pay homage to Samantabhadra.
The Master raised his whisk and said, "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are both right here. The monk drew a circle in the air and threw it behind him.
After they had paid their respects, the Master called for his attendant to bring a bowl of tea for one of the monks.

During the subsequent assembly, the Master made a gesture with his mouth as if suffering from a wind ailment and said, "Is there anyone who can cure my mouth? The assembly of monks vied with one another to bring medicinal herbs until they arrived in abundance.
When the laypeople heard of this, many also sent him medicine, but the Master accepted none of it.

After seven days, the Master himself pinched his own mouth to straighten it, saying, "For all this time, these two pieces of skin have been drumming; even until now, no one has been able to heal them.
He then sat upright and passed away.
Zhaozhou Shen’s Dharma heir, Master Ximù of Yizhou, was ascending the hall when a layman raised his hand and said, "The Master is nothing but a donkey.
The Master replied, "I am being ridden by you. The layman was speechless. Three days later, he returned and said, "I..."
Three days prior, a thief entered the Master’s quarters. The Master took up his staff and drove him out. On another occasion, the Master suddenly called to his attendant;
when the attendant responded, the Master said, "It is late at night and all is quiet; let us deliberate with him."

Longtan Xian was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Deshan Xuanjian of Dingzhou. He was the son of the Zhou family of Jianzhou. At the age of twenty, he left home and received full ordination according to his age.

He studied the Vinaya-piṭaka with great diligence and thoroughly mastered the essential meanings of the various sūtras on the nature and characteristics of phenomena. He frequently lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
At that time, he was called Zhou Jin’gang. He suddenly said to his fellow students, “A single hair swallows the ocean, yet the nature of the ocean suffers no loss;
a tiny speck is cast against a blade’s edge, yet the sharpness of the blade remains unmoved. Whether one is a learner (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), only I know this.

Later, hearing that the Zen seats in the South were flourishing, the Master’s spirit was unsettled, and he said, “A renunciant may study the majestic deportment of the Buddha for a thousand kalpas, and for ten thousand kalpas...”
"One cannot achieve Buddhahood by studying the minute details of Buddhist practice," said the son of a Mara from the South, daring to claim, "One directly points to the human mind;
seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha. "I shall tear open his den and exterminate his kind to repay the Buddha's grace! he declared.
He then took up the *Qinglong shuchao* (Blue Dragon Commentary) and departed from Shu. On the road to Liyang, he saw an old woman selling cakes and stopped to rest his shoulder while buying some.
[The Master] was offered some refreshments. The old woman pointed to his carrying pole and asked, "What text is this? The Master replied, "The *Qinglong Shuchao* (Commentary on the *Diamond Sūtra*).
The woman asked, "Which sūtra do you lecture upon? The Master said, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The woman said, "I have a question for you;
if you can answer it, I will provide you with refreshments. If you cannot answer it, you must go elsewhere. [She continued,] "The *Diamond Sūtra* says: 'The past mind is ungraspable...'"
"It is attained. Yet the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended. I do not know which mind the Elder intends to point out. The Master remained silent.
He then went to Longtan and, upon reaching the Dharma Hall, said: "I have long heard of Longtan; now that I have arrived..."
The pond was no longer visible, nor did the dragon appear. The Pond Master extended his body and said, "You have personally arrived at the Dragon Pond.

The Master remained speechless and subsequently took up residence there. One evening, while standing in attendance, the Pond Master said, "It is deep in the night; why do you not leave? The Master replied, "I take my leave," and stepped out.
He then returned and said, "It is dark outside. The Pond Master lit a paper candle and held it out to the Master. As the Master reached out to receive it, the Pond Master [snuffed it out].
[The candle] was blown out. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment and immediately prostrated himself. Longtan asked, "What have you seen?
The Master replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the world.

On the following day, Longtan ascended the seat and said to the assembly, "Among you there is a fellow with teeth like sword-trees and a mouth like a blood-basin; he would strike [me] with a single blow."
Without looking back, he said, "In time, atop a solitary peak, I shall establish my Way.

The Master then took his commentaries and sub-commentaries, piled them before the Dharma Hall, and holding up a torch, he said: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void;
to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss. He then burned them. Thereupon, he paid his respects and took his leave, proceeding directly to Mount Mí.
Carrying his sitting mat over his shoulder, he ascended the Dharma Hall, walking from west to east and from east to west. Looking toward the abbot’s quarters, he asked, "Is there anyone here?
Is there anyone here? The Master sat there without so much as a glance. The monk said, "No one, no one," and departed.

Reaching the entrance, he remarked, "Even so, this cannot be treated with such casualness. He then prepared his full ceremonial regalia and re-entered to have an audience. As soon as he stepped across the threshold—
Dongmen picked up his sitting mat and said, "Venerable Master. As Shanshan reached for his whisk, the Master gave a shout and swept his sleeves out of the hall.
That evening, Guishan asked the Head Seat, "Is the newcomer still here?

The Head Seat replied, "At that moment, he turned his back on the Dharma Hall and went out wearing his straw sandals. Guishan said, "This man will, in the future, settle himself atop a solitary peak."
"Grass Hut! To revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs—this is where he belongs! The Master resided at Liyang for thirty years.

During the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang dynasty, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he took refuge in a stone chamber on Mount Dufu. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Xue Tingwang, the Governor of Wuling, [invited him].
He restored the hermitage at Chongde Mountain, renaming it Gudde Chan-yuan (Ancient Virtue Chan Monastery).

Intending to seek out a master of eminent character to serve as its abbot, he heard of the Master’s spiritual conduct and repeatedly invited him to descend from the mountain. However, Yingtang devised a deceptive scheme, sending an official with tea and salt to falsely accuse him.

Regarding the violation of prohibitive laws: [The Master] took his teacher to the prefecture. After paying his respects and making earnest requests, he settled there and extensively propagated the style of his school.
He ascended the hall and said: "If you have no affairs within yourself, do not seek falsely. Even if you were to obtain something through false seeking, it would still not be attainment.
You need only be without affairs in the mind and without mind regarding affairs; then you will be spirit-like in emptiness and wondrous in vacuity. If one speaks even as much as a hair-tip..."
To discuss the beginning and end of these matters is entirely to deceive oneself. Why? Because a thought as small as a hair’s breadth becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms;
a fleeting emotion gives rise to shackles that bind one for ten thousand kalpas. Holy names and mundane titles are all empty sounds;
sublime features and inferior forms are all illusory colors. If you seek them, will you not be burdened? And when you grow weary of them, they again become a great affliction. In the end—
"It is useless. He gave a small-scale discourse (*xiaocan*) to the assembly, saying: "Tonight I shall not answer questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff.
At that time, a monk came forward and bowed; the Master struck him immediately. The monk said, "I have not even asked a question; for what reason does the Master strike me?
The Master asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "A man from Silla. The Master said, "Before you have even stepped onto the boat..."
"Oar! You deserve thirty blows. A monk visited; the Master asked the rector, "How many new arrivals are there today?
He replied, "Eight. The Master said, "Call them here and pin them down all at once. Longya asked, "What if a student, wielding the Mohe Mohe sword, intends to take the Master's head?
The Master extended his neck forward and said, "I'll eat you! Longya said, "The head has fallen! The Master scolded him.
He laughed heartily. Later, Baizhang went to Dongshan and brought up the previous story. Dongshan asked, "What did Deshan say? Baizhang replied, "Deshan was speechless.
Dongshan said, "Do not say he was speechless. Bring me the head that Deshan dropped so that I may examine it for you, old monk.
Only then did Baizhang realize his error, whereupon he prostrated himself in repentance and thanks. A monk reported this to the Master (Linji), who said, "The old man Dongshan..."
One who recognizes good and evil—how much time has passed since that person died? What use would there be in saving them? A monk asked, "What is Bodhi?
The Master struck him and said, "Get out! Do not defecate here. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha?
The Master said, "The Buddha is an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven (India). Xuefeng asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the school, does a student still have a share in it?"
[Yaoshan] said, "There is none. The Master struck him with a staff and asked, "What do you say? [Yaoshan] said, "I do not understand. The next day, he requested further instruction.
The Master said, "In my school, there are no words or phrases; truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Thereupon, Yaofeng attained realization.
When Yantou heard of this, he said, "The old man Deshan has a backbone as hard as iron that cannot be bent. Nevertheless..."
Within the gate of proclaiming the teaching, it is still a matter of some slight distinction. [Yunmen] said: "Whether you can speak it or not, you shall receive thirty blows.
When Linji heard this, he said to Luopo: "Go and ask him why, even if one can speak it, one receives thirty blows.
Wait for him to strike you; as he strikes, catch his staff and give it a shove. Watch what he does then. Luopo—
He questioned him exactly as instructed. The Master struck him. Xupō caught the staff and gave it a shove; the Master then returned to his quarters.
Upon returning, Xupō recounted this to Linji. Linji said, "I have always suspected this fellow. Nevertheless, do you recognize Deshan? As Xupō hesitated, Linji struck him.
He then ascended the hall and said: "To question is to err; not to question is likewise deviant. There is...
The monk came forward to prostrate, and the Master struck him. The monk said, "I have only just prostrated; why did you strike me?
The Master replied, "Wait until you open your mouth—what would that be worth? The Master ordered his attendant to summon Yixun.
When Xun came up, the Master said, "I myself summoned Yixun; why have you come here? Xun was speechless. He ascended the hall and said, "My ancestors..."
The standpoint of views is not so. Here there is neither patriarch nor Buddha. Bodhidharma is an old hirsute barbarian; Śākyamuni is a dried-up dung-club.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are dung-carriers; Equal Enlightenment and Wondrous Enlightenment are ordinary people with broken attachments.
Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are hitching posts for donkeys; the twelve divisions of the teachings are registers of ghosts and spirits; the scriptures are a rag for wiping sores.

A "Worm-Eaten Paper": Those at the stages of the four fruits, the three levels of worthiness, the initial mind of the ten stages, and those guarding ancient tombs—these are ghosts who cannot even save themselves.
When a monk came to visit him, he stepped forward and assumed the stance for sumo wrestling.

The Master said, "To be so impolite deserves a blow from this mountain monk’s hand. The monk brushed his sleeves and departed. The Master said, "Even though you act thus, you have only attained half. The monk...
He turned around and shouted. The Master struck him, saying, "I must strike you before it is right.
The monk said, "There are people with clear eyes everywhere. The Master said, "Naturally possessed of eyes. The monk opened his eyes wide and said, "A cat! and then departed.

The Master remarked, "The Yellow River clears itself only once every three thousand years. When the Master saw a monk approaching, he closed the door. The monk knocked on the door; the Master said, "Ah!"

"Who is it? he asked. "It is the Lion’s Cub," they replied. The Master then opened the door. When the monk prostrated, the Master mounted the monk's back and said, "Where have you been coming from, you beast?
Xuefeng asked, "What was the meaning behind Nanquan’s killing of the cat? The Master then drove him away with a blow.
He called out to him again, saying, "Do you understand? Feng said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Even with such a grandmotherly heart of mine, you still do not understand.
A monk asked, "How far apart are the ordinary person and the sage? The Master gave a shout. The Master was ill.
A monk asked, "Is there anyone who does not fall ill? The Master said, "There is. The monk asked, "Who is this one who does not fall ill? The Master said, "A-ya, a-ya. The Master passed away.

He addressed the assembly again, saying: "To grasp at emptiness and pursue echoes is but to weary your mind and spirit. When one awakens from a dream, one realizes it was not real; in the end, what event has actually occurred?

Having finished speaking, he sat peacefully and passed away. This was the third day of the twelfth month in the sixth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Jiexing (Realizing Nature).
