Yuan [Wude] studied under Master Shitou. He then went to visit Master Sheng at Yunfeng, who instructed him to contemplate the koan:
"The state before one's parents were born. For a long time, he made no progress. One day, Master Sheng gave him this instruction: "Ignorance is the father; craving is the mother.

You must possess the means to kill the father and kill the mother before you can succeed. Suddenly, Yuan felt as though his nostrils had been struck out. Later, when he entered the room for formal interview, Master Sheng asked: "Like..."
"This is the phrase prior to birth. The Master said, "The snow peaks are clear and cold. He asked, "What is the phrase after birth?
The Master said, "The plum blossoms exude fragrance. Sheng then offered a verse, saying: "Once again I see the heart of Heaven; the spring days grow long."
In the first month of winter, all things naturally emit their fragrance. Were it not for the clear sky over the snowy peaks so high and cold, how could the plum blossoms spray forth their scent?
At Yunfeng, holding the whisk, he gave a small discourse (*xiaocan*). He raised the following case: A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine?
Feng said, "Staring with wide-open eyes, one cannot see the bottom. The monk asked, "How about those who drink from it? Feng said, "It does not enter through the mouth. Later, the monk...
He brought this up to Zhaozhou. Zhaozhou said, "One cannot enter through the nostrils. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What of the cold spring in the ancient ravine?
Zhaozhou said, "Bitter. The monk asked, "And those who drink from it? Zhaozhou said, "Dead. When Xuefeng heard of this, he thereafter ceased answering questions.
The Master said, "If one examines Xuefeng’s nature with clarity, he understood how to swallow, but did not understand how to spit out."
Vomit! Zhaozhou understands vomiting but does not understand swallowing; thus, they cannot avoid each holding to a single view. Liang, however, is not like this. Suppose someone were to ask:
"What is it like when there is a cold spring in an ancient ravine? One might say: "It can quench thirst. If asked, "How about those who drink from it? one must strictly avoid encouraging greed.
Now tell me: when Xuefeng did not answer the question, how was that? There is no room for contention; there is ample room for yielding. To the assembly:
the single word "the Way" is fundamentally beyond speech. It is like the flavor of salt in water, or the blue pigment in lacquer—certainly present, yet its form is not seen.
On the ground of ultimate reality, not even a speck of dust can be established. Before the feet have even moved—how good!
[This] together with thirty [cases]. One does not see Zhaozhou saying: "You need only investigate the principle while sitting for twenty or thirty years;
if you still do not understand, cut off this old monk’s head. To take up such a way of benefiting others is truly beyond reproach.
It is extremely difficult, extremely difficult for various masters to realize this matter within one, two, three, or four seven-day periods. Directly—

You must apply this daily within the four modes of conduct; on this very day each year, at this very hour every year, if you can achieve even a small degree of causal continuity, only then will you not have betrayed your vow to transcend the mundane world. (He stood for a long time.)
Chan Master Yuantong Weishi was a native of the Lu clan from Dangqu. At the age of seven, he paid his respects to the Great Master Wenzi and received the tonsure.

He received full ordination from Master Juewei on Mount Si'e. He studied under numerous venerable masters before later attending Master Shengke of Huayan. During a formal session in the meditation hall, he was tested on his realization;
the Master asked him: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. When one dies and is cremated—" [the Master pressed him further].
"What is mind-consciousness? The Master raised his fist. Xuefeng Yan said, "It has died and been cremated; who is it that raises the fist? The Master again raised his fist.
Yan said, "It is indeed not without being cast from cast-iron, but where do these two pieces of skin rest?
The Master then bowed. Yan struck him. The following day, Yan questioned him again with the same words. The Master again raised his fist. Yan said, "Yesterday..."
"The path of the sun has passed. The Master said, "Each time it is picked up, it is fresh again. Yǎn struck him once more and said, "I will not let you off.
One day, Yǎn asked the Master, "What is the final word of Deshan? The Master said, "It cannot be spoken."
Yan said, "When Miqi raised that intention, how was it? The Master said, "I could not drag him in. Yan said, "Why did you, the teacher, suffer from being recorded by your disciple?
The Master said, "It is like teaching a child until he knows how to curse his father. Yan said, "You are no mistake for Huayan Yuezhong."

Thus, they met like a needle and its eye. [The Master] bestowed upon him the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), saying: "A single fist, cast from raw iron: Not obtained from others, who could transmit it?
Such expedient means I share with you; From ancient times to the present, in China, there is no other path.

The Master’s verses were quite numerous; I have collected only a few excerpts here. Regarding the World-Honored One’s first birth, [he said]: (Verse: Pointing to heaven, pointing to earth, he raised the sword and spear. How good!
How many more high-ranking men do you still crave? Even if there are those who transcend the crowd and surpass all standards, the wicked will naturally grind down the wicked.
If one can turn things around, one is identical to the Tathāgata. (Verse: Not a single speck exists; there is nowhere for conceptual understanding to lodge.

It encompasses the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity); moving vertically and horizontally, it is unimpeded. The harm caused by five thousand scrolls of paper and ink is, in an instant, cast out from the realm of the Great Man.
The Realm. The woman enters meditative absorption. (Verse: An echo transmits through the empty valley; one listens in silence within the vacant hall.

If you believe it, it exists; if you strike it, it responds. Look at this man of great power—he does not rely on the orders of a general. Before Chaos was divided. (Verse: It cannot be burned, nor can it be soaked.
I do not yet know what kind of thing this is. It is the entire body of the Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is the nest of all sentient beings throughout the great earth.
The Cave. The Old Woman Burns the Hermitage. (Verse: This old woman was full of eccentricities. You clever monk, you have not yet escaped me!
To take fire and burn the hermitage is merely to nourish yourself in vain; it has brought down a debt that will last until the Year of the Donkey.

Chan Master Samyeon Seong was the son of the elder brother of Lord Bok of Chungju. He received the tonsure under Master Jogji and, relying on Master Hwaryam, completed his full ordination (*upasampadā*), receiving both the seal of transmission and the verse of entrustment.
In the spring of the Guihai year of the Kangxi era, he resided at Longyou Temple in Puyang for over ten years.
During that time, he once composed a verse on the woman emerging from meditative absorption: "The noble are as noble as gold; the lowly are as lowly as earth. The woman and Gao Shan..."
Dàn. Each is devoid of a presiding master. (Baizhang’s Wild Fox Verse): Not falling [into views] is originally an error; not being deluded is likewise a mistake.
Vast and boundless, the triple world has no coming or going—*pī-ti-cha*.
Chan Master Dachi Cheng was a native of Jiazhou. He received the tonsure at Yungui in Guiyang and received full ordination from Venerable Lianyue.

His spiritual resonance was in accord with Huayan. Later, he resided at Longchang and established the Zhengjue Chan Monastery. When Venerable Sheng was staying at Yunfeng in Luyang, the Master went there to pay his respects.
Yunfeng ordered him to hold the whisk for a small-scale sermon (xiaocan). Holding up his staff, he said: "This here is..."
The Dharma-seat of the Abbot has now fallen into the hands of Wucheng; he can do nothing but pound the empty to refine the real, verifying the correct and discerning the false.
It is simply a matter of everyone penetrating through to this point. (He strikes the ground once. "Do you understand? Wucheng’s own gear is that of a cliff-side cave-dweller;
tonight, pressed by necessity, there is no dharma to be spoken. I shall borrow two lines of entanglement to speak briefly.
[The Master] blocked the flow of the command. The World-Honored One said, "All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom, virtue, and marks.
Zhaozhou said, "A dog has no Buddha-nature. All you venerable elders, the World-Honored One says it exists, while Zhaozhou says it does not.

Are they the same or different? If you say they are the same, there is no such thing as a common characteristic among dharmas. If you say they are different, how could there be two distinct kinds? Do you understand?
In every land and at every dust mote, the mind is one and the same; alas, why do people not seek it for themselves?
If you can directly take this up and accept it, then to play in the tide, you must be a man who plays in the tide. (He lets out a shout.)
Chan Master Bilu was the son of the Zhang family from Qijiang in eastern Sichuan. In his middle years, he received the tonsure and full ordination under Master Huijue.
He followed Master Sheng of Huayan, where he severed his worldly attachments and received formal transmission. He purchased a boat to exit the gorges and resided at Chonglong Temple in Liyang.
Upon the conclusion of the retreat period, he ascended the hall and said: "The snow presses down on the tips of the pines; the frost is severe."
The old tree is cold; white clouds, with intent, constantly seal it shut. The secluded birds, without thought, pass through the pass.
The great road to Chang’an has an iron snake lying across the railing. Departing, departing, yet in the end difficult to depart; returning, returning, yet not easily returned.
[With the whisk, he draws a circle and slashes through it. "All you practitioners of Zen, examine this closely: the straw sandals are ultimately deceived by one's own feet."
When Layman Gao Wenying, the Provincial Inspector of Justice, first arrived at Huayan, during a tea break he asked the Master: "The ancients said:
'Suppose there is a person in a tree, whose hands do not grasp the branches and whose feet do not tread upon them, yet whose mouth bites a branch.

If you ask him about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, if he answers, he loses his life; if he does not answer, he fails the question. What does this mean? The Master pointed with his finger at his own tea bowl and finished.
He then pointed to the attendant Shi Zhong. Shi immediately took the bell and poured tea. Yanguan said, "Under a powerful general, there are no weak soldiers.
Shi asked, "What do you mean? Yanguan said, "The layman's attendant also understands the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West. Shi said, "So he does."
The Master used his hand as a tongue. Yanguan said, "What do you, Layman, use as a tongue? The Layman said, "I use my tongue as a tongue. Yanguan made a gesture of alarm. The Layman asked, "Why?
Yanguan said, "It is none other than you, Layman, who can let go of your body and relinquish your life.
The Layman said, "There is no body or life to be relinquished. Yanguan said, "This old monk’s eyes have suddenly gone blind. The Layman said, "Blind! Yanguan said, "Blind!"
"Blind! The scholar said, "In that case, does this not become mere frivolous discourse? Yǎn said, "When the benevolent man sees it, he calls it benevolence.
The scholar said, "I am still like one who uses it daily without knowing it," and then he performed a ritual of respect. Later, the scholar again traveled with the layman Tù to the hot springs.
While the scholar was about to bathe and eat some cakes, the butcher said, "Master, come and join us for the *tangbing* (noodle soup) feast.

The scholar said, "This place could well be called 'Washing-the-Child Spring. Yunyan said, "Has the Nine-Dragon yet spat forth its water? The scholar said, "I regret that it does not emerge from between my ribs.
Yunyan picked up his prayer beads and made a sound of pain. The butcher said, "This old fellow has a strange way of understanding things. Yunyan said, "Enter!"
The water seeks the person; the two intentions coincide. The nine dragons spit forth water to bathe the golden body. Do not say it does not emerge from between one’s ribs;
the pain pierces through like a mountain monk’s string of beads. Inscribed on the back of the scholar’s inkstone, with a verse and preface:
Mount Jin presses in from all four sides, crushing the *kāṣāya*. Meeting on a narrow path, the secret treasury is opened. Touching and striking—originally it was not [otherwise].
Trivial! To sail together on the same boat—how could this be a minor matter? If you are willing to take it up directly, I dare to pick it up with my own hand.
Having once been issued from the Imperial desk, why need there be further pointing by a master?
If you do not wish for it, it was never here to begin with; if I do not bring it forth, it is already yours. The verse says: "The stone bestowed by the Emperor’s decree flows..."
It has been transmitted to me like an empty boat. Plucked up at the edge of Yunxi Creek, it transforms fish and dragons into companions in the heavens.
When the Magistrate of Yunxi, Di Chen Wang, a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*), entered the mountain one day prior to the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, he went for a walk with Yunfeng.
The lay practitioner asked Yunfeng for his staff; Yunfeng struck him immediately. The practitioner bowed and asked again; Yunfeng then gave it to him.
Before he had even taken a single step, the staff broke, whereupon he requested a verse. Yunfeng smiled and said, "The formation of his spirit and bone is truly marvelous;
by chance, he has met the capacity for the Mahayana. Without exerting the slightest bit of effort, he has broken one of my Yunfeng staffs."
The scholar was filled with joy and immediately prepared a formal reception upon his return. The following day, he invited the mountain monk to ascend the hall.

The monk held up his staff and said, "Last night, beholding the morning star, I attained enlightenment. I observe that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests all possess the wisdom and virtuous marks of the Tathāgata;
they have never had deluded thoughts or attachments, nor do they seek realization. Now tell me, how does this compare to Śākyamuni?"
"Is the realization the same or different? After a long silence, he looked to his left and right and said, "Suppose someone were to come forth here and say:
'The Good Knowledge of five hundred people speaks empty falsehoods! Yunfeng’s staff was already broken yesterday by Lord Tan-chan;
what further words could there possibly be? The Master smiled and said, 'I, the old monk, toward...'"
He said: "Flying rosy clouds while gazing at the Dipper; when the snow clears, the peaks return. How much is used therein? He made a gesture of fishing with his staff and asked, "Do you understand?
When the fishing pole is worn away, plant bamboo anew; do not calculate the labor, but rest as soon as the opportunity arises.
He struck the ground with his staff and descended from the seat.
Tizong was a dharma successor of Chan Master Zhan Yiqing.
A native of the Wang family from Yongning in southern Sichuan, he received the tonsure at the age of twenty under Vinaya Master Benzong.
He subsequently received full ordination in the presence of Venerable Tizong of Yunfeng and investigated his own fundamental matter. It was while striking a pillar that he attained realization.
There was a realization. A verse on seizing the opportunity says: "What has been the cause of such bitter entanglement these years? Turning it over and investigating it to the end, it is all but him.
Clearly and distinctly understood, there is not a single thing; In the final taste, there is not the slightest bit. The verse on the Old Woman Burning the Hermitage says:
"Taking it up with the hand of faith, he unfurls the crimson banner; in his giving and taking, there is a divine mechanism. Though he sells this secret, for what purpose?

He has lost the mother-born garment that clings to the body. Feng transmitted the lineage to him. Having served as his attendant and carried his bowl and robe for sixteen years, he took leave of Feng and entered Yunnan.
Residing at Ying'en Temple in Huichuan, he ascended the hall for the opening of the retreat. "In various quarters, the retreat is opened and meditation is settled. He welcomed...
The grace of ascending the hall and performing the dance startles the fierce dragons of the four seas and causes the phoenixes of the nine heavens to swoop down.

The followers of the Three Vehicles fold their hands; those of the Ten Stages clasp their fists. The myriad phenomena of the universe raise their brows and exhale their breath; the stars and constellations of the heavens shine with brilliant luster.
Microscopic lands surge up in the east and submerge in the west; all that crawls and flies brandishes its own inherent nature. This is not the work of spirits.
This marvelous function is not merely a matter of natural law. [The Master] strikes the meditation staff and says: "Do you understand?

Today, too, the soldiers follow the seal, and the generals march according to the talisman. At such a time as this, how do you speak the single phrase for 'Opening the Furnace to Wish for the Emperor's Longevity'?
The wild man has no offerings to repay the imperial virtue; he shall simply take Mount Sumeru to serve as a single stick of incense."
Liangsheng was a descendant of the Wang family of Dongwu in Shu. As a child, he received the tonsure at Huguo Temple under Master Buwo.
At the age of twenty, he received full ordination from Master Luyou. When Master Lingyin visited Huguo Temple, [he encountered him there].

He attained a realization that struck at the vital pivot and moved him to strike the rhythm of the Dharma. He traveled extensively to visit venerable masters and went to Jia Rui in Zangke, where he met Master Liangsheng;
their kōans and words were in perfect accord. He offered this verse: "Under the staff and the shout, the total capacity is received; A flash of lightning or a shooting star is already too late.
The stinking-bone robe has been cast off; Wherever conditions lead, let one act as they please. Thereafter, he succeeded [Jia Rui] to the abbacy at Songshan.
Qiu has a record that circulates in the world; its brief instructions to the assembly say: "In practicing Chan, one must be fierce and resolute; do not rest until awakening is attained.
Rouse a fine spirit and do not let the opportune moment pass. Cast down a heart of total resolve; why be constrained by years or months?"
Only when you have established yourself with a firm footing will you no longer be deluded by others. Willingly enduring the bitterest of bitterness, you must be able to penetrate the critical point.
The ancients did so; I have always been earnest about this. Become a person beyond the common crowd; your conduct must be utterly distinct.
One can realize the proof within a fixed period; at that very moment, one transcends. Penetrating beyond the heavens of heaven, one far surpasses the "white-handed thief.
As soon as one hears even a slight mention of it, it becomes vividly clear by itself. Waves surge upon the mountain peak, while the ocean floor stands utterly parched.
When Maitreya and Śākyamuni arrive, their sharp edges vanish and their tongues are tied. The three thousand worlds lay out their tangled vines, yet every nest and trap is utterly destroyed.
Striking upon this "dead-sitting Chan," it is split in two with a single stroke. Should you further propose to ask, "How is it?"—a white staff comes crashing down upon your head.
When you reach this stage, I grant that you may be called a Zen guest. I pray that before the Great Assembly, you will not suspect my words to be false.

Chan Master Tieji Chang was the son of the He family of Yuzhang; he became a monk at the age of seven. Secluding himself behind closed doors in Wengyi, he attained realization during a seven-day intensive retreat (*qijie*).
His verse of spiritual resonance says: "The single path of the perfect void is the treasury of radiance; all sentient beings within the six realms share it as well."

Throughout the three periods of time and across all ages, there is neither front nor back; it is only because of clinging to delusion that one hesitates. Clinging to the self and denigrating others is entirely delusion;
in *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra*, there is no high or low. Radiant clarity has never been obtained from another;

awakening is encountered at every turn, fundamentally free from confusion. Having departed the pass, he heard of the spiritual reputation of the Elder of Zhaojue and headed toward Shu. Upon reaching Yelang, he encountered two...

He received full ordination and formal certification from Master Sheng. He lived in seclusion for twenty years, during which time his collection of poems titled *Shanju churu ji* (Gleanings from a Mountain Dweller) circulated among the public.

Later, he went to the quarters of Master Zhang at Zhaojue Temple, where he served as the West Hall Attendant. He was appointed to ascend the hall at the conclusion of the retreat; thus, the ninety-day period ended and the hundred-day task was completed.
Lanterns were bright before the hall on the Yuanxiao Festival, and the sound of firecrackers heralded the midpoint of the first lunar month. When the monks heard this—
Awakening to the Way through sound; a layperson seeing form and discussing Chan—this is not like seeking bubbles upon the sea. Once the "measuring board" is established, it supports the heavens.

If one possesses the correct eye of universal penetration, wildflowers and spring grasses will hold the mist. Only when both Buddhist and worldly dharmas are exhausted of emotion can one lower the hand and enter the marketplace.
Regarding the single phrase for the conclusion of the retreat, how do you speak? He brushes [the whisk] once and says: "Everyone is tight."
He bound his waist-pouch and departed; do not say that the soles of his straw sandals were wide.
Hanguang’s true Dharma heir, Chan Master Foxian of Tianzhu Temple in Luyang, was the son of the Zhu family of this province. At the age of seven, he paid homage to Cihang.
He underwent tonsure and first attended Master Tishan Ti. Upon receiving full ordination, he later attained realization under Master Hanguang.
He established the Dharma at Tianzhu Chan Temple. Ascending the hall, he said: "Today, the alms bowl receives moisture; the fragrant incense of Tianzhu fills the earth.
Flowers and plants naturally blossom, and heaven and earth must likewise open and close. Lay donors provide offerings for the field of merit; when a monk arrives—"
To seize the nostrils: the function of the staff is as lively as a dragon; with one flavor, he strikes directly at the head, knocking down Indra’s flower crown.
The blue-eyed barbarian monk did not accord; the "Three Mysteries" and "Three Essentials" are but tangled vines. It is better than the "ten thousand dharmas returning to the One.
Do you recognize this One? (He draws a circle with his staff. Even where there is no elegance, there is elegance; when there is spirit, it adds to it.
Yiqi. Xiaozong Mi’s Dharma heir, Chan Master Hui of E-snow, was the son of the Nie family of Langzhong. At fourteen, he received the tonsure and went to consult with Master Shan-da. He requested—
Furthering the karmic conditions of Yunmen’s “Mount Sumeru,” he realized his place upon hearing these words. He was the Dharma heir of Master Xiaozong at Baoning Haiyun Temple.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The ocean of awakening is clear and still; the wondrous source is non-dual.

With the three gates of liberation as emptiness and wisdom as adornment, the hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates reveal the true meaning—all of this is fully manifested upon the tip of a single hair. Only...

I urge everyone to see this directly right now. Should you not yet have done so, and if you wish to attain the unconditioned realm of true purity, even if you were to turn yourself around from this very spot—[he ascends the hall]—The biting north wind pierces to the bone; a few points of plum blossom claim the vanguard of spring.
A single segment of the true mechanism is clearly revealed; alas, how can people of this age not know how to look? Elder Hui [acts] in this manner.
To announce this is like adding embroidery to brocade. Pointing his staff at the air, he said: "Without the spring breeze, the flowers would not bloom;
once they have bloomed, they are blown down by the wind."

Master Changchanghui was the son of the Lu family in Chongqing Prefecture. During a time of turmoil, he fled to Zunyi, where at the age of twenty, he took formal refuge under Master Xiandeng and received the tonsure.
Hearing that Master Boshan was opening a dharma seat at Shuanggui, he went there to receive full ordination.
He then traveled extensively to visit various masters before returning to Baoguang Temple in Xindu, where he attained realization under Master Xiaozong, who bestowed upon him a verse of transmission.

He was aware that his own virtue was meager and his conduct sparse, such that he could not contribute anything beneficial to the Dharma-gate. He remained steadfast in the path of goodness until death.

There are mountain-dwelling poems and verses circulating in the world, the gist of which says: "In the depths of clouds and water, I have divined a secluded dwelling; My livelihood is modest, yet my joy is more than sufficient.
The frost is cold as chrysanthemums bloom, making the Three Paths beautiful; The moon is bright and people are still, leaving the six windows empty. In my leisure, I come to compound medicines..."
In the medical classic, he again burned incense and read Buddhist scriptures. Within this state, there was no room for the Lion’s Seat;
he answered Mañjuśrī with nothing but silence. Sweeping the graves of his parents, he said: On this auspicious Qingming festival, I sweep the tomb mound.

Fragments of sorrowful clouds gradually surge forth. After the rain, old resentments increase before one's eyes; As thunder roars atop the grave, new grief continues. Incense is burned upon the mountain ridges.
A thousand years of stench; paper hung over the Yangtze River for a hundred generations. How many times have I chanted the "Liaoe" (Filial Piety) poem until my heart and gall burst asunder?
Gazing toward the vast sky, my vision is severed like that of a fool.
The two hidden ones, Mi and Fa, were his dharma heirs.
Chan Master Zizhou Chuan of Xiangyang was a native of Tongchuan. He resided at the Lukmon Chan Monastery in Xiangyang. Upon ascending the hall, he was asked:
"The mani jewel has long been buried in dust and soil; how can it be found? The Master said, "It shines through my old face. Another asked:
"Regarding the ordinary course of daily life, tell me, how do you make use of it? The Master said, "The bright moon draws forth the clear breeze. He then said:

The mountain range of Deer Gate is most majestic and powerful; from amidst the rubble, radiance arises, reaching the fundamental source. His countenance is solemn and manifest right before one’s eyes:
upon the tips of a hundred blades of grass, clouds and dragons arise.
Chan Master Murulin was the son of the Mi family of Jintang. From his youth, he was serene, pure, and upright; he was quiet and spoke little.

He left the household life at the age of seven and constantly kept the reality of birth and death in mind. He subsequently purchased a boat and traveled south to visit Master Er-yin at Santai in Jiahe, where he received formal certification of his realization.
Later, he returned to Long’an Xuefeng Monastery and ascended the hall to give a discourse during the depths of winter.
The Buddha-dharma is beyond conceptual deliberation; the myriad phenomena are all hidden within the snow. Only when the single red sun rises will the lanterns and the pillars all radiate their light.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Last night the frosty wind pierced through one’s very bones with its chill; the Yellow River froze over, its appearance like a mountain.
It froze the clay ox until it bellowed throughout the night, and the wooden horse was dragged out to gaze at it in competition. He then cited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
It is said: "This alone is the one reality; the other two are not true. Śākyamuni the Old Man spoke thus, yet he too only managed to say half of it.
As for that other half, wait until I have descended from the seat, and I shall give you a message.
Why? A single palm does not make a sound; a single tree does not form a forest.

Chan Master Han Yu Xian of Huoshan was a native of the Wang family of Xichong. He studied under numerous venerable masters before finally entering the quarters of Master Zixian, from whom he first received the Dharma lineage.
He subsequently went forth to reside at Huoshan in Jin. On the occasion of the opening of the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said:
"The sackcloth bag has been tied for ninety days; today it is untied, and the eight directions are open through. For the patch-robed monks, their very bodies are hands and eyes—seize!"
Clouds seize the mist and grasp the pure breeze; all you Zen practitioners, come encounter this marvel. White clouds gather and disperse across the empty sky;

the thorn-sandals on his feet are as fierce as tigers, the staff upon his shoulder is as lively as a dragon. Entering the hall: Establishing the retreat and concluding the retreat are the long-standing precedents of all quarters.
Yet the ancestral style of Buddhas and Patriarchs is a singular event: for ninety days he holds fast the secure barrier, testing the sages.
Regarding all prohibitions, there is not even the slightest room for deviation. This refines the core essence of the monk and eradicates heterodox thoughts and the thieving mind.
One will surely find one’s feet firmly planted on the ground, regardless of how one yells or roars; it shall cause the mountains to shake and the earth to tremble.
Let us repay the unrequited kindness and together assist the transformation of non-action. Entering the hall: In the bustling marketplace of the red dust, the Ancient [Way] is fully revealed.
The Buddha-mind school: within the massed form of the body, the patriarch’s true nose is revealed alone. On both banks of Pingquan, mist enshrouds the water and the moonlight is fresh.
At the peak of Gusha, colors disperse and the shadows of white clouds are exquisite. In the flower-streets and willow-alleys lies the Guanyin Temple.
Jiusi Yinfang Milihejia. Yun'e Xifa succeeded Master Binya Chan of Tongchuan;
he received the Dharma from Chan Master Yun'e of Fengxue and resided at Fahai Temple.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Since the Dharma Ocean first established itself, it has refused to encroach upon others' paths or seize their markets.
It demarcates its territory and divides its lands, taking heaven and earth as a single meditation hall. Its walking is done together with all people; its dwelling is shared with all people.

Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, whether putting on robes and eating, carrying water and hauling firewood, or engaging in every movement and action, there is no obstruction whatsoever—even unto enlightenment."
The dark void. The myriad phenomena of the universe—whether wise or foolish—each abides by their own lot.
And yet, though this is so, there is one person who does not enter the communal assembly. Pure and naked, utterly devoid of hidden stores; bare and unadorned, without front or back.
Sometimes, atop a solitary peak, he roars at the moon and chants with the wind; sometimes, before the bustling marketplace, he appears with the head and face of a spirit or a ghost. His tongue...
Supporting the Brahma Heaven, his eyes empty the four seas; when moving, he is like drifting clouds; when still, he is like the spirit of the valley.
[The Master] strikes a circular shape with his whisk and asks: "Do you recognize this person? Throughout his life, he has laid bare his liver and gall toward others;

yet those who know him are treated as if they do not. At Lingtai Temple, ascending the hall: A single phrase is without partiality, cutting through nails and iron; all myriad functions are brought to rest, utterly transcending.
Laluṇi: Attaining the wondrous by following the flow; a single style across a thousand miles. When great function manifests before one, one plays upon the stage as the occasion demands.
A jade mirror contains the autumn; a frozen pool reflects the image. A dragon-slaying sword emerges from its scabbard; ten thousand miles away, corpses lie scattered.

How can one linger within the mass of great fire? The diamond circle allows no grasping. To touch it and turn away is already to fall into the realm of merit and achievement; to grasp it and immediately act—this is the way.

Having early established his path, he possesses such wondrous insight as to serve as a vessel for the sea of suffering. His hidden and manifest aspects are fully revealed, and his literary style and spiritual track are of one accord.
Ascending the hall at Fengcun Temple: The spring is deep and things flourish; the sun is warm and the breeze harmonious. Swallows rejoice and orioles sing;
the times are clear and the Way is prosperous. Prajñā circulates, for the Dharma is fundamentally without concealment. Striking the meditation seat, he said: "This sound is not [the sound]."
Sounds: toiling in vain with ears pricked. Form is not form; it is difficult to discern and distinguish. At Haibao Monastery, ascending the hall, one dons frost and treads in straw sandals;

across the clouds, three thousand miles away, one lets go of the whole body, which naturally accords with a state of carefree detachment. From within his sleeves, the golden mallet is cast forth into the open sun.
The chamber of Vimalakīrti is opened wide in eight characters. Those who dwell therein grasp the sovereign authority beyond the threshold; they wield the hook.
There is bait upon the head. Bestowed upon Buddhas and Patriarchs, it illuminates their function; the scale lacks its stars, yet it opens the true eye for devas and humans.

To examine the core of a monk—should one recognize the appropriate timing and distinguish between fortune and misfortune, and instead of acting immediately, stir up the matter, I shall give thirty blows to his heels.
Why? Because under the gate of Haibao, no command is issued in vain.
Chan Master Huanxiu Gan was the son of the Hu family of Long’an in western Sichuan. At nineteen, he left the white robe for the monastic life; at twenty, he received full ordination.

He traveled extensively to study under various masters throughout the land, attaining realization at each of their assemblies. In the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era, he went to Shaolin to pay homage at the ancestral pagodas.

Passing through Fengxue, he visited Master Yunge, with whom his spiritual resonance was so harmonious that he was granted the seal of transmission. In the Guiyou year, he began teaching the Dharma at Jingyang.

At Xingfu Chan Temple, at the request of the assembly, he ascended the hall to address them: "Plucking the weeds and observing the wind for twenty autumns, his entire faculty remains unmoving as he dwells in confident ease.
Without cause, he has mounted the Flower King’s throne and shattered the three mysteries to receive those of the highest stream.

When the Dharma-vehicle is once proclaimed, the Three Baskets are rendered inexpressible; when the Ultimate Way is expanded, a thousand paths converge on a single track. All currents are cut off, pervading every mote of dust."
Spontaneously encompassing all lands, it turns the sublime pivot; it subsumes both existence and non-existence while relying upon the transmission of the pointing instructions.

Its radiance transcends sun and moon; its wisdom surpasses the holy and the mundane. In movement and stillness it is impartial; in concealment and manifestation it is never obscured. The skull constantly dries the world.
The touch of the nostrils reveals the family style; it is subtle, dense, and serene. It provisionally opens up Dongshan’s five ranks, where the dark mechanism is perfectly integrated.

It seeks to transcend the three births of Muzhou and Yangshan. A single character barrier surpasses the high antiquity of Yunmen; the meaning of the six phases grasps the spontaneous realization of Fayan.
Seizing both the environment and the person, it is direct and exhilarating; establishing both guest and host, its great function turns like the heavens.
Seals on water, seals on mud, seals on space—those who are not masters find them difficult to discern. It is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor any thing; only through realization can it be known.
Like the earth universally supporting all, like the sky universally covering all, the true mechanism is laid bare and the myriad dharmas are fully revealed.

At such a time as this, tell me: how would you express the single phrase for the opening of the hall to offer blessings to the Emperor? *Jig'yang ge'yang wang* (The Song of the People Beating the Earth).
The Emperor’s power was such that, through the continuation of poetic hymns, he celebrated the harmony of the times.

As for Chan Master Guyue Lang of Dangshan, a successor in the Dharma lineage, he was the son of the Yang family of Hezhou. Having traveled extensively throughout all quarters, he encountered Master Ruohan.
Che encountered Chan Master Dangshan for certification. He resided at Rui-lin Yuan in Taoyuan. Ascending the hall, he said: "Wearing only straw sandals, there is no need for a boat;

the matter beneath one's heels becomes increasingly submerged or floating. Even now, though drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry, one cannot yet discern whether the flow over the bridge is the water flowing.
In the small assembly (xiaocan), he suddenly held up his whisk and said: "This is the first step of the ultimate path. [If you] have not yet realized it—"
"This person has passed away and finds no place to rest. Quan said, "I shall entrust this matter to you. Chew it slowly; its flavor is like that of *ge-ru* (yellow myrobalan).
He set down his whisk and struck his knee once.

The Venerable Chan Master Gusu was the son of the Hu family of Chengdu. He received the Dharma succession from Master Dangshan. On the occasion of the Buddha-Bathing Ceremony, he ascended the hall and said:
"Two stalks of candles for the sun and moon; a single stick of incense for Mount Sumeru. With these manifest things, I make offering to the King of the Dharma."
Looking at the assembly, he said: "This is this mountain monk’s way of exhausting his filial piety.

If you all have any rare delicacies or extraordinary dishes, do not hesitate to bring them forth, so as to repay the unrepayable debt of gratitude and together celebrate the longevity of the Buddha, the Awakened Sovereign.

He then ascended the hall to make offerings before the portrait of Chan Master Danxia, saying: "The former Śākyamuni was not at peace; the future Maitreya has not yet arrived. I offer my worship solely to this natural old man."
First, he did not value that Yi’s wisdom was of great talent; second, he did not value that Yi’s Way was complete and his virtue fully prepared.
What he now values is this: Yi heard the announcement of death and departed; upon hearing of the bestowal of precepts, he quickly withdrew.

He rode upon the Holy Monk and received his title from Mazu; he burned the wooden Buddha to ward off the cold at Huilin. Setting aside all such matters of coming and going for a moment, let us consider his current station as a single instance.
"How shall one raise this phrase? He made a sweeping gesture with his whisk and said, "The doors and windows of seeing and hearing are without obstruction.

He snatched away Pang’s head-wrap and said, "On the Lantern Festival, I ascend the hall. Grasping my staff, I say: On the fifteenth day of this month this year, I shall not beat the ordinary broken drum;
I shall light the lamp that dispels darkness so that everyone may see it clearly. Suddenly, the oil is exhausted and the lamp goes out."
"What about the remainder? [Ni-ru-kou]. "The staff has eyes as bright as the sun; over hills and dales, on level ground or in the plains, go wherever you will.
At Shengquan, ascending the hall on New Year’s Eve: "A year is completed in three hundred and sixty days; having reached this evening, the count is finally finished.

Every household nails up peach-blossom talismans; every family burns crackling firecrackers. Those who see off the old are frantic with haste; those who offer for the deceased wail in bitter grief. How fine!"
He laughed at the people of the world, who for the most part are pursued by temporal conditions; only the monk Shengquan remained serene, as if unaware.
He cast down his staff and descended from the seat.
He was a dharma successor of Daxiong Peak.
Chan Master Suan of Shu was the son of the Xie family of Jianzhou. He left home to become a monk in his middle years and inherited the Dharma from Dayong.

He resided at Baoguo Hermitage in Chengdu. When the Elder of Zhaojue provided a vegetarian feast, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Baoguo has just opened this field of battle for the Dharma; the assembly of traveling monks fills the hall, breaking new ground.
Though there is not even a single *dan* or *shi* of grain stored in the kitchen, there are naturally those of lofty wisdom who will join together to promote it."
He introduced Master Dahui Zonggao, who went to Jiangshan to visit Chan Master Ying’an Huo. Entering the hall, he cited the kōan of the ox passing through the lattice window:
"This public case has resided within the belly of Jiangshan for many years.

Had it not been for my Dharma-uncle, the Elder Teacher, who encouraged and corrected me, I would never have dared to bring it up in my entire life. Today, before this assembly of gods and men, I produce it."

He made offerings to his Dharma-uncle, the Master, and addressed the assembly, saying: "Great assembly, since the head, horns, and all four hooves have already passed through, why is it that the tail cannot pass?
Where does the crux lie? After a long silence, he spoke on their behalf:
"A torch before every door. Originally, matters are of one house; they are to be chanted and harmonized together. As the saying goes: "When wine meets..."
Drink with those who know you; recite the poems for those who understand them. I, this humble monk, dare not cite the ancients to judge the present.
This is the Elder of Zhaojue who has condescended from his exalted position to the lowly, assisting in the propagation of the Dharma and upholding the Buddha-dharma.
As for the phrase "to receive beings and benefit living things"—how do you speak it? He strikes the meditation staff and says: "A solitary egret at Hengtang takes flight obliquely, a few birds."
Yingping Guashuaoshao (Silver Pitcher Hanging from the Tree Tip).
Xianggu was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Meixue Zong of Jinchun Temple; he was the son of the Xie family of Shehong and received the Dharma transmission from Chan Master Xianggu.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mountains and shadows are deep and secluded, with few visitors; the wild waters and layered cliffs share the same springtime.

Today, in these mountains and fields, we once again open the ancestral banquet and the Buddha-sun hangs forth once more. If we hold fast, tiles and pebbles sleep amidst the clouds; if we let go, the lanterns break into a dance.
How can this compare to Great Scholar Bo in the Realm of Non-birth, who takes his ease in lofty slumber, carefree and joyful?"
Ningzhen’s dharma heir, Chan Master Tianran Hui of Xiping Temple in Nanlong, was the son of the Liu family of Nanchong. Due to the chaos in Shu, he was mixed among the ranks of soldiers.

At the age of eighteen, he grew weary of the world as being like an illusion and resolved to transcend the mundane. He paid his respects to Rusheng to receive the tonsure and become a monk. His precepts were perfected.

[He was] fully equipped [with realization]. He traveled to visit various masters of the different quarters. Later, he relied upon Master Ningzhen, who probed him deeply and struck him with painful blows until he died and returned to life;
he subsequently received certification from him. On the occasion of the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall and said: "It is the first day of the year; all things are new.

Sending off and welcoming in, one sees the host and guest. Suddenly picking up his staff, he said: "Only this dark, shimmering thing does not follow the seasonal calendar nor conform to human sentiment."
"Sometimes he strikes the wind and beats the moon; the head of Mount Sumeru cracks and the blue seas ache.
Startled, the tiger of the South Mountain leaps away, and the Great Dipper is caught in a chain of misfortune, receiving a great fright. But tell me, where does the point of profit or harm lie?

He then struck the ground with his staff and said, "Were it not for one who has experienced many battles on the field, how could he hoist a banner a hundred feet high? He then descended from the seat.
Master Wen Chan of Lianchi, the dharma heir of Kuai Xue Guofa, was the son of the Luo family of Dangqu. At the age of seven, he received the tonsure under Master Hanxu;

at twenty, he went before Venerable Fangru to receive full ordination. After traveling extensively to consult various masters, he returned to Baoning, where he established the Lianchi Hermitage for himself.
Rest. One day, Master Kuai Xue visited; as their karmic conditions met, he was granted a formal transmission (jibie).
When Layman Chou offered a Dharma robe, [the Master] ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it is born only by relying on conditions.

In the midsummer heat, the cold wind is piercingly fierce—this is the condition. But tell me, what is the Dharma? Raising the robe and showing it to the assembly, he said: "Do you understand? This robe..."
The affairs of the mundane world are fully present in every person; they are inconceivable. Who is lacking anything?
Why must you go to another's heap of manure and straw to seek what bowl? Therefore it is said: "Without leaving this very place, it is ever serene;
if you seek it, you will know it cannot be seen."
Yunqiao Shui was a dharma successor of Chan Master Canggu Guì;
he was the son of the Li family from Jingzhou in Huguang. At the age of seven, he paid respects to Master Huanshi and received the tonsure.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination under his own teacher. He traveled extensively to visit various masters throughout the land, eventually arriving at Shuanggui to harmonize with Yunqiao.

Furthermore, as their karmic conditions coincided, he bestowed upon them a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). In the Bingyin year of the Kangxi era, the local gentry and officials of Dazhou requested that he reside at Longxing Chan Monastery.
Upon ascending the hall, he suddenly presented his staff and called to the assembly, saying: "Do you understand? This [staff] reaches up to heaven and down to earth;
it is inherently nameless—who would dare to forcibly assign it a name? At times it shakes the earth and emits light, as bright as the blazing sun."

At times, he effaces his traces and hides his whereabouts; black as ink, he does not belong to the colors blue or yellow. Adapting to whatever vessel contains him, he can transform and manifest, appearing horizontal or vertical.
Ultimately equal, he is truly peerless. Reaching back to antiquity and extending to the present, he vertically exhausts the three periods of time.
Then, holding up his staff horizontally, he said: "Precepts, concentration, and wisdom—the ancestral master’s barrier—all fit perfectly upon this single string."

[The Master] stepped forward. Again, Zhuo said: "Do you understand? If you can realize it here and now, the immeasurable Dharma-gates and the wondrous meanings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will be established from this point on.
If this is not yet the case, you must buy more straw sandals and travel the pilgrimage routes."
The thirty-eighth generation descendant of Dajian (Daikuan), Chan Master Yunlin De of Luohan Temple, was the dharma heir of Shigu Hui.
He was the son of Dong [surname] from Tongjiang. He paid homage to Master Xin Tian and underwent tonsure and dyeing of his robes. He then went to visit Shigu...
Master Gu succeeded to the Dharma and rebuilt Fanglang Arhat Temple, which was the place where Chan Master Mazu Daoyi shaved his head.
He ascended the hall. A monk asked, "What is the realm of the arhats? The Master said, "Heaven-reaching green bamboos are dense;
sky-filling ancient cypresses are thick. The monk pressed further, "What about the people within that realm? The Master said, "A single hall of the Great Hero (Mahāvīra)."
Ten people from Dachi advanced and asked, "When person and environment do not stand, what then? The Master said, "It is you who have failed to reach such a state.
He then continued, "A single blow, a single shout, a single fist, a single foot—this directly points to the very marrow of Linji and fully reveals the strategic maneuvers of Deshan.
There is not a single extra dot of the ancients, nor a single stroke lacking in the present; it is entirely like grass being laid low."
The wind blows. Like a tiger wearing horns, wherever it strikes or brushes against, its horizontal pivot kills or gives life.
If you have not yet escaped this, the mountain monk cannot help but add further footnotes. (He strikes the ground once with his staff and lets out a shout.
This too is a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes. (He strikes again and says: "Mistake! Mistake!"
Jingju Yemou Chanshi (淨居月目禪師) was a native of Le (樂) in the Zou (鄒) clan. At the age of seven, he received the tonsure at Baa Yue Temple (巴岳寺).

He attended upon Master Shigu (石谷和尚) to receive full ordination and subsequently received the transmission of the Dharma. Later, he resided at Jingju Temple (淨居寺) in Longmen (龍門). He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
A monk asked, "What is the environment of Longmen? The Master said, "The two pools of water beneath the Qingfeng Bridge.

The monk pressed further, "Who is the person within that environment? The Master said, "Rising at sunrise and resting at sunset. The monk pressed again, "I have received your instruction regarding the person and the environment;
as for the ultimate vehicle of the ancestral teaching, what is it? The Master struck him. The monk said, "Blind stick! The Master struck him again.
He struck [the floor] and said, "There is indeed a blind fellow here who eats! Then he continued: "At times I opened an inn to stave off hunger and cold;
at other times I drew water from the Dragon Gate to till the fields. As for the Buddha-dharma, I would rather let it rot away entirely than speak of 'old woman's Chan' from now on."
Chan Master Cangtonghua was the son of the Feng family of Qijiang. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and received full ordination under Master Miyu at the age of twenty.
He was certified by Master Shigu and made seclusion his constant practice. His poems on mountain dwelling have been circulated in the world.
Its summary says: "The mountains stretch on and on; the waters flow on and on. With a single staff, wander at will through the depths of the clouds.
Plucking pine blossoms from the trees, they may serve as food; when autumn returns, lotus leaves can be made into a cloak. Magnificent is the Buddha-dharma, a mirror that clears away the dust;
vast and boundless is the passage of time, sending forth the traveler’s boat. If you wish to suddenly transcend these illusory scenes, you need only constantly tend this ox of the mind. Furthermore:
He said: "Clouds, streams, and mountains—each and every one is a painting; bamboo and trees, growing in dense clusters, cannot be painted.

One must laugh at the dull nature of those who dwell in the mountains; a single mattock is sufficient for a lifetime. In his later years, he returned once more to Shimen Temple in his native district.
On the eve of his departure, he spoke this verse: "When I came, yellow chrysanthemums sifted gold; When I go, green mountains spread white. If you think back on this skull..."
A skull. Having been a guest ten thousand times over, today he kicks down Mount Sumeru, squeezing the void until it bleeds.
In the city of Nirvana, there is no one to know him; he laughs to death the ancient Maitreya of Tuṣita Heaven.
Zizhi Zangfasi [Pei]tong delivered a discourse for National Protection Temple’s Chan Master Tianran Gui. "Today is the eighth day of the first lunar month;
everywhere the Buddha-dharma is being proclaimed, yet National Protection Temple alone does not do so. When seeing people, it merely scolds them. He suddenly seized his whisk.
He said: "If you can realize it right here, then every land and every atom is the realm of Vairocana; the sound of the stream and the song of the birds are the gate of Avalokiteśvara’s principle.
If this is not yet so, your nostrils will continue to hang downward as before. He struck his whisk and descended from the seat.
On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascended the hall and said: "I shall not sing old melodies; I intend to beat fresh drums and pipes. The mouth of the wordless youth is agape."
The tongueless child can understand speech; at ease, he plucks the stringless lute. The ocean waters surge with waves and the mountains rise of their own accord.
But tell me, how does one play the stringless lute? [He makes the gesture of playing the lute with his staff and asks: Do you understand?
If you listen with your ears, it will ultimately be difficult to comprehend; only by hearing the sound within the eye can one truly know.
Chan Master Wēn Qióngmù of Wànfú Temple in Jǐnguān was a native of the Dèng family in Yíbīn, Róngzhōu. At the age of fifteen, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk.

He constantly reflected on the impermanence of this body and traveled to visit various masters throughout the land. Upon hearing that Upādhyāya Zǐzhī was opening the hall for formal instruction, he set out with staff and alms bowl to seek him out.
He served as an attendant in the quarters for fifteen years and was subsequently granted certification of realization. Later, while residing at Wànfú, he ascended the hall and said: "In the past..."
When people gather stones to preach the Dharma, my current preaching of the Dharma is likewise empty. Like a spark from a stone, a flash of lightning—it is difficult to find a place to settle.
[The Master] suddenly grasps his staff and strikes it down, saying: "Only this one thing is bare and naked, radiantly brilliant.

Sometimes it mingles with mud and water, dancing in villages and singing folk songs; sometimes it stands alone on a solitary peak, hanging beneath the moon and suspended among the stars. When it moves, it enables Avalokiteśvara."
Śrī-Ābhāsvara binds his tongue and hides his blade; in stillness, he leaves the Old Śākyamuni with no ground to stand upon.
But tell me, where lies the benefit or the harm? After a long silence, he said: "Study! At Huguo Monastery, for the sake of Master Tianran, the assembly requested him to ascend the hall.
This curved wooden seat is my Dharma brother Tianran—neither can it be gathered together, nor can it be split apart."
It has now fallen into the hands of Wanfu. Within this, he moves freely in all directions, unifying both function and illumination.
Then, holding up his whisk, he calls to the assembly, saying: "Do you see? Here, my elder brother Yan manifests the marks of a Great Man upon the tip of a single hair."
"To you all, I shall now speak the final word. He struck the meditation seat again and asked, "Did you hear it?
Then, for your sake, he revealed his entire being in its nakedness. "If you do not realize this, you shall not escape ten thousand blessings;
I must send forth another message. He cast down his whisk and said, "Remember this single hair-whisk; when it comes back, its roar shall shake the three thousand worlds."
Yushong Yi was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Yushong Erzhu of Fuzhou. He was the son of the Fei family of Yuzhou. Initially, he studied under Master Posue;

though he could not recognize a single character, he practiced the dhūta austerities. Later, he visited Master Yushong at Mount Muni, where he attained realization through the master’s staff and was subsequently certified.
Later, he resided at Cimingsi on Mount Sha’e. Ascending the hall, he said: "The great function is sung alone; the traces of the thousand sages have vanished.
All streams are cut off; even the clouds of the staff find no path. Which truly correct patch-robed monk can manifest the great function and deploy the great utility?

Within the flash of a spark or a bolt of lightning, they 'crack' and 'peck' together, wielding authority over gods and humans and weighing the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Striking and singing proceed in tandem."

Killing and bringing to life are both manifested; the nests of ordinary and sage are shattered, and the roots and sprouts of birth and death are severed. Yet, even this is not yet the matter that lies above.

What, then, is the matter that lies above? The Imperial Edict has been issued and is spread throughout the world; the General has brought the lands beyond the frontier to a state where smoke and dust vanish.
Shuyun Chai was the Dharma heir of Chan Master Shexiang Nu;
he was the son of Long of Dingyuan. Having traveled throughout half the world, he attained realization under the guidance of Master Linye.
Upon returning to Shu, he met with Master Shuyun, who certified his attainment. He ascended the hall and said: "The phrase that points directly upward—"

A thousand sages are left speechless. A single stroke of direct encounter is realized everywhere as it is. In every turn, movement, bowing, and rising, the natural splendor of one’s original ground is laid bare.

In a cough, a sneeze, or a casual wave of the arm, the monk’s functional handle is fully revealed. Those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence are like fine steeds that, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, pursue the wind for a thousand *li*.
Those of middling or inferior capacity are like the dog Han-lu, who chases after clods of earth and forever forgets his way back home. And yet...
Now, let us set aside the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.

We shall simply instruct each and every one to possess a majestic bearing like a king, to cut off the myriad divergent paths at their source, and to firmly grasp the very nose-ring of the monk. To penetrate clearly the true eye of the crown and to look through the pivot of the patriarchs—tell me, what is this pivot of the patriarchs?
The four fields are bitterly cold with nowhere to lodge; with hair disheveled and robe open, one arrives.

In the Painting Hall. Ascending the hall: He opens the treasury of radiant light and manifests the eternally abiding principle. The great earth is utterly free from a speck of obscuration; the four seas are as clear as if washed.
The myriad phenomena of the forested world are all contained within this very space. Do not speak of beholding the morning star, for it deceives and deludes foolish men and women.
Ascending the hall: The forge is opened wide; demons and Buddhas are instantly melted down. The tongs and hammer are raised high; saints and commoners [are forged].
Sentiments exhausted; every one with scorched heads and blistered brows, everyone with skin cracked and flesh melted.

Even refined gold of a hundred smeltings must lose its luster upon reaching this point. (He strikes the meditation staff. "Bringing forth a golden ball from the furnace, it shatters the iron gates of everyone's faces."
Chan Master Limei Can was a native of Luyang. Having received the Dharma from Master Shuyun Xian, he resided at Zhongyan on Jinchuan.
Opening the furnace, he ascended the hall and said: "This matter is inherently possessed by every person; why need one seek it elsewhere? At every turn one is crowned by the blue sky;
at every step one treads upon solid ground. This mountain monk does not speak falsely, yet for the time being, there is no principle [to be grasped]."
These are the two points. Thus, Layman Pang said: "Spiritual powers and wondrous functions are simply carrying water and hauling firewood.
If you can penetrate this thoroughly, the task of your lifelong study will be complete. If this is not yet the case, straighten your spine upon the long meditation couch;
do not nod off to sleep. Shake off your lethargy and simply observe the wearing of clothes and the eating of food, the carrying of water and the hauling of firewood.

What, ultimately, is this? Examine! The Buddha ascends the path; entering the hall for the sermon: For ten years I have resided within this forest monastery; Fortunately, this morning the Way of the Buddha is fulfilled.
Rivers, mountains, clouds, and moon are all matters of indifference; I seek only the golden-scaled fish to ascend the straight line.
Since the passing of my late master, I have been moved by the melancholy of rise and fall. This unworthy one exposes the family’s shame, yet strives to raise up the broken sandalwood staff.

The Basin. To repair what is damaged and supplement what is broken in the house, one must first find the right person. At the moment of the simultaneous "sucking" and "pecking," there appears to be a cause from three lifetimes.
Now, I wish to transmit the household utensils; let humans and devas bear witness to this oath. I release three arrows, which together shall strike a flock of birds.
Thereupon, he summoned Tao Ran, Yongchu, Langxu, and the other three, saying: "The pivotal mechanisms of the patriarchs and sages..."
Sharing the same marketplace, a single path of circular light; ten thousand spirits follow the same track. [The Master] lets out a shout and says:
"Tell me, does this enter into that number? A bright full moon hangs by the cliff’s edge; a few fragments of lingering clouds dangle from the mountain peak.
[He] strikes the meditation seat once and descends.

Chan Master Shuguang, the Dharma heir of Daye, was a native of Qishui. He entered the highest peak of Mount Emei to seclude himself from the world, remaining there for over twenty years without descending the mountain.
One day, wishing to descend, he struck the drum and ascended the hall; when his ninety-day retreat concluded, he skillfully manifested [his departure].
Hiding one's clumsiness; day and night, with earnest diligence, one hides skill within clumsiness. One raises and tames a water buffalo whose horns are towering and rare in this world.
Today it strides freely, leaving its tracks upon the moss; it makes the old fellow Huang laugh to scorn on the level fields. The form that departs from the world is fundamentally formless;
even to speak of it is to have no speech. All the people in the great earth find it difficult to grasp; for seventy-nine years he has dwelt here.
"Saha. With a snap of his fingers, the passage of time was like awakening from a dream; with a single step, he kicked over Mount Emei.
"This side and that side are both one and the same. He let out a shout, cast aside his brush, and passed away.
Hanzhu Ming Chan Master of Huiling Temple in Shihong, a dharma heir of Erdu Tai, was the son of the Zeng family of Luzhou. He received the dharma from Erdu Tai.
Entering the hall, he ascended the seat and said: "After the rain, the moss is pure; when ascending the hall to preach the Dharma, who can understand this condition? The birds cry..."
Placing the Flower Branches. Small Assembly. The first beat of the poison-smeared drum; the third strike of the bell that falls to the ground.
A phrase that overcomes the enemy and transcends the crowd—a live snake finally transformed into a dragon. *Duḥ!* (A sharp exclamation).
Chan Master Chunbei De was the son of the Li family of Fengdu.

Fakongzheng (Fa-k'ung-cheng), a Dharma heir of Chan Master Suerui (Su-erh-p'ei), was the son of the Liu family from Ningxia in Shaanxi. At the age of seven, he paid his respects to Chan Master Shunhe (Shun-ho) and received the tonsure.

when the gates of the multi-storied pavilion opened, the great capacity was finally contained within the oceanic treasury.

The hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings and immeasurable Dharma-gates are all, in their entirety, manifested before one upon the tip of a single hair. Each and every one is nothing other than a manifestation of enjoyment. Great!

If this is not yet the case, we cannot help but provide a circuitous lead and auxiliary support. He brushes his sleeves once and says: "Seven years."
Departing from the Master, he roamed upon the sea; returning, the season was precisely autumn. By the hedge, chrysanthemums revealed the phrases of the Three Mysteries;

the fragrance of cassia buds floated with a subtlety beyond the mundane. Lion Peak is like a painting; one’s gaze lingers upon this magnificent scenery. Within the pool of clear water, the dragon exerts its power;
it has seized the clouds and mists to fill its sleeves. *Heh!* (A shout).
Siddeng Yin was the dharma heir of Chan Master Yinnan Guang.
He was the son of the Shen family of Jinchuan. At the age of twenty, he paid his respects to Master Siddeng to receive the tonsure.

He attended him for three years at the mountain retreat, by which time his realization had grown increasingly profound. When Siddeng emerged from retreat, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). After a long period, he obtained certification of his attainment. Siddeng then entered...

After his period of meditative stillness, he traveled extensively throughout various regions. He then returned to the pagoda of Master Shou at Xingguo Temple, where he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.
One day, the Great Being Li Mei of Zhongyan and the Layman Tongde invited him to ascend the hall and offer a formal sermon, presenting him with Dharma robes.
At the summit of Mount Dayu, it was once held up but could not be lifted. Layman Deshan brought it forth on his entire tray.

Chan-practitioner Muyue accepted it directly in person. This is truly what is meant by: "That which is equal in food is also equal in the Dharma. Furthermore, regarding the phrase for praising the meal, how would you say it?
Leaning on his staff, he said: "The land of Wu ends at the river; beyond the bank, the mountains of Yue abound."

He again addressed the assembly, saying: "It is by the grace of my elder brother, the Venerable Master Limei of Zhongyan, who has opened the gate of expedient means and revealed the true aspect, universally gathering in humans and devas so that each may possess their own inherent nature.
This present occasion surpasses even the first stage of Sudhana’s journey;
without traversing the mists and waters, one ascends Maitreya’s pavilion. Without relying on cultivation or realization, one shall next fill a seat among the thousand Buddhas."
Do you understand thoroughly? "The embroidered mandarin ducks are displayed for you to behold; the golden needle is not handed over to others.
This is the successor of Shexiang Ne, the thirty-ninth generation under Dajian.
Chan Master Yuan Tong Da Lang Xizhi was the son of the Yang family of Yucheng. Having received formal certification (*yinke*), he resided at Huxi Temple in Sanyingsi.

Beyond the necessities of sleep and food, he wove *kauśeya* silk to bestow upon those who came from the four quarters. While residing at Yuantong, when his dharma robes were brought forth for the morning assembly, he held up the robe and said:
For over twenty years I have studied this state of being a fool; Unexpectedly, calamity has come upon me. Grievances sink to the bottom of the sea, forming layer upon layer of knots;
On this day, neither humans nor devas can push them open. Residing at Longzang Temple in Xinfan, he ascended the hall and said:
"Today is the first day of the seventh month. Monks, seek the core essence! The summer heat has not yet faded, And the autumn scenery already presses in. When one arrives home, for oneself..."

"By the way, there was much exertion on the journey. With a single sweep of his whisk, he looked left and right and said, "Setting aside for a moment what happened on the road, how would you say it when you arrive home?
"The one who is the lord of the myriad phenomena does not wither along with the four seasons. Upon concluding the retreat, he ascended the hall.
Opening the barriers and releasing the locks, he let loose the herd of oxen. Since they are no longer bound, let them roam at ease. This is it; take heed!
Avoid touching east or west; do not offend the sprouts of the crops. *Ei!* Next year there will be new branches once more;
one blast of the iron flute calls them back. Evening discourse. Jingqing has six "scrapings. Monks fear the slippery path.
If you wish for the two to correspond, the deep awl must prick with pain. A secretary asked, "What is 'scraping the dust off the fur'? The Master said, "The wind blows."
"Grass bends down. [The student asked: "What is 'scraping the hair from the skin'? The Master said, "A red blade and a branding iron. [The student asked: "What is 'scraping the skin from the flesh'?

The Master said, "Pouring boiling water over snow. [The student asked: "What is 'scraping the flesh from the bone'? The Master said, "Ding the butcher dismembering an ox. [The student] said, "As for the marrow, how would you scrape that?
The Master said, "Casting off the hand, one arrives home; yet people do not recognize it, and instead harbor resentment."

His feet were thin and his straw sandals wide. On the evening of the first day of the tenth month in the year Jisi (1489), seeing that the grass before the Dharma Hall was overgrown, he used a hoe to clear it away.
Suddenly, setting down the hoe, he said, "In a future life, you must do some more. Having finished, he entered the Abbot’s quarters.

The next morning, when an attendant hurried in, the Master had already passed away while seated. Tears flowed from both eyes, and his countenance remained as if alive. He was thirty-three years of age at his death.
He lived to the age of seventy-four. His stupa was erected at his native mountain.
Zu Bi was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Cangxi Yue of Baoning; he was the son of the Li family of Cangxi. Having lost both parents in his youth, he saw a verse on the wall.
He remarked, "If this body does not attain liberation in this life, toward what other birth shall I turn to liberate it?

From these words, he conceived a resolve to transcend the mundane world, yet he found no freedom. He encountered an elder master and requested instruction, who directed him to investigate the koan of the "Pine Tree.
Finding no point of entry, he vowed to leave the dust of the world behind. Hearing that Master Yuechang was expounding the Dharma, he went to attend upon him for three years. One day, he heard...
Upon hearing the sound of the drum, he attained realization. He received formal certification (in-ka) from Master Zu Bi while serving as the head seat (zuòyuán).

He resided at Tiānwáng Temple in the Jùqìng Prefecture of Dīnnán. On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall and said: "The primary truth (prathamārtha-satya): before the World-Honored One left Tuṣita Heaven, it was already proclaimed.
Before the old monks of the world emerged from their abbot’s quarters, it was already proclaimed. Before Venerable Yuè picked up [the whisk]..."
The staff! The proclamation is finished. If you wait until he ascends the curved wooden platform, it will already be two or three steps behind.
To further require this mountain monk to chatter on would be even more irrelevant. Nevertheless, the nature of these immeasurable great men is pungent;
they fill a ladle to the brim and pour it over Siddhārtha, pointing at heaven and earth while vainly claiming supremacy—only to be caught by Yunmen.
"I wish to strike him dead. I wonder, among this assembly, is there anyone who does not feel resentment? After a long silence, he held his staff horizontally across his chest and said:
"The green mountains only love to grind through antiquity and the present; the clear waters have never washed away right and wrong."
Chunbei De was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Fachuang Yuan; he was the son of the Song family from Wan County in eastern Shu.

Having received the Dharma from Master Chunbei De, he resided at Huangling Chan Monastery in Yiling Prefecture. He spoke these words of Dharma to the practitioner Anshi Hui, saying: "Since ancient times..."

If a person draws near to a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and applies themselves with diligent effort and austerity—neglecting sleep and forgetting to eat—they will surely investigate and clarify the matter within the seam of their robes until they penetrate it from top to bottom. Thus, they will emerge from the cage and leave the nest;
free and unencumbered, they will casually utter a word or display a device that shakes the earth and startles heaven, serving as a standard for a thousand or ten thousand generations.
I shall not, for now, fail in my resolve to study the Dharma.
Farewell. *Jinjiang Chandelu*, Scroll Fifteen (End). Postscript.
To begin with, that which is truly eternal has no form from the start and is fundamentally beyond comparison. When released, the myriad practices are perfected;

when withdrawn, the thousand mechanisms are stilled and eliminated. Bodhi, Nirvana, True Suchness, and Buddha-nature—the diamond circle and the thorny chestnut, the banner of radiance and the lamp of the sun and moon—all these various distinct realms flow forth from within this and fill it completely, manifesting by attaching themselves to things.

It is named "Difficult to Transcend," for its innermost depths are hard to penetrate. Nevertheless, by relying on heaven, one attains loftiness; by relying on earth, one attains tranquility; by relying on the sun and moon, they alternate in their illumination.
Although it is said that all things are impartially reflected therein, it still cannot completely dispel the darkness of the dim path.

By relying on the lamp, however, one can shatter the gloom of a thousand-year-old chamber. To speak of its essence, it is solitary brilliance shining alone; to speak of its function, it is a continuous flame linking radiance. This is what is meant by "the profound..."

All these are clarifications, yet this clarity is ultimately inexhaustible. This book is not called a *Chan Lu* (Record of Chan), but is titled *Chan Deng* (Lamp of Chan) so that it may be transmitted without end.
Is this not the lamp of the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' life-force of wisdom?

From the World-Honored One holding up the flower and Kāśyapa’s smile, down to the severing of the arm to find peace of mind, and the realization that "the bright mirror is not a stand; defilement cannot stain it," it is "this very mind."

The Buddha gave a single shout that deafened the ears, manifesting the great function of his spiritual capacity. Under his ribs, he returned the fist, planting the Banner of Radiant Light amidst it like a net of precious threads;
thus, light interlaced with light, universally encompassing the entire realm. This was our Original Teacher, Master Chang.
Since first receiving the mind-seal from the venerable master Shuanggui, he has sat in the seat of enlightenment seven times to propagate the fundamental tenets.
Finally returning to Sichuan, the Regional Commander Zhang Kunyu, together with his current officials and subordinates, requested that he reopen the ancestral monastery of Yuanwu.

For over thirty years, in the intervals between responding to sentient beings and engaging with the world, I have gathered fragmentary writings and broken scrolls from amidst the ashes of the kalpa, collecting the essential teachings of various masters and compiling them into a single work titled *The Zen Lamp of the Jinjiang*. This was done in the autumn of the Guiyou year.
He commanded Chengsheng to carry bundles of straw down to the east. At Lengyan, he used jujube wood for his hearth.

Taking the masters of past and present as his companions, from within the essence of true permanence, he verified and clarified the great matter of cause and condition. Together they unfurled a single banner of radiant light and linked together a single lamp of inexhaustible illumination.
Although it is said that the time since the Sage departed is remote, the assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly undispersed even now. Thus...
This is my teacher’s painstaking effort to preserve the Dharma. He lamented that the distant past lacked verifiable evidence and waited for the transmission to have its own source.
