which includes the Biographies of Eminent Monks and Divine Monks, compiled by Zhāojié Zhàngxuě, the Śramaṇa Tōngzuì.
Compiled by Chesheng Zhulang of Qingcheng, edited by Hushengyou of Huanchan, Shaoxing;
based on the *Daoyin* by the son of the Marquis of Puyang.
He was endowed with a blessed nature and dwelt in a state of profound integrity. Possessing inner brilliance and expansive wisdom, he reached the pinnacle of refinement in his mature years.

His collected works are most extraordinary. From the time he was a mere child with hair like fine silk, his exceptional appearance flourished uniquely. His observance of filial piety and love, and his character of compassionate obedience, were fully realized therein.
At the tender age of seven, he encountered the sorrow of his mother’s passing; he abstained from grains and cut off all liquid food, nearly extinguishing his human nature.

Once he reached adulthood, his virtuous conduct earned him praise throughout the local districts. After completing the mourning period, he resolved to repay his boundless debt of gratitude, and his aspiration to leave the household life became known to others.
He did not move from there, but instead went to Lingyan Temple to seek a teacher for his tonsure. He devoted himself to recitation and study;

before even ten days had passed, he had mastered two fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The entire assembly was struck with amazement and called him a divine child (*śiṣya-kumāra*); eminent elders and renowned scholars alike sighed in admiration.

He immediately began studying the Vinaya. Furthermore, regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha* transmitted by Dharma Master Song at Pengcheng, he subsequently organized it into sections and chapters according to the rules and precepts.
He required that young śramaṇas first practice the Vinaya, and only those who were proficient in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* were permitted to enter and listen to his lectures.
Although the Master’s years of ordination were few, his practice and conduct were so eminent that he alone was preeminent among the assembly and held in high esteem.

Whenever he expounded the *Śatyaśāstra*, his mastery of its principles was profound. Later, he withdrew to Mount Tai for four autumns. Thereupon, taking up his staff, he emerged from the mountains and traveled alone toward the west;
eventually returning to Shu, he resided at Duobao Temple. When both the monastic and lay communities heard of his reputation for the Way, they requested him to open [the school].
While the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* were being lectured upon, there was the Dharma Master Baoxian, a native of Donghai.

His cultivation and learning were comprehensive and extensive, and he was particularly proficient in the Mahāyāna. Having long been renowned during the Sui dynasty, Master Xian remained composed amidst such fame; yet the more one looked up to him, the more lofty he appeared.
Whenever he arrived at the Master’s lecture hall, he would solemnly alter his demeanor. The Master raised his voice and deployed his eloquence, exhausting the subtle and reaching the profound.
Duke of Deng, Dou Jin, Generalissimo of Yizhou; Duke of Zanguo, Dou Gui, Vice Director of the Administration Commission; Duke of Sheng, Gao Shilian, Chief Secretary;

and Lu Chengqing, Duke of Fan yang, along with former and current chief officials and governors of the southwestern region—all men of national renown and court excellence, possessing great prestige and high rank—united in their illustrious reputation, together expressed their reverent admiration. [They] submitted this letter of thanks.
After his ordination, he went to the mountain temple of Pengmen, which had previously been destroyed and whose courtyards were in a state of decay.
The Master lamented this and undertook its restoration; before two years had passed, it had flourished as a magnificent garden of enlightenment.

Furthermore, reflecting that the subtle words of the ninefold canon—the very standard upon which the three realms rely—were in danger of being lost and hidden away within the Dragon Palace, he subsequently carved the secret volumes of the *Tāla* palm-leaf manuscripts onto the northern cliffs of the temple.

they shall endure as long as the kalpa itself. Thereupon, the pure principles were widely propagated and the lofty achievements were far-illuminated.

There, he assisted Master Xuanzang in translating scriptures, collating the Sanskrit manuscripts, and serving as a verifier of the meaning. Whenever there were difficult passages, they deliberated upon them together.
The Dharma Master Kai, the presiding master of Huiji Temple, was keen-witted, refined, and erudite; his reputation resounded throughout Hongdu.

He was the first to establish a Dharma assembly and requested that the profound mysteries be expounded. Monastics and laypeople from the imperial capital all came to seek instruction, looking upon one another with joy as they gained insights never heard before.
The Master investigated the subtle points of historical records and was especially fond of the *Laozi* and *Zhuangzi*. He savoring their essence and imbued himself with their richness;

he encompassed the four beginnings within his rhythmic style and synthesized the five musical notes within his literary compositions. Consequently, his lectures and expositions were comprehensive, penetrating both internal and external domains.

His specialized studies included the *Nirvāṇa*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Laṅkāvatāra* Sūtras, as well as the *Daśabhūmika* and *Bodhisattvabhūmi* Śāstras.

Tanzhi [studied] treatises such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, as well as the Vinaya of the Four Divisions (*Caturvarga-vinaya*).
Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he had already composed commentaries upon them; thus, his essential tasks were complete.

Jingmai was a native of Zitrong. In his youth, he was modest and self-restrained; as he grew older, his aspirations and conduct became lofty. He specialized in the rigorous investigation of the sutras and śāstras, penetrating their most subtle depths.
By nature, he was grave and steadfast, never engaging in frivolous associations. He always chose his destinations with care when traveling. During the Zhenguan era, he arrived at the capital region.

The Master was selected among the elite and resided at Ci'en Temple. Together with Xuanming, Jue, Bianji, and Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain, he held the pen to compose the texts.
He translated the *Benshi jing* (Sutra of Past Deeds) in seven fascicles; later, the Master, along with Shenfang, received the oral transmission for the transcription.

At both the Yu-hua Palace and the Sutra Translation Hall of Ci-en Monastery, he was universally esteemed for his adaptability and mastery of circumstances; thus, he attained a profound understanding of the scriptures.
Later, he composed the *Yi-jing tu-ji* (Record of the Catalogue of Translated Scriptures) in four fascicles.

This work systematically categorizes the titles of scriptures from ancient and modern times, the ranks and positions of the translators, those translated singly versus those retranslated, and those of doubtful or spurious origin—all arranged with meticulous order. The Way of the Teacher is like the gathering of fish and dragons in a deep pool.

On the tenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, at Ānguó Temple, he sat cross-legged and passed away with a serene countenance. His stupa was erected to the left of the stupa of Buddhāpālita and to the right of the tomb of Empress Níwá.
The epitaph for the stupa was composed by the Inner Attendant, Grand Marshal, and native of Tiānshuī, Zhào Sīkǎn, who commissioned his disciple Shàn... [to inscribe it].
The stele was erected at the site of the stupa. He lived to the age of fifty-six and had thirty-six years of monastic seniority.

Shenhui was originally a son of the Shi clan from the Western Regions; his grandfather had moved the family residence to Fengxiang in Qizhou. The Master possessed an innate nature of profound understanding, and his brilliant wisdom emerged from within.
Like a great block of jade, he did not polish his brilliance, so those of his time did not yet know him. It was only at the age of thirty that he entered Shu.

He visited the Great Master Wuxiang, who possessed sharp faculties and attained sudden enlightenment, entering into a profound resonance with the Mind-Seal (*citta-mudrā*). Wuxiang sighed in admiration, saying, "The Way of my school rests with you.

Thereafter, his virtue was full and his wisdom vast; he flourished as a patriarch of the Chan school. Through still illumination, he extinguished objective realms and transcended to realize the state beyond thought.

He realized that the mind itself is Buddha and saw no separate body. When he remained in a state of profound stillness, his physical form was like wood or earth; yet when it came to his wondrous functioning...

Muzhi. Like the movement of clouds and the falling of rain, the simple folk were transformed by his influence; beholding his countenance, they turned toward goodness, and hearing his words, they reformed their errors.
As for those whose minds were clouded or fettered, he cleared and purified them, leading those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities to enter the Way according to their respective portions.
On the twelfth day of the eleventh month in the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he manifested illness and passed away while sitting upright in the lotus posture at the age of seventy.
Fifteen: At thirty-six years of Dharma seniority, the śramaṇa Nadi attained the Way of his teacher and transmitted it to future generations.
At that time, Wei Gao, Prince of Nan’gang, took refuge in the Master and received the essentials of his Chan teachings. He erected a stele for him, composing both the text and calligraphy himself.
The Chan school esteemed this highly.
A native of Nanyin, surnamed Zhang, he possessed a nature of clear awakening and attained the profound essence of Caoxi.

Lacking any means of verification, he met Chan Master Shenhui of Jingzhong Temple, whereupon his mind finally reached accord with the truth. This is what is meant by "the brocade of a finished pattern, washed to increase its beauty."
Like a dragon holding a torch that travels to dispel the darkness, the Master then departed the gorges to travel extensively for study.

From Jiangling, he entered Shu, where, on the banks of the Southern River in Shu, he cleared the weeds and tied up a thatched hut. The multitude all turned to him with devotion and reverence; gradually, he established a Buddhist monastery. This was at the beginning of the Zhenyuan era.
Later, when Gao Si-kong Chongwen pacified Liu Pi, he changed the name of this temple to Shèngshòu (Holy Longevity). Originally, it was named Bǎoyìng (Precious Response).

When the Master’s period of transformative influence was nearing its end, he manifested his passing and entered *nirvāṇa* at the beginning of the Chángqìng era. A stupa was constructed and he was interred to the right of the temple.

During the Huìchāng era, the stupa was destroyed. During the Dàzhōng era, [the temple] was restored on the old site of Bǎoyìng across the north bank of the river, and the temple was rebuilt under its original name.
As for the Holy Life: the Master had a disciple named Yifan, who revived the Chan teachings.

There was a son of the Feng family from Zitrong in Dongchuan; when he reached the age of study, he went to Fugan Temple in Chengdu to serve the Bodhisattva Dinglan, who was none other than the Master Xuanzong.
One day, the Emperor wrote upon the boy’s robe with a brush, saying: "This child..."

"You have a karmic affinity with me; it is because of this that you shall receive my name. In the ninth year of the Dazhong era, when Bai Gong Minzhong was appointed as the regional governor of Yibu, he invited the Master to establish a *śīla*-platform at Jingzhong Temple.
Responding to this summons, the Master traveled to the capital to lecture and transmit the Sutras and Vinaya.

After five years since his full ordination, he traveled throughout the realm and visited Chan Master Shenzhao of Xiaoma, where he attained awakening and realized the essential principle. Thereafter, he resided at...
He spent several summers at Mount Hua in Chuzhou and subsequently traveled to Mount Wuyi. At that time, the Provincial Inspector Li Hui constructed a meditation hall for him.

In the third year of the Qianfu era, he went to Daisai Mountain in Longquan, Jin’yun, where he established a monastery; he then submitted a petition to the Ministry of Sacrifices to request an official plaque.

His title was Long’an. He resided there for eighteen years, after which he moved to Lianyun Yuan. The Prefect, Lu Yue, invited him to the separate cloister of Kaiyuan Temple in the prefectural seat, where he was provided with the four requisites.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the Dingmao year of the Tianyou era, he manifested illness and passed away at his residence.

His age at death was seventy-three, and his years since ordination were fifty-two. By the imperial decree of Emperor Xuanzong, he was entrusted to the regional administration for funeral arrangements.
Yang Xi, the Minister of Works, presided over the funeral rites. The cremation took place in the southern garden of the monastery. Several hundred grains of śarīra were collected;

subsequently, forty-nine grains, along with a jar of remains, were enshrined in a stone stūpa. In the third year of the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty, the year of Yisi (945 CE), Vinaya Master Wentai composed the inscription for the stūpa.
Jiànyuán was a man of unknown origins. His conduct was consistently refined and clear, and he encompassed the path of the Vinaya. As a model for the bhikṣus, his upright form cast a straight shadow.
Later, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, which became known as the "Superior Assembly. He provided food daily for a thousand people;

the rice and millet were always overflowing in the granaries and storehouses, never being exhausted even as they were drawn from them. From summer through autumn, there was never a time of scarcity. Such was the nature of his mysterious spiritual resonance.

That mountain monastery was frequently the site of miraculous responses. Once, Chan Master Huiguan saw more than three hundred monks carrying lotus lamps, ascending into the air and departing like falling stars as they passed by.
During the Kaiyuan era, Duke Cui Ning of Ji suspected this was sorcery and delusion;
he personally entered the mountain and prohibited the lighting of fires within a thirty-li radius in all four directions. When the third night arrived...
More than a hundred lamp-stands appeared, accompanied by a crimson light extending for a thousand feet. Lord Ji suddenly prostrated himself in worship, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, a golden hand emerged from among the pines, measuring approximately six or seven feet in length; two bodhisattvas of yellow and white hues flickered within it.
Furthermore, on the tips of the cypress trees in front of the courtyard, a single lamp appeared during the day, its brilliance like the sun, spreading horizontally across the sky.
About three *li* from Boli Mountain, there was a precious pearl approximately one *zhang* in diameter, brilliant and lovely to behold.
From the western ridge, a great rainbow bridge suspended itself; upon the bridge, Buddhist monks—both old and young—emerged at intervals. Two torches blazed brilliantly in the sky.
They appeared as if welcoming and seeing off one another. Below were four bodhisattvas, standing in pairs, both emitting bodily radiance six or seven *zhang* high.

Furthermore, within the pine forest ahead, a Buddhist temple suddenly appeared; on its lintel were inscribed the two characters "Three Studies" (*sanzhē*) in seal script, from which hung two embroidered ribbons.
Between the eastern groves, a golden mountain emerged at night, and when the moon was at its zenith, two lamps—one of gold and one of silver—appeared.
It was erected beside the tomb of Dharma Master Zhixuan. Whenever the third month arrived, Wei Nanjiang Gao would go to the temple to perform a great vegetarian feast for three hundred bodhisattvas.
The bodhisattvas would manifest their forms, holding lamps and incense, and lead the way as he offered them by inserting them into the incense burner at the mountain gate.
Both Bai and Zhongmin witnessed these auspicious omens. Consequently, they restored this temple. In the eighth year of the Dazhong era, its name was changed to Kaizhao.
Master Yuan’s spiritual influence was as potent as the land itself; his disciples transmitted his lectures, and he remained the preeminent authority in Dongchuan.
Zhixuan, whose courtesy name was Houjue, was the son of the Chen family of Hongya in Jiazhou. His great-grandfather, Tu Nan, served as the Magistrate of Shehong County in Zizhou.

His mother, Lady Wei, dreamed that the moon entered her womb, and he was born as a result. While being nursed, whenever he saw images of Buddhas or the forms of monks, his face would invariably brighten with joy.
At the age of five, when his grandfather commanded him to compose a poem on flowers, he immediately said: "Flowers bloom in full redness upon every tree."
"Flowers have fallen from ten thousand branches, leaving but a single one remaining. Tomorrow it will surely be carried away by the wind.

The Patriarch sighed in lamentation and said, "I raised this grandson, hoping he would pass the imperial examinations to wipe away the shame of two generations. Now I see the boy's resolve; he is not one who will 'bequeath his legacy' to his descendants.
He will certainly follow the Empty Gate (the Buddhist path), which will go against my expectations. At the age of seven, he indeed encountered Fatai and Fashi.
The Master was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Ningyi Temple. His residence was adjacent to the temple, so he would go daily to the lecture hall;

upon hearing the Dharma discourse once, it was as if he beheld his past causes. That evening, he dreamed that the Buddha stroked his head with his hand. Upon waking, he informed his grandfather and requested permission to leave the household life.
His relatives observed his resolve and realized it could not be diverted, so they granted him their consent. At the age of eleven, he shaved his hair and became a novice.

Following his master, he went to Sian Temple in Tangxing County, where he was granted the *Mahāvaipulya* Sūtra in forty-two fascicles, Master Huiyuan’s commentaries, and Master Biankong’s exposition on the Perfect Meaning;
together they comprised one million two hundred and fifty thousand words, all of which encompassed the most profound mysteries.

At the age of thirteen, he already surpassed his fellow monastics with his gestures and speech, manifesting the air of a mature elder. At that time, Prime Minister Du Gong Yuan-ying was stationed there as a regional commander.
In Western Shu, having heard the Master’s reputation, [the authorities] ordered him to ascend the hall at the Puxian Pavilion of Daci Temple to preach and discourse.
Both the monastic and lay communities numbered in the tens of thousands daily; they listened with focused attention and devoted hearts, their expressions of awe and admiration never ceasing.

From this time on, the people of Shu no longer addressed him by his given name, but called him "Chan Bodhisattva" instead. According to tradition, the Master’s previous incarnation was named Zhixuan of Sanxue Mountain in Hanzhou.
He lectured on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, which moved the earth to transform into lapis lazuli. He received full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the Vinaya Master Bianzhen at Jingzhong Temple;
as soon as he had heard the *Vinaya*, he subsequently mastered the *Abhidharmakośa*. Thus, he inherited the lineage of transmission from Vinaya Master Shangu of Changshan.

Furthermore, following his preceptor, he descended the Three Gorges, traveled through Jingzhou and Xiangyang, and reached Zisheng Temple in the Imperial Capital. There, he became a leader among the three studies throughout the four seas.

This was a place where people from all quarters gathered. As the Master expounded upon the sutras and śāstras, monks and laypeople looked up to him in admiration; the shoes outside his door were piled up daily in dense rows.
When Emperor Wenzong heard of this, he summoned him to the palace for an audience and consultation, finding him highly satisfactory.

Furthermore, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* under Dharma Master Xìn of Ān-guó, and also researched secular classics and literature, such that there was no discourse among the hundred schools of thought with which he was not proficient.
He was not well-versed in the comprehensive [scriptures]. The Master often lamented that his native accent was unfit for lecturing and expounding.

Consequently, while reciting the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraḥ* at Mount Xiang’er, he dreamed of a divine monk who cut off his tongue and replaced it with another. The next day, his speech suddenly transformed into the Qin dialect.

There was a man named Yang Maoxiao, a great scholar, who sought to investigate the Inner Canon under the Master; he even aspired to emulate Xie Lingyun by composing a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. He produced many...

Whenever he took up a volume to resolve doubts, [the Master] would analyze and judge them accordingly. He sent a letter stating: "In these present times, who among the 'dragon and elephant' masters within the realm is other than you?
Furthermore, Yang Rusi of the Ministry of Justice, Yuan Zai of the Left Vice-Minister, and Yang Rusi of Chang’an all visited his door, intending to join the Lotus Society.
Once, while the Master was sitting in meditation, he saw Mao Xiao wearing purple robes and a green crown, appearing three times.
When the rites were concluded, he ascended into the air and departed. Xuán had someone keep watch over Mào Xiào. That evening, he instructed his son, saying:
"I have long wished to shave my head and don the black robes, drawing water with a pitcher and carrying my sandals to serve Master Xuán. What has hindered me is this official cap and sash.
When I am laid to rest, entomb me in a purple *kāṣāya* and a green lotus-flower crown. It was only now that his prior vision was verified. (Wǔ)
The Emperor ruled the realm. Initially, he held the teachings of Śākyamuni in high esteem; later, however, he accepted the counsel of those who were deluded by demonic influences.

He sought to offer sacrifices to Mount Penglai and constructed a lofty terrace to pray for spiritual transcendence. Although the censors submitted remonstrances and the ministers repeatedly spoke out, the Emperor’s resolve ultimately could not be turned back.

On the occasion of the Dayang Festival (Qingming), the clergy and the Daoists assembled at Linqide Hall. The Emperor alone summoned the Master to debate with a representative of the Daoist school, asking:

"Can the state of transcendence be attained through cultivation, or not? The Emperor folded his hands and cited the principle from the Laozi regarding the governance of a great state being like cooking small fish.

He engaged in a dialogue with the Daoist priest on this point. The Master set forth that the root of a sovereign’s governance lies in the teachings of transformation; he then spoke of the Transcendents.

This art is a lofty pursuit monopolized by solitary commoners dwelling among the mountains and forests; furthermore, it necessarily relies upon past causes (*pūrvakṛta-hetu*) and is therefore unsuitable for a sovereign.
His eloquence flowed like a river from its source and surged like the ocean, totaling several thousand words, such that those who heard it were struck with trembling.
This greatly offended the Emperor’s will, and none among his attendants failed to show dejection on their faces. The Left Protector-General, Qiu Shiliang, [intervened].
Yang Qin-yi, the Inner Grand Councilor, admired his talent and eloquence but feared he might soon face dismissal. He thus secretly urged him to compose a poem praising the Emperor.
Master [Hanshan] composed five stanzas on the spot; the final stanza read: "Birth in heaven arises from the karma of heaven;
One need not seek immortality to attain it. The crane’s back is precarious and the dragon’s spine is slippery; May Your Majesty remain for another thousand years."
Upon reading the poem, the Emperor gained a slight understanding. Although the Emperor did not accept his loyal admonitions, he praised his insight and eloquence.

The Master then returned to his old mountain in Ba and Min. He continued to provide himself with towels and combs as usual, yet his observance of the precepts became even more refined and clear. He then set out on a small boat toward the regions of Lake Xiang.
At that time, Yang Han-gong, the Imperial Secretary for Remuneration, was serving as the Inspector of Guilin and invited him to stay at Kaiyuan Temple.

The temple belonged to the reign of Emperor Xuanzong’s ascension to the throne. Lord Yang, having risen from the position of Inner Chancellery to command the Left Guard Army, deemed his merit in establishing the imperial decree to be great and requested the restoration of the Indian (Tianzhu) teachings.
He submitted a memorial seeking to trace the master’s reputation and whereabouts. The Master again donned his tattered robes and returned to Baoying Temple in the capital.

On the occasion of the Shouchang Festival, he lectured and offered praises; the Emperor bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* and appointed him as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) of the Three Teachings. The Emperor—
He established the Faqian Monastery using his former residence as the site. By imperial decree, the Master was appointed to reside in the Yuxu Pavilion of the monastery.

On the birthday of the Emperor in the third year of the Dazhong era, the Emperor summoned Counselor-in-Attendance Li Yisun and Palace Attendant Yang Han-gong; monks and nuns were assembled in great numbers to debate the Dharma, which greatly pleased the Emperor’s heart.

Consequently, he petitioned that all abandoned monasteries throughout the realm be rebuilt by imperial edict, leading to the grand restoration of Buddhist shrines, for which the Master exerted great effort.
He ordered a court painter to depict his likeness within the palace; such was the esteem in which he was held.
He was a close friend of the Chancellor, Lord Pei Xiu, and together they vigorously promoted the restoration of Buddhism, extensively carrying out works of benefit and salvation.

In the spring of the second year of Guangming, Emperor Xizong fled the chaos for Western Shu. Later, he dispatched Guo Zuntao bearing an imperial edict, and [the Master] traveled by palanquin to the temporary capital. The Emperor received him...

In their discussions, he demonstrated a profound understanding of the higher mind. Tian Lingzi, the Commander of the Left Army, along with various high-ranking officials, sought his counsel with great diligence and respect.
The Emperor, wishing to honor his excellence, ordered the various scholars to compose a title for him, but none satisfied His Majesty’s wishes. Thereupon, the Emperor took up his own brush and wrote:
"I have received from the Master the instruction on the principles of 'opening, showing, awakening, and entering' regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*. To awaken is to perceive; it is clarity. To awaken..."

He attained the Great Way and awakened to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. It is further said that awakening occurs in a single kṣaṇa, while non-awakening lasts for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, awakening is the realization of the meaning of attaining Buddhahood through the True Vehicle (Saddharmayāna). I now bestow upon you the title "National Teacher Wudada" to express my intent.
The Master declined the honor repeatedly but was unsuccessful; he then requested to return to his former residence at Jiulong.
The Great Master Wuxiang was the third son of the King of Silla. He shaved his head and received the full precepts at Gunnam Temple in his native country.
In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he crossed the Eastern Ocean and arrived in China. Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang summoned him for an audience.
He was attached to Chanding Monastery. Later, he entered Zizhong in Shu to visit Master Chan Master Zhishi.

There was an extraordinary man named Chuji who had once been summoned to the palace by Empress Wu Zetian; she bestowed upon him a nine-panel *mona* robe. He possessed the power to know future events with absolute certainty and without error.
Before the Master arrived, Chuji said, "A guest from outside will come to meet me tomorrow. On that very day, the Master arrived.
Master Ji asked, "What is your name? The Master replied, "Formless. That night, he bestowed the *maṇava* robe upon him.
The Master then entered deep mountain ravines and rocky gorges to practice *dhyāna*. There were two black calves whose horns were locked together; they pressed close to his body with great urgency.

They thrust their hairy hooves into his sleeves, their coldness like ice. When they reached his abdomen and pawed at it, the Master remained entirely unmoved as he continued to enter into meditative absorption.
He had intended to stay for five days, but suddenly the snow reached over a zhang in depth. Two fierce beasts came;
the Master washed himself clean and lay naked before them, vowing to offer his body as their food. The two beasts sniffed him from head to foot and then departed.

Having lived in the mountains for some time, his robes were tattered and his hair was long. A hunter, suspecting he might be a strange beast, prepared to shoot him. The Master said, "I am a practitioner..."
He was a man of the Way. The hunter then desisted. Later, he entered cities and towns; by day he stayed among tombs, and by night he sat beneath trees, practicing the dhūta austerities.
People gradually came to hold him in high esteem, and they constructed a vihāra before the cemetery. The Regional Inspector Zhang Qiu Jianqiong both came to pay their respects.
It coincided with the time when Emperor Minghuang fled the capital for Shu; he invited the Master into the inner palace to provide for his needs. At that time, Cheng...

Yang Yi, the Magistrate of the Prefecture and County, suspecting him of being a sorcerer and a deceiver, issued a warrant to have him expelled beyond the borders. He further ordered twenty-odd men to drag him away.
As they drew near to the Master’s person, everyone was seized with trembling. In an instant, a great wind suddenly arose;

sand and stones flew about as the wind rushed directly into the hall, blowing aside the curtains and rolling up the drapes. Yang Yi prostrated himself in submission, and when his repentance was complete, the wind ceased. [The Master] was then escorted back to his former residence.
Consequently, he exhorted donors to construct the Jìngzhòng, Dàcí, Pútí, and Níngguó monasteries, as well as hermitages, bells, and stupas in outlying districts beyond counting.
He initially resided at the main quarters of Jìngzhòng Monastery.

There was a man of great strength there known as Shělì (Abandoning Strength), who felled firewood to supply the monastery kitchen; it was unknown where he came from. One night, he suddenly arrived carrying a sword.
Xie Xi stood hesitating by the side of the meditation seat. He perceived something descending from the wall, whereupon he sprang up and struck once with his sword;
the giant monkey’s body and head were severed upon the ground. He then dragged it away to bury it, smoothing the earth over to erase all traces before departing.
At dawn, the Master summoned Xie Xi to thank him for cutting firewood, but he was already nowhere to be seen. [The Master] once pointed and said:

The cypress tree in front of the stupa said, "When this tree is level with the pagoda, the temple shall be destroyed. When the monastery was abolished during the Huichang era, the tree was indeed exactly the same height as the pagoda.
He also said that there were two small ponds in front of the temple; the one on the left was for soup and the one on the right for rice.

If offerings for the midday meal were insufficient, he would have them dredged and deepened until they were sufficient. His words proved true, and his divine wonders were many such as these. Thus it is said:
In the first year of Zhide, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-seven.
Daijia, the son of Wang Shi from Jinshui County, left the household life while still a youth; he frequently displayed strange and eccentric behavior, and his father gave him the name Daijia.
Toward the end of the Tianbao era, he practiced ascetic discipline with great diligence and styled himself a dhūta. When Emperor Xuanzong went on a tour of inspection, [he encountered him].

Having shaved his hair to become a monk, he cleared a path and cut away the brambles twenty *li* from the county seat to dwell alone among the mountains and marshes; later, a Buddhist monastery was established there.

This mountain contains many sacred traces. Originally named Shicheng Mountain, when Emperor Minghuang reached Jianmen Pass, the mountain deity manifested its form to welcome the imperial carriage and declared its surname to be Li.
By imperial decree, it was granted the title of "Grandson. Later, [the Emperor] ascended Mount Wudan to the east.
From the terrace, he gazed afar and saw auspicious clouds and purple vapors coiling and binding within the realm of space. He asked those around him, "What place is this?
They replied, "It is Mount Shicheng. Thereupon, he realized the intention behind the mountain deity’s protection and guardianship; he subsequently renamed Yunding to Ciyun Temple.
The Master later passed away at this temple.

Huishong left the household life at Fading Temple in Pei County. It was during the Yongping era of the Later Han dynasty that the Buddha-dharma first began to spread to China, and thereupon the Zhide Jing Monastery was established, where divine light frequently manifested.
Reaching the time of the Song dynasty monk Huichi, who departed from Master Huiyuan, his dharma-elder, at Mount Lu, he vowed to convert the regions of Min and Shu.
At that time, Qiao Zong, being unrighteous, ordered several men to take up blades [to kill him].
He intended to slaughter the one who held [the image], but the holder merely snapped his fingers; the multitude was so startled that they fled in panic, falling prostrate.

In the fourth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the temple was renamed Fading Temple. It contained a sacred image of Maitreya. During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a piece of withered wood suddenly arrived, floating down the river.
At night, it emitted a brilliant light. Consequently, a statue head was carved [to house it]. During the Zhenguan era, Dou Gui served as the Regional Inspector (Changshi).
At Jianmen, the light from the Buddha’s head appeared; he led it to the prefectural seat. Although Dou Gong ordered several hundred men to go and retrieve it, they were unable to lift it.
He then ordered a divination to determine whether it could be established at Foding Temple. A single person was able to lift it.

Consequently, Dou fashioned a Buddha image, and the Regional Inspector Gao Shilian erected a hall to house it. Later, a monk named Fan’ai erected a stupa there and obtained a giant crab with two legs remaining after its body had been consumed.
This pagoda has many miraculous occurrences; some people even brought wine and meat [to offer].
Once, while intoxicated, he went before the Buddha; immediately upon seeing him, he perceived a calamity. During the Tianbao era, the Master practiced with even greater austerity at the temple.
Before long, the stupa was struck by a thunderbolt, which uprooted its central pillar and cast it outside. Suddenly, a small piece of wood took its place.
The assembly all marveled at this, unable to fathom the cause. The Master then prostrated himself before the sacred image of Maitreya, appealing to the devas and nāgas for explanation.

"It is only fitting that you feel awe and reverence. Why did you suddenly strike and seize the central pillar of the stupa? Thus we know that when the common woman cried out, thunder struck Lord Jing’s terrace;
there was truly something that moved the spirits. One day, amidst sudden thunder and fierce winds, it shook again just as before.

Upon looking back, it was seen that the dragon deities had returned the old pillar and reinstalled it as it was. At the moment the pillar was being replaced, dark clouds gathered from all sides, and...
Four divine beings supported him with their bodies so that he stood level with the stupa. Such was his power to move things.
Before the destruction of the temple during the Huichang era, seven śarīra relics emerged from atop the *cakra* (the pinnacle of the stupa), and a white light filled the sky, flying westward;

this was witnessed by all throughout Shu. When the stupa was about to collapse, a crimson light appeared in the midst of the heavens. When it was reinstalled, its jujube fruit flourished once again. Thus spoke the Master.
He eventually passed away at the monastery.
Chujì was the son of the Xiū family from Zhōuzhōu in Shǔ. He served as a disciple of Chan Master Bǎoxiū, serving his master with diligence and maintaining few desires.

He did not compete with others and was naturally proficient in the profound and mysterious mysteries. Residing in the northern mountains, he practiced the dhūta austerities. Empress Wǔ heard of his reputation and issued an imperial decree for him to enter the palace, whereupon she bestowed [gifts] upon him.
The monk Mouna Saṃgharakṣita took his leave to return to the mountains. For forty years, he did not set foot in a village;
he remained constantly seated in silent meditation without sleeping. A tiger would crouch beneath his seat, and he was held in high esteem by the common people.

Those who came to study his Way gathered there in great numbers, and thus he manifested many extraordinary wonders. For instance, the Great Master Wuxiang came from the kingdom of Silla to visit Meditation Master Xichen.
The Master had previously cautioned the assembly, saying, "A guest from abroad shall arrive tomorrow; you should sweep and clean the grounds to await him.
Indeed, on the following day, a guest from the East Sea arrived. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, the newly appointed Governor Wang Ye was originally a Daoist priest (a *huángguān*).

During the Jingyun era, he once performed minor meritorious service as an *zhishi* (prefectural governor). Upon concluding his term in that commandery, the Buddhist monk Bao harbored a malevolent intent.
He took up his official duties and issued an order for all śramaṇas within the jurisdiction to assemble; however, only the Master did not descend from the mountain.

Someone urged the Master to go and attend the assembly so as to avoid becoming a source of calamity. The Master said to his disciples: "Though you have left the household life, you still do not yet understand karma. I—"
Before he has died, what can King Yè do to me? When the day of the King’s official mourning period arrived, the assembly of monastics had all gathered.
Someone remarked, "Only Chují has treated the regional lords with contempt and failed to come offer his congratulations. King Yè was slightly incensed;

having forced the monks to ascend the hall and take their seats, he was about to voice his grievances and ask the Master for the reason behind his refusal, when a look of resentment suddenly arose. The monks were all—

His thighs trembled, and he suddenly collapsed to the ground. His attendants supported him back to his residence, but upon reaching the trees behind the hall’s screen, there was a sound like that of being slapped on the cheek;
at the hour of *youzhong* (the fifth watch), his breath ceased. From this point on, everyone said that the fault lay with the Daoist who had unjustly accused him, leading to this end.
The Master passed away in the first month of the twenty-second year of the Kaiyuan era, at the age of eighty-seven.
Zizhong has revered him to this day.

Dàchuān was a man of unknown origins; he lived in silent seclusion, his integrity and resolve becoming ever more rigorous. He never opened a grave for himself, and his words were never spoken in vain.
At Xīxián Monastery in Hánzhōu, he practiced the four *ārya-vaṃśas* (Noble Lineages); as his asceticism intensified, [he went to] Miánzhú...
All people revered him as their master. When his end came, he lay outside the temple; the laypeople prepared a bed and carried him back into the monastery together to perform the funeral rites.
Just as the bier was being lifted, suddenly two deer led the way as if acting as an escort.

As they first crossed the threshold of the gate, the temple plaque suddenly fell to the ground. People from near and far were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration. Furthermore, on this mountain...
Spiritual wonders do not tolerate coarseness or vulgarity. There was a monk named Fazang who was not careful regarding his monastic conduct and frequently committed transgressions.
A divine being hurled him down the mountain for about seven *li*, yet he suffered injury only to his toes. From that time on, he reformed completely and observed the precepts without fail.
At the beginning of the Dali era, the northern mountain turned into a golden color; upon it appeared pavilions and towers where Bodhisattvas practiced the Way for a brief moment.

Suddenly, he mounted the clouds and ascended far away. The Master had long resided in this temple; as both man and site were endowed with spiritual power, he left behind his shadow for veneration, treating it as if it were a sacred shrine.
The Indian monk Nanda—whose name means "Joy" in the language of China—was of unknown lineage. His character was eccentric and unconventional, yet he maintained a profound reverence.
Màn had no fixed abode. During the Jiànzhōn era, he traveled to Mǐnshǔ. At that time, Zhāng Wèigōng invited him to serve as the governor of Chéngdū.
The Master declared, "I have attained the *yàoxù sānmèi* (如幻三昧, illusion-like samādhi). I can enter water without getting wet and throw myself into fire without being burned."
He could transform metal and stone, manifesting infinite transformations. When he first entered Shu, he traveled together with three young nuns;
at times he would drink heavily and sing wildly, and at other times he would gather crowds to preach the Dharma. A military commander loathed this and ordered them to be arrested.

When the Master was captured and brought before him, the commander said, "This poor monk merely takes refuge in the gates of the Sangha, yet he possesses secret medicinal arts. Thereupon, he pointed to the three nuns and said, "These women are all skilled in [these arts]."
She performed songs and dances, which the garrison commander greatly admired. He subsequently invited her to stay and held a banquet with wine and meat, where they drank and sang together.
He provided her with a tunic, trousers, and a hair-knot, and applied rouge and powder to each of the three nuns. They sat in a row;

their sidelong glances and playful laughter were of a transcendent grace that surpassed the world. When they were half-drunk, the Master said to the nuns, "You may perform a dance for the Commandant," and so she stepped forward slowly.
They performed a dance; trailing scarves like swirling snow, they rose with sudden agility, their skill surpassing all others.

When the music ended, the dancing did not cease. The Master then rebuked them, saying, "These women are possessed by wind-demons. Suddenly, the Master rose and seized the sword of the garrison commander.
The crowd, thinking he was intoxicated by wine, all fled in terror. He then struck off the heads of three nuns, which fell to the ground; the blood flowed for several *zhang*. The garrison commander—
Greatly alarmed, he called his attendants to bind the master. The master smiled and said, "Do not act so hastily. He slowly raised the three nuns, which were actually *zhongzhu* walking staffs;
the blood was merely the wine he had been drinking. The master continued to sit and enjoy his banquet, while he sent someone to cut off [the king's] head.
His two ears were nailed to a pillar, yet there was no blood at all. His body sat upon a mat; when the wine circulated to him, he would pour it into the severed openings.
His face would turn red, and he could sing with his mouth while clapping his hands in time with the rhythm.
When the banquet concluded, his body rose of its own accord, went to the pillar, and replaced his head; immediately, there were no scars. He could often speak of people's fortunes and misfortunes.
This was a riddle; it was only later that he understood it. A man in Chengdu provided him with offerings for several days, but the Master suddenly did not wish to remain.

The man then bolted the gate to detain him, but the Master immediately entered through a crack in the wall. As they pulled him back, he gradually disappeared until only the corner of his *kāṣāya* remained. After a moment, he was gone.
On the following day, they saw the shadow of a monk painted on the wall, appearing exactly like the Master. Two days later, the painting gradually faded away.
After seven days, there were ink traces in the air; by the eighth day, the traces had vanished.
Someone saw the Master already within the borders of Pengzhou early on that morning, and his subsequent whereabouts remained unknown.
Huai-kong was the son of the Liang family from Langzhou. In his youth, he entered the monastic life at Guangfu Monastery on Mount Qi-sha in his native prefecture.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to study under Chan Master Daji, attaining a state of pure clarity and profound understanding.

Later, he went to Anfeng Mountain in Pengcheng, where he hung up his staff and remained in silent contemplation. Within a few years, he established a great monastery there. Once, a monk arrived, traveling through the air.
He arrived and circumambulated the walls without ceasing; at times he stepped upon lotus flowers, and at other times he walked upon the ground.
Whenever people looked up at him, after several days he took his leave of the Master, saying, "I shall return to rely upon you in three or five years. Having spoken, he vanished from sight.

The Master passed away in the first year of the Xingyuan era at the age of eighty-eight. It was not until the second month of the first year of the Changqing era that he was finally enshrined in a stupa.
As for Dingguang, his origins were unknown; from the time he entered the Dharma, his character was unconstrained. He subsisted on coarse food, abstaining from midday meals, and wore simple clothing.

Having completed his years in the world, he was destined to bring about transformation and guidance in the regions of Yong and Shu. However, he suddenly encountered the suppression of Buddhism by Emperor Wuzong and was compelled to revert to the Confucian tradition.
When the sun of the Buddha’s teachings shone once more and the ranks of the Sangha were restored to their proper order, the Master joined in the reconstruction of monasteries.

Consequently, he cast a great bell weighing over ten thousand catties of refined gold. On that day, as the bell was being struck and the crucible heated until the ashes flew upward, auspicious smoke arose from the blazing furnace.
Two rays of light issued from the *cakra* of the stupa’s pinnacle, drifting upward like a rainbow. The multitude all gazed toward them;
the five colors surged and intermingled as if in resonance, and as one drum was struck, another responded. This was the stupa where King Aśoka had enshrined the Buddha’s *śarīra*.
At the beginning of the Taihe era, the Nanman leader Meng Zodian plundered and entered Yicheng, stationing his barbarian troops within the temple.

Inside, the corridors were all filled with the fumes of roasting meat, causing the monks to flee in all directions. At that time, four plumes of thick smoke issued from the top of the stupa, rising straight into the void.
When night fell, the Mian and Tan tribesmen, witnessing this extraordinary marvel, immediately forbade all acts of defilement.
Zhiguang, surnamed Cui, was a man of unknown origins. His vessel of virtue was inherently intact, and his roots in the Way were uniquely firm.

His transformative influence was grand and elegant, and he manifested extraordinary traces of his practice. Whenever those suffering from various ailments sought him out, he would take a single piece of bamboo as a staff, point it at the site of their pain, or strike it once;
there was no one who did not recover instantly. To the point that those who were paralyzed stood up, and those who were lame ran.

At the beginning of the Qianning era, the Wang family first established their control over Chengdu. Luo (name lost), the Prefect of Ya Commandery, resigned from his post and traveled to visit the ruler of Shu, bringing the Master with him.
The Wang family had long been aware of his extraordinary arts and addressed him as the "Holy Master.

Previously, during the Xiantong era, the Nanzhao king Jintan Chuo had come to besiege Chengdu, nearly capturing it. At that time, a Heavenly King appeared in the form of a śramaṇa, approximately five *zhang* in height.
As his eyes emitted streams of light, the Mian troops immediately retreated. Consequently, the people of Shu erected a five-zhang statue of a monk at Baoli Temple north of the city.
Later, it was destroyed by the Minister of Revenue, Niu Yu. Subsequently, as military fires followed one after another, there was only fear that the statue of Vaiśravaṇa would collapse.
The Wang family then said to the Master, "Your extraordinary arts and moral influence move the people; you may [rebuild] the Baoli [statue]."
The Heavenly King said, "No. There was a former Minister of State named Lu Zeng who dreamed that the Heavenly King said to him: 'Have my image repaired.

Just as he was beginning the work, this letter suddenly arrived requesting that you use your Dharma-power to complete it. The Master accepted his command and moved to stay beneath the Heavenly King’s pavilion on a small bed in a corner.
Every day, the sick crowded at his door; he collected two or three hundred thousand coins in alms each day."

He provided funds and further spoke to encourage others to contribute timber. Within ten days, all the materials had been transported and piled up, which he entrusted to the three administrators (sangang) to oversee.
Initially, when the Master was at his home temple in Yajun, he resided in a single small room within the Kadi Shrine Hall; the door was low and the thatched roof was humble.
He did not permit women to enter the gate. He possessed only a single bamboo bowl; for every meal offering, he would accept twenty *wen*, which he invariably cast into the bowl.
Once it was full, he would place it in the Buddha hall, strike the bell to assemble the community, and distribute the contents equally between himself and the others.

Whenever he was invited to a meal, his intention was to accept only twenty *wen*; even if the offerings were more, he would not take them. Having finished eating, he would depart, and there was no [further exchange].
He announced this. Thereafter, his spiritual efficacy increased further. Whenever he encountered a sick person, a single pinch and a single shout would cause them to rise.

At times, he would have paper money burned, or have food and drink picked up and scattered [to the spirits]. When he encountered those suffering from extreme pain and distress, he would twist paper, dip it in water, and apply it; they too were cured.

In the first year of the Guanghua era, when the construction of the Hall of Heavenly Kings was completed, he followed the banks of the River God’s pool and chanted incantations over food to feed the fish.
After a night had passed, more than ten billion fish floated to the surface of the water and died;
they were all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whereupon they returned to express their gratitude for the Master's kindness.

Yuanshang was a native of Shu. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and extensively mastered both Buddhist and secular classics. He was skilled in literary composition and was celebrated at the time as a "prodigious child.
Internally, he cultivated the monastic precepts with such integrity that none could find fault with him. In the first year of the Longshuo era, he passed away due to illness.

As his body was being prepared for cremation, a rainbow, resembling a length of silk, appeared within his chamber and ascended straight into the void. Furthermore, the bells at the corners of the temple rang without being struck.
The wind blew spontaneously, and every night there were sounds of drums and horns; these continued for over a hundred days before they ceased.
From then on, birds and sparrows no longer perched upon his dwelling. In the fourth year of the Xianheng era, sweet dew descended upon the lecture hall.
When the Master passed away, his disciples collected his writings, totaling more than thirty fascicles, which were then published for the world.
Fǎróng was the son of the Yán family from Lángzhōu. From his youth, he preferred simplicity and naturally loathed ornate clothing.

When his father instructed him to take up the brush, he would instead paint images of the Buddha; even in his play, he would gather sand to build stupas. Everything he did was nothing other than Buddhist practice.
At the age of thirteen, seeing the deportment of the monks, he earnestly sought to leave the household life and relied upon Huìxiū of Chánglè Monastery.

The Dharma Master underwent tonsure and became proficient in the recitation of the sutras before receiving the precepts. He studied and lectured on the *Nanshan Lüchao* (The Vinaya Commentary of the Southern Mountain).
Later, while traveling as a wandering monk, he met Chan Master Pují of Mount Song; the Master’s spiritual peak was solitary and lofty, and [Falin] was secretly entrusted with the seal of the mind.

He went to Funing Temple in Yiyang, where he vigorously revitalized the school’s tradition. Students arrived like deer in great numbers. In the ninth year of the Taohé era, he manifested illness and passed away.
He was eighty-nine years old at the time of his death. His disciples carried his sacred seat into the stupa.
Guànxiū, whose courtesy name was Deyǐn, was the son of the Jāng family of Dēnggāo in Lánxī, Jīnhuá. At the age of seven, his parents held him in great affection.
He entered the monastic life under Chan Master Yuanzhen of He’an Temple in his home county. While still a child, he would recite one thousand characters of the *Lotus Sūtra* daily;
whatever he heard with his ears, he never forgot. Together with Chumu, he underwent tonsure and lived in neighboring temples.

They would regularly discuss poetry across their fences and chant it to one another, such that all monks who saw them were struck with wonder. After receiving full ordination, his reputation for poetry grew prominent.

Moving with the times, he went to Yuzhang to study the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, both of which he mastered in their profound meanings. He was diligent in his lectures and expositions.
Wang Cao, the Prefect of his home commandery, held him in high esteem; subsequently, the Prefect Jiang Xiang established a platform for ritual purification, repentance, and the precepts.
He appointed the Master as the supervisor of the ritual altar. At the beginning of the Qianning era, he traveled with his aspirations to visit Qian Shu, the Prince Wusu of Wuyue.

He presented five poems, each consisting of eight lines, which greatly pleased the Prince. The gifts bestowed upon him were also generous. When the Prince established his regime by eliminating usurpers, the imperial court honored him as a meritorious subject.
Consequently, a separate hall was erected and a stele inscribed to record the names of the generals and officers who had collaborated in the pacification of Yue. Thereupon...
The poems of the Master were engraved on the back of the stele; his esteem was such as this. He was skilled in fine brushwork and attained the six principles of painting.

He excelled in ink and water, and his works were worthy of admiration. At the request of the Qiang family’s pharmacy at Zhong’an Bridge, he produced a set of Arhats, saying that for each figure he painted, he would invariably pray for a dream to obtain the likeness of a true sage before completing it; these were unlike ordinary styles. From there, he traveled to Yí.

Hui-xi’s spiritual path harmonized with that of the Venerable Master Lan of Tang’an Temple. Later, he desired to ascend Mount Nanyue and traveled north to pay his respects to Cheng Rui, the Military Governor of Jingzhou.

Initially, Cheng treated him with great courtesy and provided him with lodging at Longxing Temple. At that time, the Palace Secretary Wu Rong was in exile; the two met and frequented one another’s company, discussing both the Way and poetry.
Wu Rong composed a preface for the Master’s collected works in the third year of the Qianning era. Shortly thereafter, the Master was falsely accused.
He slandered the Master to the military governor of Jing, leading to the Master’s dismissal from Gong’an. In deep melancholy, he inscribed a phrase upon his inkstone:

"Only when entering the case does the body find peace. His disciples urged the Master to go to Shu. At that time, the Wang family was plotting usurpation and was summoning worthy scholars from all quarters;

they were overjoyed to obtain the Master and treated him with great courtesy, bestowing lavish gifts and honors. They conferred upon him the title of Chan Yue Da Shi (Great Master Chan Yue). The Ruler of Shu constantly...
He was called the "Attaining-Attaining-Come" (Dededeilai) Monk. At that time, Wei Ai proclaimed his noble title. What he excelled at were songs and satirical verses;
their subtle and hidden meanings served the purpose of edification. His stylistic modulation was no inferior to that of Li Bai or He Zhizhang.
In the second year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he passed away at his residence at the age of eighty-one.
*Jinjiang Chandelu*, Scroll Sixteen;
*Jinjiang Chandelu*, Scroll Seventeen.
Yong’an was a native of Hongya in Jizhou. He was diminutive in stature, his complexion was dark and sallow, and his speech and manners were coarse and vulgar. However...

His capacity for awareness was vast and expansive; generally speaking, it was beyond measure. During the eighth year of the Dazhong era, he went to Chengdu to pay a visit to Bai Minzhong, the provincial governor.
He requested that the governor petition the throne for a temple plaque. Because his legs were so frail, he arrived by sedan chair.
No one had ever seen him enter a latrine and subsequently urinate; thus, people at the time called him the "Master Without Leakage" (Wulou Shi). He was then settled at Sheng... [text ends].
He remained at Shousi Temple for ten days. A memorial was submitted to the Central Secretariat ordering five or six monks to take turns guarding him day and night to observe his conduct.
His internal and external diet was roughly the same as that of ordinary people, yet he showed no intention of disrobing or departing from the two practices [of meditation and recitation].

After carefully calculating the accumulation of his movements over ten double-hours (*yāma*), it was impossible to discern where he went or how he moved. Lord Bai, the Minister of Education, submitted a petition for the temple’s official registration; upon its arrival, [the matter was settled].
He took his leave and returned home. When Lu Qiu, the Judicial Official of Meiju, met him, he regarded him as nothing more than a young novice monk.
Others said, "This master is already over eighty years old."
The man known as Wangming was an unknown person who lived among the Zhongliang Mountains, some several dozen *li* west of Baoci.

There, several peaks turn inward and support one another, their emerald-green cliffs merging with the sky; he dwelt in their midst. His conduct was eccentric and his speech unconventional, yet those who saw him constantly were not startled, while those who suddenly encountered him found him strange.
Ordinarily, he was extremely fond of wine and meat, and his coarse behavior was practiced openly. Furthermore, [he possessed] a net... [text fragment].

He presided over all affairs and frequently acted with moderation; he was known as the "Elder Master" (Shangzuo). At that time, the entire community of monks followed his example. The Master, aware of this, sighed and said:
"With an unpurified mind-ground, how can one dare to practice 'reverse conduct' (nigamana)? Reverse conduct is not the domain of ordinary people.
There is a proverb that says: "Gold is tested by fire; wait until I have passed my own test. During the Kaicheng era, he suddenly made large cakes and summoned his disciples.
He said, "Come with you all to the Śītavana forest. Outside the city, there were many tombs and burial mounds in the mountains and fields where people discarded their corpses.
The Master sat upon the ground, spread out a flatbread, wrapped it around a putrid, decaying corpse, and began to eat it as if it were food. This was the height of bold and spirited conduct.
The monks who were traveling with him all covered their noses, spat on the ground, and fled. The Master shouted loudly, "Are you able to feed yourselves?"
"Only this flesh can serve as fodder for other flesh. From this point on, the monastic community was awakened and transformed into one of refined austerity; believers flocked from near and far.
At that time, the Right Vice-Director Liu Zhongying, while serving in the Liang Prefecture, personally went to pay his respects and honor him.

At the time of his passing, he was approximately eighty or ninety years old. A true image of him remains at the mountain temple; to this day, throughout the regions of Liang, Yi, and the Three Commanderies, people simply call him "Xing."
The former Elder’s extraordinary traces and miraculous deeds have not yet been detailed.
Fajah was a native of Jiangdong. He traveled through Min and Shu and resided at Fazhu Temple, which was built by Prince Xiu of the Sui dynasty.
Inside the temple was a śarīra stupa erected by Emperor Wen during the Renshou era. The Master harbored great compassion and frequently [performed acts of] defiance.

He knew of their arrival and spoke without the slightest error. Once, while in his room, he said to his disciples, "Outside there are more than ten thousand people, all wearing hats and with bodies hunched and contorted;
they are coming to beg for my salvation. Go quickly outside the temple to find them.
The disciples marveled at how their master’s words were so contrary and confused. While they stood about in hesitation, dozens of people appeared.
A person carrying a bamboo basket arrived with a conch shell inside. The Master asked, "Is this it? He ordered that money be taken to redeem it and threw it into the water.
Luoseng Shu was a man who had attained the stage of *phala* at Shengshou Temple; he once fell ill while staying at Mount Wutai and passed away there. The assembly gathered together.
The monk was unfathomable; yet, he gazed upon him without ever showing the slightest negligence. When the ninety-day period of retreat was nearly at an end, his illness was cured.
At the moment of parting, [the monk] said: "I am deeply grateful for the care you provided during my suffering. Now that I have recovered, it is entirely due to the Master's power.
I reside on Mount Chalung in Jiulong County, beyond the Sword Mountains (Jianwai). On a future day when you travel abroad, do not forget me."
They visited one another. In his later years, he arrived in Shu and traveled to visit various peaks, inquiring everywhere among the elderly woodcutters.

They all said, "We have never heard the name of this mountain. He sighed and said, "Alas! How deluded are these sickly Chan practitioners. As he was about to turn back, he encountered a mountain boy who said:

"I am the one who gathered sand at that cliff," he said, and immediately led the way forward. Suddenly, they beheld a temple and pagoda standing solemnly in the void, with corridors and galleries surrounding them in dignified order.
Indeed, they encountered the man from whom they had previously received medical care; he came to the gate and recounted their past history.

As the sun was about to set, he said to him, "This monastery cannot be reached except by one who has attained the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*). By virtue of our karmic affinity from former lives, we have met here this once."

He stopped and said, "May I stay for one night? The master replied, "That cannot be. [The monk thought,] "Since he has been so diligent in his cultivation and realization, how could this be difficult for him?
He then ordered an old servant boy to escort the master back. As the monk looked back, he saw only the steep and precipitous cliff face.
The landscape was merely a vast expanse of cypress and hinoki trees. This was during the Zhong era of the Kaicheng period.

At that time, National Teacher Wudao Zhixuan, while compiling his biographies, encountered the monk Kesì, who was exceptionally skilled in geomancy. He commissioned Kesì to select a site for his future burial plot.
He found the front peak of Danjing Mountain; the mountain resembled the form of a city’s battlements, and though it rose and fell in undulations, its center was level and firm.
Peace. Shortly thereafter, an elderly villager said, "According to ancient tradition, this is Mount Chalongsan.

Xingzun was the second son of the Min King of Fuzhou, the Wang clan. After Zhuangzong of the Later Tang ascended the throne, he entered Luoyang to present local tribute and remained there in the capital guesthouse.
Toward the end of the Tongguang era, as Mingzong was about to enter the city and military chaos ensued, he [Xingzun] consequently...
He cut his hair and adorned himself, changing his robes to become a monk, and went into hiding in Ba and Shu.

By the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty, his appearance was that of a man over seventy years old, yet his physical vigor did not decline. Whenever anyone inquired about his age or seniority in the monastic order, he would invariably remain silent.

He resided at Kuangguo Chan Monastery in Langzhong, maintaining the community solely through the Vinaya rules; people were unaware of whether the Master’s spiritual capacity was superior or inferior. There was a Mr. Li...
Zijia ordered them to observe a fast. While they were eating and drinking, he suddenly rose and went out the door, shouting and clamoring as if to reprimand someone.
He said to Li, "Tonight there will be a fire starting from the southeast and reaching the northwest. Instruct all the neighbors and households to prepare for it."
That evening, as expected, everything was reduced to ashes without a trace remaining. The assembly gathered to ask for the reason, and he replied:
"Yesterday, a woman dressed in red passed by carrying a torch. This old monk regretted that I could not catch up with her."
Sengjian’s surname was Wang; he was a native of Jingzhao. From his youth, he was perceptive and wise, and his speech and demeanor were far superior to those of his peers.
In the eleventh year of the Dazhong era, he successfully passed the imperial examination under Du Shenquan. Feng Juan, the Director of the Imperial Library, was a fellow graduate from that same year.

During the Qianfu era, when the rebels of Chao were rampant, Sengjian followed the river currents to escape the chaos and arrived at Zhugong, where he sought refuge with Cheng Rui. [Cheng] Rui then launched an attack...
Finding no success in the Huaihai region, he shaved his head and entered the monastic life. At that time, Lei Man held sway over Jingzhou and Xiangyang;

Zhao Ning defeated and destroyed him, and Zhu Wen (the Founder of the Later Liang) dispatched Gao Jichang to exterminate [Lei Man’s forces]. Jiangling subsequently fell under the control of the Gao clan. The Master sought refuge in the regions of Kui and Xia.
In the third year of the Tongguang era of the Later Tang, he traveled to Shu to seek out Feng Juan, but found that he had already passed away. He then resided at Jingzhong Monastery.
He resided at a temple where his beard and hair were white as snow, yet his complexion was ruddy and radiant; he moved about with such ease that people could not fathom his true intentions.
Master Diandian was a man of unknown origins. During the Guangzheng era of the Meng clan’s reign, he lived in seclusion on Mount Dayi in southern Qiong.
He frequented the market stalls and shops. Although he had donned the dyed robes of a monk, he was constantly like one deranged.

Whenever he encountered others, he would invariably point at them with a knowing look; thus, he was known by that name. When invited to a vegetarian feast, he would consume wine and meat without distinction, taking this as his constant practice;
even the common folk did not find it distasteful. As evening fell, he would purchase yellow and white hemp paper, pens, and ink, and place them [in his bag].

He tucked it into his sleeve and returned home. After traveling several *li*, he arrived while still deeply immersed in his state, having fallen asleep by dusk. Although the room where he lived had an outer door, it lacked four walls;
once inside, he closed the door so that no one could enter. Initially, a young neighbor monk followed him on tiptoe to observe him.

He saw [Huiyuan] holding a candle, sitting with legs spread out, with paper and brush set before him. He was scolding someone and writing in large characters, though the meaning of the text remained unintelligible.
The character [of the figure] often let out a sudden exclamation, as if making a decisive judgment or disposition.

After a long time, as he gazed intently at the boundary between light and dark, there appeared a shimmering array of figures like people standing in formation, resembling officials of the Underworld. Their tunics and robes were not the attire of this world.
Those who witnessed this withdrew in terror. When questioned about the matter the following morning, he grew angry and did not answer. Several years later, the people of Qiongze all...
People marveled at his divine anomalies, and his ultimate end remained unknown.

Dinglan was the son of the Yang family of Chengdu; originally from the bustling marketplace, he belonged to the class of violent butchers and wine-sellers, yet Heaven had bestowed this nature upon him.

He repented of his past transgressions and vowed to join the sixfold harmony of the Sangha. He traveled to propagate the Dharma throughout the three regions of Shu, where at that time everyone took refuge in him with faith.
He constructed a monastery named Shengshou (Holy Longevity), but as its karmic conditions had not yet ripened, he concealed it among common laborers.

His parents had died early, leaving him without the means to perform funeral rites for them; whenever he encountered their anniversary, the Master would weep until he was choked with grief, often even stripping himself naked [in his mourning].

He entered Mount Qingcheng. Mosquitoes, gadflies, horseflies, and flies bit and gnawed at his skin and body, yet he said, "I am giving away my internal wealth (the flesh of my body) to repay my parents for their labors.

He drew blood to transcribe scriptures, and later he even cauterized his arms. Eventually, he reached the point of plucking out his ears and gouging out his eyes to feed them to birds of prey and fierce beasts.
Thereafter, he could no longer walk without being supported by others, and he stumbled and fell whenever he touched objects. Later, a strange man appeared and took hold of him.
He held up an object that was like a pearl; it appeared within the hollow of his eye socket, and for a moment he gazed at it as before.
A voice from the unseen announced: "The King of the Southern Heaven has returned the master’s eye-pearl. People near and far were struck with amazement. He often said to others:

"I have heard in the *Sūtra of Good Precepts* that this is called the 'Unsurpassed Gift. I vow to practice it diligently to swiftly attain the supreme fruit. In the third year of the Dazhong era, [the Emperor] Xuán...
The Emperor issued an edict for him to enter the palace to receive offerings, honoring him with exceptional courtesy out of reverence for his spiritual responses.
His disciple Youyuan constantly attended to him at his side. In the second month of the sixth year, he again vowed to set fire to his own shoulders.

Although the Emperor repeatedly exhorted and encouraged him, saying that he was already advanced in years and should instead focus on long-term cultivation, the Master did not accept the decree; he subsequently set himself ablaze and passed away. Youyuan submitted a memorial regarding this.

He was requested to change his name and a stupa was erected for him; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Juexing" (Awakened Nature) and his stupa was named "Wuzhen" (Realization of Truth).
In the capital of Shu, it is now commonly referred to simply as the Dinglan Stupa Courtyard, where the incense and lamps have never ceased until the present day.
Hongzheng was surnamed Chang; it is not known where he was from. He resided in a monastery between Min and Shu.

Previously, he had suffered from a chronic illness that was deep-seated and persistent, but once it had subsided, he made a vow to constantly recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, setting a standard of twenty recitations per day.
He maintained this practice with such diligence that there was never any neglect. At that time, while his neighbor-monk Shouxian was sitting in meditation at night, he saw two ghosts.

The messenger held a written document in his hand and said privately to his companion, "We are to arrest the monk Hongzheng. One messenger said, "Because he was silently reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there was a great and extraordinary protective power nearby;
we had no way to approach him. Furthermore, I am concerned that the deadline will be missed. Now I have devised another plan:
there is a man named Chang standing by the east gate of the Directorate who shares the same surname as the monk and has also previously been a monk."
"A monk has arrived; take him away with you to block the entrance to the hall. When Shōken heard this, he was struck with wonder and recorded the incident.
The next day, he secretly questioned the gatekeeper, Chōkō, who replied that Kōshō had already died. Shōken had previously been devoted to the *Amitābha Sūtra*, but later changed his practice.
The Master’s final end remained unknown.
Xiongjun was the son of the Zhou family of Chengdu. He was skilled at lecturing and preaching, yet he lacked any moral discipline.

He misappropriated the offerings of the faithful for improper purposes and was generally full of craftiness and deceit. He behaved only with negligence and recklessness; furthermore, he once changed his clothes and entered military encampments, fleeing there to escape danger before returning to the monastic order.
During the Dali era, he died a sudden death and entered the underworld, where he was summoned before the King of Hell. After being subjected to a severe reprimand, he was led into prison.
He departed. Jun raised his voice and cried out, "If I, Xiongjun, should fall into hell, then the Buddhas of the three periods would be speaking falsehoods.
I have read the *Amitābha Sūtra*; even those of the lowest of the lower grades who commit the five heinous crimes can attain rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations at the moment of death.
Although I have committed sins, I have not perpetrated the five heinous crimes. As for my recitation of the Buddha’s name, its number is beyond measure."
There was another man, a neighbor of Xiongjun, who had been taken by the same calamity. He had been chanting the Buddha’s name for several days and was also on the verge of death.
When he was about to recover, he spoke to Xiongjun, saying, "If you see any monastics or laypeople in the city, please tell them: I have already attained rebirth in the Western Land.
Having finished speaking, he ascended a precious platform and departed directly toward the west.

Qingxu was the son of the Tang family of Zizhou. By nature he was resolute and decisive, yet stubborn and cunning, difficult to guard against. Suddenly he turned his heart toward the Dharma and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
His three karmas were brought into harmony, and he never grew lax. Once, while he was chanting in the mountains and forests, seven deer became tame and submissive, as if listening intently;
when his voice ceased, they departed. Furthermore, when a neighboring house caught fire and the connected roofs were reduced to ashes, [he remained unharmed].
Only the Master’s dwelling was passed over by the flying flames and sparks; it suffered not the slightest scorching.

In the second year of the Chang’an era, he traveled alone to Wuzhen Temple in Lantian and stayed in the Northern Courtyard of the upper section. Previously, there had been no well or spring there; as human effort could not reach it, water had to be drawn from a distant stream.

Carrying jars and bearing buckets, the labor involved in transporting it was extreme. At that time, the Great Master of Huayan, Fazang, heard of the Master’s miraculous efficacy in upholding the sutras.
He then prayed for a spring. Immediately, he entered the Maitreya Pavilion and burned incense; the sound of his recitation continued until dawn on three occasions.
Suddenly, as if in a trance, he saw three jade maidens on the flank of the mountain to the northwest of the pavilion, who were gouging the earth with knives, and water emerged wherever they worked.
The Master remembered the location clearly and immediately rose to dig there; indeed, he obtained sweet spring water that was inexhaustible when used.

In the fourth year [of his stay], while at Shaolin Monastery, there was a Buddhist chamber at the foot of the mountain that was very spacious, yet no one dared to approach it, as it was said to be the dwelling of ghosts and spirits.
Once, a Vinaya Master, relying on his own observance of the precepts, went there at night to recite the Vinaya; he saw a giant who pierced him with a spear.

He fled down the mountain in a state of utter distress. After hesitating for a moment, he fell unconscious. There was also a monk who recited the *Kṣitigarbha-vajra-mantra*, who was highly revered by the community at that time.
