The crowd said to him, "Your power of incantation is peerless; could you stay there overnight? He replied, "What is there to fear in this?

Thereupon, he took his incense and lamps, entered the dwelling, and sat there reciting the mantra. Suddenly, the deity emerged, seized him by the feet with its hand, and threw him down into a mountain stream.
For seven days he remained silent, his spirit clouded and his body prostrate. When the Master heard of this, he said, "A ghost or spirit of the lower realms dares to act thus!
He immediately went there and recited the sutras as usual. At night, he heard a most violent sound from the east of the hall; he then recited the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Dharani.
Again, he heard what seemed to be two oxen fighting within the hall, and the Buddha images all trembled. Since the dharani had no effect, he returned to [reciting] the...

At the first *qì* (unit of time) of this sutra, all disturbances subsided and all signs of influence vanished. From then on, those residing there suffered no more afflictions, and the deity eventually departed.
In the second year of the Shénlóng era, he entered the palace by imperial decree to pray for rain; after twenty-one days, snow fell.
Because the situation was not yet resolved, Zhōngzōng deemed it necessary to seek further prayers at the temple. He immediately offered earnest supplications within the Buddha hall, and furthermore—
He practiced the "refining of a finger. After only one night, rain fell for a thousand *li*. His finger returned to its former state.
Whenever he encountered great floods, the temple buildings were all submerged, yet his monastery suffered no harm. In all such instances of miraculous response, it was always like this.
An anonymous person from Kaishua Temple in Hanzhou previously entered the temple and saw auspicious signs appearing one after another.

He then vowed to practice self-sacrifice and asceticism as his goal. Suddenly, while burning incense within the hall, he briefly beheld the ground and the buildings all turning the color of lapis lazuli.
A five-colored cloud from the Bodhisattva vehicle descended into the courtyard and said, "You are most steadfast and resolute; you shall certainly attain the Way.
I have come to bear witness for you. Wangming prostrated himself in worship, but after a short while, the cloud vanished.

When the temple monks arrived, they found that the entire courtyard had turned the color of lapis lazuli. They sighed in wonder without ceasing, and the monk thereafter redoubled his diligent practice.

Fei Changfang of Chengdu had originally been ordained as a monk, but during the Zhou dynasty he followed secular customs. He was extensively learned and profoundly mastered the subtle and profound principles of the Dharma.

During the translations of the Kaihuang era, he participated in the selection and promotion of texts. By imperial decree, he was summoned to the capital to assist in the compilation and revision of scriptures according to established precedent.

Because the catalogs of scriptures from successive dynasties were scattered and difficult to collect, and because the years since the initial rise of the Buddha-dharma had seen its records fall into neglect, he compiled the *Sanbao lu* (Record of the Three Jewels), volume one.

Fifteen fascicles. Beginning from the early years of Emperor Zhuang of the Zhou dynasty, the upper section records the *jiǎzǐ* (sexagenary cycle) dates, while the lower section records the reign titles (*niánhào*), along with the number of sections, fascicles, titles, and scrolls of the various scriptures translated by successive dynasties.
These are presented separately in narrative form; those that are currently in circulation are included, while those that lack distinct verification are omitted.
Once the catalog was completed and submitted for imperial review, an edict was issued for its implementation, and it has since been circulated throughout all regions.
Huizhao was the son of the Chen clan. His lineage originally descended from Taichou in Yingchuan; he moved to the countryside of Danyang to escape the chaos.

By nature he was tranquil and detached, possessing few desires. He was grave and resolute, speaking little. Having lost his father at a young age, he grew up under the care of his elder brother. His devotion to seeking out virtuous friends became renowned throughout the villages.
At the age of twelve, he grew weary of the world, left the household life to receive the full precepts, and immediately traveled to the capitals of Jingzhou and Yangzhou to study under masters.
When Master Min lectured on and explained the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, his resonant voice reached the ears of all, and [Zhuangyan] recorded nearly every word.
He said to his fellow student Huifeng, "I have been bathed in the Way for few days, yet I have come to know its essential purport. It seems there is a karmic affinity from a former life.

Is it not that what I have heard is shallow in meaning, or is it because of the excellence of this teaching? Thereupon, he went to listen to Master Zang of Kaishan lecture, and suddenly awakened to the underlying principle.
When he was told about Xuán, he devoted his whole heart to studying and admiring him. That very night, he had a dream in which he went to Kaishan Temple and gathered several bushels of plum fruits.
As he reached out to eat them, he first encountered the branches and leaves. Upon waking, he realized: "I am precisely meant to follow this teacher;
I shall surely reach the utmost depth. Shortly thereafter, Master Zàng passed away, and Master Chuò of Longguang Temple succeeded him in transmitting the teachings.

He immediately turned back to listen. Since he lacked the original text of the treatise, the authorities prohibited him from staying. He possessed only a single blanket, and as it was the dead of winter, he spread it out to use as a writing desk for the treatise.

Enduring the cold with his teeth chattering, he was finally able to attend the lectures. His mastery of both the words and their meaning was such that his singular brilliance stood preeminent above all others.

At that time, he refuted the view that the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is inherently existent, employing the categories of the coarse and the subtle to dismantle their arguments. Thus it was said:

This constitutes a profound interpretation; he possesses a divine mind. When the Prince of Wuling of the Liang dynasty was dispatched to govern Western Shu, he heard that the region abounded in scholars of doctrinal studies (*yi-xue*).

He insisted that only those of eminent understanding and broad reputation could be entrusted with the proclamation [of the teachings]. After the assembly deliberated and recommended various candidates, none met his expectations.
The Prince said, "I recall a gathering of the Dharma from years past; there was a monk from the Cang region named Dharma Master Shao who would truly be fit for this selection. If he were obtained...

Traveling together, [Dao’an] thought that [Huiguan] might be able to revitalize the teachings in the frontier regions, so he invited him to Shu. There, he lectured and exhorted the assembly at various monasteries with a flow like a river.
Once, while delivering a lecture at Longyuan Temple, he sat in meditation as the discourse drew to a close; in his room, he had a visionary encounter with a deity.
A woman in blue robes appeared just as he was dressing. She paid her respects and said, "I pray that the Dharma Master will always remain here to propagate the Dharma;

I shall protect and assist you. Having spoken, she vanished. Consequently, he sat for several sessions in succession, during which his clear insights became increasingly profound and complex. Previously, while in Yangdu, he suffered from a chronic illness;

though he applied himself with constant diligence, it persisted. Upon arriving in Shu to lecture, all his ailments were cured. Those who understood the matter believed this was due to the protection of the temple deity.
At that time, at the Dharma assemblies in Chengdu, three or four Dharma-drums were always struck simultaneously, vying with one another to open wide the Gate of the Profound.
The Master’s disciples were so numerous and flourishing that none could surpass this in magnificence.
Baoyuan was the son of the Chen family of Langzhong. At the age of twenty-three, he left the household life in Chengdu and resided at Luotiangong Temple.

Desiring to study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* so as to become a master of its propagation, he found that the local teachers in his home province were of shallow skill and could not satisfy his aspirations.

In the first year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Longguang Temple, where he received the instruction of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) from Dharma Master Sengmin. After traveling through various regions...
After several years, Sengyi became quite deeply immersed in his spirit. Daomin said, "This gentleman follows his own nature with remarkable acuity; his wisdom and discernment surpass those of others.

My only regret is that he is inconsistent and erratic, and his conduct is volatile and impetuous. Had he encountered a person of broad learning who treated him with superior hospitality, he would have become a renowned scholar of this age."
If he does not meet with his time [of death], he will not die a natural death; he will surely bring disgrace and ruin upon the Great Dharma.

The Master was excessively fond of wrestling and was prone to drinking and harboring resentment; he was frantic all day long and showed no deference to others. Although Daomin repeatedly admonished and exhorted him, the Master instead treated him as an enemy.

Consequently, the Master changed his ways and followed Zhizang again to investigate the former deeds of his predecessors. He established his own lecture hall, and his wealth and resources were distributed [to support it].
Zhan applied himself with redoubled diligence and industry, far exceeding his usual efforts. He would often say, "A man of great character should make others serve him;
how can he long remain in service to others? He then extensively transcribed commentaries on the scriptures and purchased books from Wang Zhengnan, which he bound together in a single chest.

Having set his mind on returning to the West, Huiji of the same monastery teased him, saying, "In the past, because the 'Blue Box' (Qingxian) of the Xie family did not reach you, you were unable to compose [the *Shishuo xinyu*]."

The literary record states: "Recently, when the Minister’s white basket failed to arrive, it was judged that there was no principle to be expounded. The Master said, 'This is by no means so; this is merely a staff for beating dogs.

Consequently, he took his case-folders and returned westward to reside at his former temple, where he established the definitive principles of the doctrine. Both monastics and laypeople held him in deep reverence."

Thereupon, philosophical assemblies were frequently convened, with several hundred listeners in attendance. [The Master] was self-important regarding his reputation and conduct, and had few friends or confidants.

The śramaṇa Zhixun, who had traveled to study in the capital, was proficient and quick-witted in the Śāstra of Numbers (Saṃkhyakārikā). When they returned together to their native land, [the Master] sought to form a close bond with him, but the teacher did not permit it.

Later, when the temple’s treasury incurred an official offense, the Master relied on his own high reputation within the province, believing he would be exonerated by the public. He used his own body...

His time had come. His fierce and violent nature did not subside; yet, as the matter reached its conclusion, he realized that defeat was certain. Consequently, he left the city walls and, along the road, took his own life with a blade.
He was sixty-one years old at the time, which was the seventh year of the Putong era.
Baotuan was the son of the Zhao family of Anhan. Later, he resided at Suxi in Changlong, Mianzhou. By nature he was benevolent and yielding, and his wisdom was brilliant and clear.
Even as an infant he displayed extraordinary qualities; his parents wished to test his discernment, so they laid out various silks, flowers, fruits, bows, arrows, and writing tablets before him.
The Master immediately brushed aside the cakes and fruits and took up the writing tablets. The assembly [witnessed this].
They marveled at this and all knew that he would surely achieve great success. When he reached the age of seven, he happened to visit Baxi;
the Regional Governor, Yang Tiao, asked him, "I have heard that you read extensively; for what reason is your name 'Laozi'?

The Master replied, "It is because my hair was white when I was first born. Yang Tiao secretly marveled at this. At sixteen, he served under the Prince of Pingxi of the Liang dynasty. Initially, he was a Daoist novice.
My son, before you had studied the Buddha-dharma, Pingxi recognized your spiritual capacity and commissioned you to oversee the construction of meritorious works.

There, you encountered Buddhist scriptures; you rejoiced in their literary elegance and esteemed their profound meaning. You proceeded to examine, read, and recite them, whereby the distinction between delusion and awakening became increasingly clear.

Constantly seeking the Buddha-dharma to dispel your ignorance and obscurity, you finally entered the monastic life at the age of twenty-four and immediately received full ordination. First, you listened to...

For several years, from beginning to end, he gained a general mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka regarding what constitutes an offense and its avoidance. He then turned his attention to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, transmitting it to others without weariness.

He did not begrudge sharing his personal notes; whenever there was a need, he would provide them immediately. He investigated the text with focused intent, analyzing each section with meticulous care.

Later, he also attended the lectures of Dharma Master Shao, through which he thoroughly mastered the profound meanings and purports. When Prince Wuling heard that the Master had convened a great assembly in the Mahā Hall, he requested him to preach on the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*.
At first, he had not yet fixed his mind upon it, as there were originally no commentaries or sub-commentaries. Only then did he apply his mental efforts to extract the phrasing and principles;

the words and meanings harmonized perfectly, and those who listened filled the hall. He privately recorded these teachings and thereby composed the draft of the commentary, which was widely circulated in the world. Later, he returned to Fuchuan.

He transformed both the clergy and the laity, providing continuous instruction through both secular classics and Buddhist scriptures. He led those on heterodox paths back to the truth, such that nine out of ten households were converted.
Furthermore, he compiled medical prescriptions to treat various sufferings; yet when people offered him gold or silk in gratitude, he accepted nothing at all.

Consequently, there were those who, moved by his righteousness and cherishing his virtue, renounced worldly life to become monks. Others, whose circumstances or obstacles prevented them from doing so, observed the eight precepts for the remainder of their lives.
Although the Master’s Way spread throughout the Jinglu region and his influence wafted across the Min and E mountains, his aspirations remained humble; he sought only to propagate the True Dharma.

With sincerity as his guiding principle, he did not compete with others for status. Seeing that the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* had not yet been widely disseminated within the borders of Shu, he desired to compose a commentary so that later students would have a place of refuge.
He entrusted the responsibility for the sutras and vinaya to others and retired to the mountain to undertake the composition, yet the community again...

I searched for it, which caused much disturbance; only after two years did I finally succeed, without any obstacles whatsoever. When I first reached the *Gaganagañja-parivarta*, I did not understand its meaning.
Closing my eyes to contemplate it, I was unaware that my body had risen into the air about three or four feet above my bed.

Suddenly he attained great enlightenment; ultimately, his literary wisdom emerged. His writing could not fully express [his realization], yet based on this, one can say that his resolve and strength were beyond compare.

He was indeed the son of the Gong family from Langzhong in the sea [of Sichuan]. Having left home at a young age, he possessed far-reaching aspirations. He encountered the flourishing state of the Buddha-dharma in the capital of Yangdu.

He then made a solemn vow to descend the gorges. Upon arriving in Jinling, he followed Master Yun to study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. He attended various lectures on the sutras and other texts, quickly establishing a reputation for purity.
Consequently, he led a separate assembly of his own, and his followers became numerous. At that time, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty held the Dharma in high esteem.
While he was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he commanded his teacher to debate the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The teacher then ascended the debating dais;

although they engaged in a back-and-forth exchange of arguments, the teacher continued to hold a brass incense burner. The Emperor remarked, "Although the Dharma Master has severed stinginess and greed, he will not grasp an incense burner unless it is made of brass.

The teacher replied instantly, "Your Majesty occupies the pinnacle of the imperial throne, yet you do not wear your crown and hairpin unless they are adorned with pheasant feathers. The Emperor was greatly pleased, and the entire assembly [applauded].

He was filled with wonder. Later, upon returning to Shu, he resided at Xie Temple and greatly propagated the study of the scriptures. When Prince Ji of Wuling established his seat of command at Jingluo, his reverence and affection for the Master were unending.
He frequently stayed overnight with the Master to request discussions on profound principles, forgetting both day and night.

At dawn, as the King was about to wash his hands and the sun’s shadow had just begun to appear, the King remarked: "The sunlight glows upon the plastered walls like the interior of a city; the wind stirs the *śāla*-pole."
The bell rang; only then did they realize they were inside the monastery. That morning, the king’s carriage canopies had come to meet him, and his horse neighed again.

The Master said, "From afar I saw the canopies move and rejoiced at meeting Chen Si; suddenly I heard the horse neigh and celebrated the encounter with Nāgārjuna. They emerged together, smiling with delight.
As the king ascended his carriage, he said to his attendants, "Listen to the words of Dharma Master Hǎi; they cause me to linger, unable to depart."
His eloquence was boundless and versatile; he served as a model for such excellence. Zhou Shi governed the regions of Liang and Yi, while Master Yong presided over his own domain;
both deepened their profound respect for him, elevating him far above the ranks of ordinary men. At the age of eighty, he said to his disciple Faming, "I am about to depart.
I have no anxieties regarding what lies ahead, but I grieve only that after my passing, the stupa planned for me might fall into ruin. I shall leave my body exposed to be devoured by birds."
During the Jiande era, he was indeed expelled and banished. Today, the temple buildings lie in ruin, with only a single hall remaining where the statues still stand.
Zhi-fang was a native of Zizhong;
his ancestors were from Eastern Wu, but his distant forebears served in the western region of Shu, where they eventually established their family. He was a child... [text fragment ends].
When Zhi was young, he entered the monastic order at Longyuan Temple in the prefectural seat under the tutelage of Master Lun.

Early on, he associated with Bao Hai and together they went to the school of Master Yun in Yangdu. His intellectual eloquence was sharp and incisive, and his reputation spread throughout the Yang and Yue regions.

Whenever he lectured and analyzed the meanings of words and phrases, his refined and elegant discourse flowed like a spring; consequently, laypeople and monks who took up paper to transcribe his teachings often numbered in the hundreds.
When he first lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, upon reaching the sublime and wondrous "Jeweled Stupa" chapter, he completed his exposition on the meaning of the King’s [relics].
He then remarked: "Why need one seek such sublime wonders only in the lands of past Buddhas? Even this blessed ground of the Yangdu capital is most magnificent.
Such is the Seven-Storied Pagoda that rivals the sun and moon for brilliance; the Nine-Storied [Pagoda] of Tongtai that vies with the mists and clouds for color; and the Fangjing [Pagoda]..."

The lotus petals hang downward; the circular rafters are laid out askew like lotus flowers. It resembles the dwelling of Anavatapta to the south and is akin to the subduing power of Nikha to the north.

Having heard it with my ears and seen it with my eyes, I hope that these accounts may be placed side by side. Those who have recorded this have kept it secret and brought it back, causing the people of Yizhou to sigh in wonder and utter cries of amazement.
Thus, when his words emerged, they formed complete chapters, appearing as if pre-composed; such was the marvel of the Ocean of Jewels.

[The interlocutor] came to pose a difficult challenge, bringing forth his eloquence and brilliance. Thus, Hai asked: "When you transformed this region three times, changing its filth into purity, were you also able to transform ordinary beings into sages?
He replied: "Transformation Buddhas are exceedingly numerous; because they are narrow, they must be expanded. As for ordinary beings and sages, they are naturally so."
"Why trouble yourself with such changes? Again he posed a difficult question: "If that were so, then sixty minor kalpas would be like the duration of a single meal;

this would be visible only to the sages, while ordinary people could not see it. If both ordinary people and sages could see it, then from the perspective of the ordinary person, both would be sages. The Master laughed and said, "When did I ever say such a thing on my high seat?
This was merely you speaking for yourself and posing a difficult question to yourself. Haijue’s words failed him, and he retorted with a verse: "A wooden dipper with three corners..."

"What do you mean by 'Wise Square'? he asked, and upon hearing the sound [of the voice], he replied: "How can broken tiles and a filthy pond be called a sea of jewels? The crowd laughed loudly and dispersed.
When his illness became severe, Hai (Ocean) came constantly to visit and console him. Zhifang then apologized, saying: "I was unable to maintain my health, leading to this deep-seated ailment.
I rely on your kindness in coming so often to inquire after me; I wish to be reborn in Sudarśana, where we may always wander together. Shortly thereafter—
A rare fragrance filled the room. He passed away at midnight in Yibu at the age of over ninety.
Xuánxù, surnamed Sāng, was a native of Chengdu. Having been a monk for a long time, he had mastered the path of the Dharma;

the *Nirvāṇa* and *Satyasiddhi* were the schools he studied, and he constantly lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, guiding and enlightening the ignorant. However, his demeanor was lofty and austere, and his deportment was dignified and composed.

In the course of conversation, his responses were swift and adaptable. He was proficient in non-Buddhist texts and skilled in cursive and clerical scripts. From time to time he composed verses, continuing the excellence of former masters.
Furthermore, he was humble enough to lower himself before others; whenever there were youths, whether monastics or laypeople, who possessed literary talent, he would summon them to converse with him.

He treated those he loved with intimacy. Yet, toward princes, kings, eminent lords, renowned scholars, and men of great virtue, he stood out with an air of haughty independence, never deigning to take them into account;

his spirit was even loftier still. His eloquence was comprehensive and as swift as a flash of lightning. There was one Xiao Pingzhong, a subordinate official in the Eastern Secretariat of Zizhou and the grandson of Xiao Gao, whose vast learning and intellectual acumen were peerless at the time.

When [the Master] went to visit him for conversation, his literary... (Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary, ending abruptly with "文" [literature/text]. The translation reflects the available portion.)
He gathered his followers to show them [the monk]. Pingzhong Shangzhi said with composure, "I have long admired your lofty character for disregarding the various nobles.
Now that I am honored by your visit, I feel deeply ashamed that I am no worthy recipient. The Master said, "The nobles are arrogant and haughty; I must respond to them with arrogance.
Your Excellency is broad-minded in your affection, so I answer you with broad-minded affection. Zhong said, "The Dharma Master has never been like this before; why is it suddenly so today?"
"However, I suspect this is empty talk; I fear it is not a factual record. He replied, "I, a poor monk, shall judge your truth or falsehood just as you judge the truth or falsehood of Xu.
They shared a laugh together. He once composed an inscription for the Bao Yuan Temple, in which he criticized Laozi and Zhuangzi, saying:
"Laozi is called a Sage and Zhuangzi is titled a Philosopher. To hold a firefly up to the sun, or to use a mountain to compare with [the vastness of heaven]..."

The dust belonged to the River-Jiang Daoist, Feng Shanying. He passed by the temple to pay his respects; upon seeing [the inscription], he loathed it and said to the Master, "In literary composition, each person speaks of their own excellence.
To maliciously slander others—your intentions are truly unknown. If you do not remove and change this, I am an Imperial Messenger and shall report this immediately to the Emperor.
The Master replied, "The style and substance of literary composition are not something you understand. If you were to report this to the Emperor..."
"Envoy, if you wish to intimidate me with your authority, my temple appoints a person annually to manage the estate; this is an imperial authorization and also an imperial decree.
You wish to petition against me, but the person managing my estate is also capable of petitioning against you. Although Ying was deeply resentful, he could do nothing about it.
Daoji’s surname was Lü; he was a native of Dongping in Henan. By nature, he possessed innate wisdom, and his reputation for precocity was well-established.
At the mere age of fourteen, he traveled to Pengcheng with his books, listening extensively to various masters. As he heard their teachings, he perfected his virtue;

when discussing profound doctrines, his understanding transcended the words themselves, and when analyzing novel insights, his thought soared beyond the written text. Thus, Xu and Xu [the two masters] spread his fame.

Minglue’s principles were so profound that the rivers and seas esteemed his righteous guidance; consequently, his peers held him in the highest esteem and those who had attained prior cultivation looked up to him as their superior.

Yang Su, the Grand Marshal and Chief Minister of State under the Sui dynasty, possessed great talent for governing the realm and held total authority over the scales of power. Having once received Minglue’s pure teachings, he personally prostrated himself in respectful homage.
As they discussed the principles of the Dharma, Yang Su sighed with choked emotion and turned to his fellow ministers and elders, saying: "Master Ji is the very foundation of the Buddha-dharma."

Subsequently, he was invited to reside there. Having personally encountered renowned monks, he found few who could equal him as a peer. He was thus invited to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) to lecture and propagate the *Śata-śāstra* (*Xinlun*).
Having long since received his illustrious influence and already possessing a foundational understanding of the essential path, he wielded his skill across all Buddhist schools with ease;

his profound insights were preeminent, enabling him to discourse with a torrential flow like a cascading river, his responses resonating like rolling thunder. At that time, in the first year of the Daye era, the reign of the Sui dynasty was at its zenith, and the study of the Dharma flourished.
Surpassing wind and clouds, the gentry stand as lofty as mountains. All of them embrace the scriptures and frequent the lecture halls, seeking the Way and knowing its ultimate destination.

Following one another like the tracks of a carriage wheel, they gather like scales from near and far. Thus, he compiled the *Zaxin xuanyang* (Mysterious Chapters on Miscellaneous Minds) in eight scrolls, including various excerpts, to be transmitted to the world.

Having mastered all the gateways, he followed the guidance of the ancients; yet while all previous works were woven and analyzed with great detail, his words soar to the heavens, providing a comprehensive narrative.

His style was both elevating and tempering; his model surpassed that of antiquity. From that time on, he became the leader for all within the four seas, and the flourishing *Huiri* (Wisdom Sun) Monastery was established as his seat.

All who observed his spiritual aura took him as their teacher, and those who followed his guidance knew how to return to the source. Because the Master’s honor was preeminent beyond comparison and his refined resonance transcended the world, in the fifth year of the Daye era, an imperial edict summoned him to come and reside [at court].
Thereupon, he expounded profound discourses before the Emperor, fully satisfying the Heavenly Will. The Sui Sovereign then relinquished his worldly governance to the profound [Dharma].

The Confucian official was about to visit the Buddhist headquarters to oversee the assembly of scholars. He personally presided over the debating arena as his imperial carriage moved slowly, the sound of flutes filling the royal highway.

The imperial banquet was briefly suspended as he halted his progress to pay respects at the gates of the teaching institution. Since the Great Dharma flowed eastward, this gathering has been the most magnificent spectacle.
At that time, those who had donned their robes of debate were all enjoying great reputations; yet, when it came to ascending the Dharma seat, each excelled in their own way.

A hero whose liberation finds its ultimate refuge, he bowed together with his teachers to become a profound sovereign. His fame rested upon the expectations of the multitude; his virtue unfolded as a grand design for governance.
First, he established the great framework of the state; subsequently, he illuminated the imperial majesty. The hundred officials and ministers all marveled at his rare and sublime voice.

When the Sui dynasty fell and its mandate was lost, bandits ravaged the Central Plains. Seeking the rites among the four barbarian tribes, Confucius had issued his directive; thus, [the Master] beat the drum and set forth toward Nanzheng. He unfurled...
He taught in Ximin, whereupon those from Ba and Shu flocked together like birds in flight, gathering from afar as soon as they caught sight of his presence.

There was none who did not clear away the drifting mists [of ignorance], so that the heterodox and the orthodox were clearly distinguished. He studied the Mahāyāna, propagated the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, rectified what had been previously transmitted, and compiled what had been lost.

His realization surpassed that of former times, and his fame spread throughout the realm. Because he perceived that his disciples found it difficult to follow his path and that those inheriting his legacy were prone to lose their way, he further composed the *Da...* (Great...).
The *Shengzhang chao* (Commentary on the Chapter on the Vehicle) consists of eight fascicles. Its phrasing is consistently pure and profound, and its moral teachings are systematic and comprehensive.
Thus, those who peruse its volumes or step upon its carriage are as if ascending the Dragon Gate; it is truly believed that there will be a day when one gradually advances like a great bird.

Therefore, in the capital during the Zhenguan era, this work was transcribed and circulated by monks renowned throughout the realm, serving as a true seal of authentication. Yet, because the succession of generations is impermanent and human life is but a temporary sojourn.
While preparing a commentary on the treatise, he passed away suddenly. He died at Fugan Temple in Yibu in the second month of the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, at the age of over sixty.
Lingrui’s surname was Chen. He was originally from Yingchuan, but had become a resident in Chenxiang, Yichang, in the region of Shu. His ancestors had intermarried with the Li clan.
On the eighth day of the second month, his mother attended a vegetarian feast held at a Daoist temple and prayed for a son.

Upon returning home, she dreamed that she was sitting beneath a pine grove when a bowl made of the seven treasures flew down from the treetop and entered her mouth; she immediately felt [a sensation].

While pregnant, she took no pleasure in the five pungent vegetables. After her delivery, whenever she consumed meat or strong flavors, both mother and child suffered from headaches; consequently, she observed the fast.
At the age of eight, her parents took her to a Daoist master and had her recite the *Buxu ci* (Verses on Wandering in Emptiness).

Her face bled, so she returned home and entered the fields, where she encountered the Dharma Master Zhisheng. She then said, "My family lineage honors the Dao, yet I myself wish to honor the Buddha. She followed the Master.
He left the household life and was taken to Shengye Monastery in Yizhou to become a śrāmaṇera. Within a single summer, he mastered the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* through oral recitation.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, Master Yin of Goguryeo entered Shu to lecture on the *Sanlun*. He subsequently became a disciple of Yin.

His constant practice was the Mahāyāna. Later, he followed [the imperial court] into the capital, where he traveled about listening to various teachings. At the end of the Daye era, he returned once more to the region of Shu and resided at Faju Monastery.
In the second year of the Wude era, Master Gao of Anzhou traveled up to Shu and lectured on the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* at Dajianchang Monastery.
The Master attended these dharma assemblies for three years, after which he returned to his original residence, where he constantly propagated this sūtra for another two years.
"Granted. There is a follower of heterodox teachings in the monastery, a partisan of the *Tattvasiddhi* school, who resents this discourse on emptiness and constantly undermines my mind.

He intends to harbor malice toward me. The Master was staying in his room, leaning against the northern wall. At the first watch of the night, he returned to his bed; restless and unsettled, the hair on his body stood on end.
He moved to the southern bed and sat there until the third watch, when he suddenly heard something outside the northern wall striking and passing through."
He went to his sleeping quarters to look; it was a lacquered bamboo shafted spear about twenty feet long that had been placed as if on a bed, its point piercing through the body.
Having failed in his attempt to kill him, the assailant then hired a thief with a silver ingot to enter the room. The Master sat by a desk, searching for the man but finding no one;
there was only a suit of armor at the place where he usually sat. The Master realized that this was an act of malice intended to harm him.
He was immediately transferred to Longji Temple in Yichang, Mianzhou. His physical appearance was dark and short, standing only five chi tall.
Wherever his words reached, he prioritized comprehensive insight; he constantly lectured on the Mahāyāna as his primary vocation. In the first year of the Zhenguan era.
The Dhyāna Master Xian of Tongzhou served as a patron (*dānapati*), providing all necessary supplies for the Master’s entire life.

On the night of the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month in the seventh year, the Master dreamed that he was welcomed by figures in official robes and cap, and Xian departed for the Western Land. The bowls of the disciples were all empty and contained nothing.
On the thirtieth day, the temple bells and chimes all rang out simultaneously. At the third watch, Xian sat upon the meditation seat.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. The Master traveled extensively, preaching and chanting, and his transmission of the Dharma continued without interruption.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month in the twentieth year, at the third watch of the night, a great wind suddenly arose. The assembly heard a voice say:

"Dharma Master Lingrui will go to a great kingdom in the South Sea in the tenth month of next year; he shall be reborn on the western slope of Mount Guangming as an emanation of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva."

On the third day of the tenth month, when the appointed time arrived, the elders and juniors, monastics and laypeople of the entire monastery saw banners and flowers descend from the sky, and Bodhisattvas filled the temple.
Yet the Master remained seated in his room reading a sutra. A monk outside informed the Master that banners, flowers, and extraordinary fragrances were pervading the temple.

Upon hearing this, the Master took up his scripture and went out to look; he stood with a composed countenance until the end, remaining firm and upright without falling. They then supported him back to his room and laid him down.
At the third watch of the night, he suddenly rose and sat cross-legged as if returning to life. The Prefect personally presented him with incense as an offering.

Monastics and laypeople escorted him back to Mount Dongdu, where a great assembly was convened. At that time, he was eighty-three years old. Indeed, his purity was such that from childhood he had never consumed meat or pungent vegetables;
it is said that he received such a reward for this.
Sengfu was the son of Wang of Qixian County in Taiyuan. In his early twenties, he was austere and diligent; his discernment surpassed that of his peers.

Having passed the age of elementary study, his realization had matured into a vast capacity. His fellow villagers marveled at his excellence, and those who lacked benevolence kept their distance from him. By nature he loved tranquility, yet he traveled regardless of the distance.

Carrying provisions, he sought out teachers to inquire about what he had not yet mastered. There was Master Bodhidharma, who was skilled in clarifying contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and followed the flow of worldly distractions.

He dwelt in mountain caves and grottoes, inquiring into matters with profound and extensive depth. Upon leaving the household life, he never asked a question twice; everything was integrated within his breast.

Seeking out the origins and tracing the ultimate threads of the teachings, he established himself as a patriarch of the school of meditative discipline (*samādhi*). Later, he traveled extensively among lecture halls, becoming proficient in both the *sūtras* and the *śāstras*. His studies were solely for his own edification.
The Sage is without words. During the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, he traveled south to Yangyuan and stayed at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong.
He admired its groves and marshes as an excellent place for his mind to find repose. His conduct was as steadfast as ice and frost, and his words were always trustworthy.

His three robes and six requisites never exceeded what was necessary. When he entered the villages in accordance with the season, both monastics and laypeople looked up to him in reverence; furthermore, he was invited by princes and nobles.

The Master was humble and free from self-importance. Although the imperial palace was but a few paces away, he never once went to pay his respects. Having become a model for all beings, he was the object of devotion for both the clergy and the laity.
Emperor Gao of the Liang dynasty, who had long admired his pure character and held him in high esteem, ordered craftsmen to construct a residence at Kaishan Temple to accommodate him.
Fearing that the Master might harbor thoughts of seclusion in the mountains and forests, the Emperor would often find him wandering leisurely about the gate. Carrying...
Leaning on his staff, he sighed and said: "In a room with walls of earth and a thatched roof, with a door of wild grass and a window like a jar, sitting upright within it is still sufficient for joy.
Why should one prize broad palaces and despise thatch-roofed huts? Furthermore, to be at peace yet capable of moving on is what the ancients esteemed;

why must one remain stagnant here merely to indulge the pleasures of the ears and eyes? Thereupon, his heart turned toward the Min Mountains, and he set out to behold Mount Emei, meeting [them] in the West.

Marquis Chang Xiao Yuanzao was dispatched to govern the Shu region. [Huiyuan] immediately donned his robes and attached himself to him. Upon reaching Jingluo, although the road passed through the Nine Bends, he did not forget the Three Contemplations.
Furthermore, because he had cherished the scriptures since his youth, he would hold his scrolls in silent contemplation, moving with them as the hours of dawn and noon passed.
Consequently, the Chan teachings of the Yong and Shu regions flourished greatly from that time on. After a long while, he returned to Jinling and once again resided at Kaiyuan Temple.
"Excellent. Previously, at Mount Huyi, a divine being appeared and bestowed the *Huiyin sanmei* (Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom) upon the rustic man He Gui, saying:
"You may give this scripture to Prince Nanping and have him observe a seven-day fast for his illness."
If one does not understand this method, one should consult it with a secondary source to investigate it. It turned out that this was indeed a practice he had previously performed;

Nanping subsequently carried out the ritual fast and sacrifice, and his illness was immediately restored. Is this not a case where internal causes and external conditions combine, mutually giving rise to one another?
He passed away not long after at Kaishan Temple at the age of sixty-one; this was the fifth year of the Putong era.
He was interred outside the eastern gate of the Lower Dinglin Monastery. The Emperor mourned him and issued an imperial decree bestowing posthumous honors.

Initially, there were those who urged him to cultivate merit through material offerings, but the Master spoke with a stern voice, saying, "To prolong one's life with wealth and goods is far removed from the Way. Consequently, he donated all the household articles within his quarters as alms.

"Regarding the Sangha of the four quarters: after my passing, you should simply abandon me in the mountains and valleys to be nourished by the offerings of birds; do not prepare a coffin or a grave mound, for that would contradict my intent.
His disciples wept and could not bear to follow this command, intending instead to carve a stele to commemorate his virtue.

However, Princess Yongxing, who had long possessed faith in him, submitted a memorial to the Crown Prince requesting that he compose the inscription. An imperial decree was issued, dispatching the Prince of Xiangdong to do so.
Yi erected a stele for him at the monastery.
Tanxun was of the Yang clan, a native of Huayin in Hongnong; later he moved his residence to Hedong Commandery. From his youth, he delighted in the Way.
Having long been confined within the cage of worldly life, at the age of twenty-two, he finally renounced secular affairs and traveled far to seek seclusion among the crags.
Upon reaching Linluoquan Temple on the northern side of Mount Bailu, he met Chan Master Tanzhun and received the tonsure. After another year had passed, he completed his full ordination.

He maintained strict discipline in his self-cultivation, taking the study of the mind as his primary principle. His resolve was singular and fierce; though his companions preceded him, he remained fully prepared.

Regarding the precepts: he also recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. When early summer arrived, he returned to his master to pursue his settled practice. Learning that the monk Chou was residing at Canggu Valley, he went there to inquire about the Vinaya.

Chou, who was himself a master of the mountain of meditative concentration as previously described in the earlier records, had already paid him respectful salutations from afar due to the fame of his reputation.

Since their dwellings were in different forests, their spiritual refinement reached its ultimate depth; yet, wishing to manifest this through personal meeting, he frequently sought an opportunity to visit.

Separated [from the world], yet because the path was rarely trodden by humans and the ridges abounded with wild beasts, I had long dwelt in seclusion; my nature thus became unaccustomed to the dust of the mundane world.

When coming and going to seek clarification of doubts, there was no way to follow the trails of woodcutters. I simply gazed toward the azure valley as my guide for travel; though thorns, brambles, sand, and gravel were difficult to traverse, I did not find them hard to cross.

Amidst the vast crags and deep recesses, I climbed and ascended by clinging to the rocks; my will remained fixed on right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), never allowing myself to follow a deviant path.
"Penetration. Furthermore, one may extend benefit to others through side-paths; yet because these are circuitous, they obstruct direct progress.

Although my current drifting fingers find it difficult, I must advance straight ahead to measure my practice. To employ this subtle intention, following objects and attaching to the mind—is this not excellent? He would often say:
'Rather than losing the Way and merely achieving success, it is better to accord with the Way and remain unsuccessful. Therefore, he traversed heavy obstacles."

Difficulties were endless. After three summers had passed, he moved to Lùtǔgǔ to practice dhyāna. Coincidentally, a dried-up spring gushed forth once more, and deer and elk gathered around the monastery.
Thus, he obtained fine water and tamed beasts, daily providing for himself and his neighbors. His disciples, who followed him in study, congratulated one another on this auspicious omen.
At that time, while seeking instruction, he went briefly to Yúnmén; encountering thick mist and gloom along the path, he lost his way. Fortunately, he relied upon the mountain...
The divine revealed the path; thus he finally understood his original course. This was a manifestation of spiritual resonance within the netherworld, where divine intelligences provided protection.
Once, a thief came to steal vegetables; as he was about to leave the garden, he was stung by a swarm of bees.

When the Master heard of this, he went to rescue him and treated him with a compassionate heart, thereby saving his remaining life. On another occasion, a man from Zhao arrived from afar and paid him reverent homage with great earnestness, saying: "Because..."

Having died of illness and revived, he was thus graced by divine favor. When he went to see King Yama, who interrogated him regarding his offenses for which he ought to enter prison, he relied upon the Zen Master Tanxun, who came to petition for his life;
consequently, the King released and pardoned him. Having never understood how this had come about since his birth, he sought it out and only then investigated the matter.

Furthermore, while traveling in the mountains, he encountered two tigers fighting, which did not cease for a long time; the Master then took up his monk’s staff to separate them, using his own body as [a barrier].

Yi said, "We dwell together in these woods and thickets; there is no great cause for conflict. It would be fortunate if we each took our own paths. The tiger lowered its head and accepted his command, then withdrew in silence.
On many occasions he encountered bears and tigers contending with one another, and the circumstances were much the same.

Yet, when he dwelt alone amidst the brambles and thorns, he was the only trace of humanity to be seen. Birds did not scatter in alarm, and beasts regarded him as a companion. This, moreover, was the manifestation of his hidden virtue moving all living things.

He employed this to achieve benevolence. How could one not praise him? Whenever he entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he would remain for a period of seven days. A white tiger would enter his room and make it its dwelling place.
He dwelt alone in a quiet courtyard for no less than ten years; his traces of meditation were such that few could emulate them.

From then on, his transformation spread throughout the region north of the Yellow River, where he extensively propagated the Chan school. People traveled there with staffs in hand and provisions wrapped about them, returning like scales of fish and gathering like mist. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty held him in high esteem.

His virtuous reputation inspired profound sincerity and reverent devotion. An imperial decree was issued by Yuanshou, the Minister of the Three Departments, to personally escort the imperial letter along with offerings of incense.

In the nineteenth year of the Kaihuang era, his wind-disorder suddenly intensified, and he passed away at Bajian Mountain Temple at the age of eighty, having completed fifty-five years of summer retreats.

The monk Yuan was surnamed Li and was a native of Qi.
His family had long been immensely wealthy, renowned throughout Ba and Shu. When the Master was first born, the heavens...
Copper coins rained down into the courtyard; the entire household gathered them together until every place was filled.
His father grew weary from carrying the money and cried out, "Stop! but the coins no longer fell. The rice stored in the granary reached only halfway up when it suddenly overflowed.
All his relatives, both near and far, marveled at such fortune. From childhood until adulthood, his character and resolve were extraordinary; he moved with calm composure.

Whenever he sat, he was invariably in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). His gaze radiated outward, emitting a brilliant, flickering luster. His complexion was as smooth and lustrous as jade, yet his countenance appeared like refined red copper.
His voice was like a great bell; when it resounded, it seemed to shake the forest. On the soles of his two feet, the marks of the wheels (*cakrāṅka*) were clearly defined with ten spokes.

On his two hands, the nine-petaled *svastika* patterns were as distinct as if they had been painted. At the age of eighteen, he stood seven feet tall. His father marveled at these signs and granted him permission to leave the household life (*pravrajyā*). (2)
He was escorted by his parents as far as Kanghyeong-sa Temple west of the city to undergo tonsure; this is the present-day Bogeun-sa Temple.

He sought out enlightened masters extensively, and whatever sutras or treatises he read never failed to remain in his memory. He gathered all knowledge within his breast, revering the precepts and maintaining his simple nature; he wore robes made of coarse cloth.
Aside from his flask and bowl, he accumulated no other possessions. He was a close associate of Dharma Master Yi of the same monastery;
both were the most eminent and talented among the monks of Shu Commandery. Accompanying one another, they entered the capital to extensively seek out new and extraordinary teachings.

There was a śramaṇa named Sengbao of Zhuhui Monastery whose path of dhyāna was profound and subtle, and whom the Emperor held in high esteem; [Daoxuan] relied upon him to study meditative concentration, whereupon he suddenly understood the ford. Having traveled through...

Regarding the fluctuations of heat and cold: having meticulously examined the meanings of the words, Master Yanliang refined his studies to establish the Way. Yi was extensively proficient in the classics and arts;

from the *Qiu* and *Suo* to the cursive and clerical scripts, there was nothing he did not devote his attention to. When Emperor Wu of the Zhou abolished the teachings, he returned to his former monastery and partitioned the eastern wing of his quarters to serve as a private residence.

The remainder was offered to the government. When the Sui dynasty’s mandate opened, the construction was renewed and restructured. As the master craftsmen were felling timber, rain fell continuously for two months.

The Master held his incense burner and offered prayers; as soon as he spoke, the sky cleared. For the pagoda, a golden plate was required, so he again petitioned the underworld. Following his words, they immediately began digging.

Upon opening the hidden treasury as commanded, there was sufficient gold, and the surplus returned to its original cave. Considering the power of such merit, it is remarkable throughout both ancient and modern times.

I have not heard of such a thing. He constantly provided for the solitary and orphaned, never opposing the wishes of others, and assisted those from far and near; his distribution of wealth was like flowing water.
Furthermore, as many people were being drowned in the waves of the Jinshui River, he intended to construct a flying bridge across the southern road. Hardly had he struck upon this plan when—

All matters were gathered together. Formerly, Zhuge Wuhou pointed within the two rivers to construct the Seven-Star Bridge and to forge three iron *dui* (gongs), each eight or nine feet long and about three feet in diameter;
people called them "iron spears. He intended to strike the bridge pillars with them, and once their use was finished, he cast them into the river.
Whenever one needed to pray at the shrine, they would emerge from the water. When the Master was constructing the new bridge and was about to erect the pillars, those gongs spontaneously...

However, he swam across the water to reach the bridge-head; when the bridge was completed, he again threw himself into the water. The songs and chants of the clergy and laity concerning this still linger in people's ears today.
Both masters Sengyuan and Fayi served as models for all beings; morning and evening they inquired after the Dharma, never failing in their entrusted devotion.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Renshou era, at the hour of the tiger (3–5 a.m.), Master Fayi said to his disciples: "The three realms are without..."
"Permanence! I am about to depart. Having finished these words, his spirit withdrew; Fuyuan remained at his original dwelling. He was sixty-nine years old.
When Master [Falin] heard of this, he said with deep sorrow, "Master Yi has already passed away; how could I remain alone? Shortly thereafter, he fell ill.
His remains were buried together with those of the other master, and on the fourteenth day of that same month, he also passed away. He was eighty-four years old. This occurred on the seventeenth day.
They were buried together at Jiulitang. A stone was inscribed to record this at the temple hall; Chen Ziliang composed the text.
Fajin resided at Yunüsi on Mount Xiying in Mianzhu County, Yizhou, and was a disciple of Master Huī.

Later, he received the ten precepts from Dharma Master Ding. He was reverent, diligent, and sincere, making humility and respect his primary concern. He devoted himself solely to the practice of seated meditation.
Behind the temple was a bamboo grove where he frequently sat; four tigers and leopards would circle him on both sides. The Master told them not to reveal his spiritual capacity.
Later, as he practiced the contemplation of water (*āpasmṛti-bhāvanā*), his family members went to gather firewood and saw clear, pure water upon his rope bed, which they picked up.
He placed two white stones in the water. When the Master returned to the monastery at dusk, he felt a distinct pain in his back.
He asked his family members, "Did you place any stones there? They replied that they had. The Master instructed them, "Go and remove those stones tomorrow morning.

At dawn, while the Master remained in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the family members saw that the water was as clear as before; they immediately removed the stones, and his pain vanished instantly. Thereafter, he practiced meditation without ever leaving this spot.

Shan Huixi was a native of Pei in Yizhou. His surname was Zhao. He entered the monastic order in his childhood and was proficient in the phonology and prosody of the classics. His literary compositions were elegant and well-structured.
He shared equal renown with Rongzhi of Zhenxiang Temple in Mianzhou; both were śrāmaṇeras who stood out for their exceptional talent and brilliant promise.
Later, while composing verses in rhyming succession with the śrāmaṇera Daowei of Dashi Temple in Chengdu, he encountered a verbal disagreement with Wei.
Consequently, he withdrew from worldly affairs and settled his mind in the practice of dhyāna. Upon reaching the age for full ordination, he extensively studied the sūtras and vinaya;

he extracted their essence and used it as his primary standard. He thoroughly investigated the ultimate truths of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, and was especially devoted to the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*), which were his primary object of contemplation.

Huiyuan once challenged Dharma Master Sengji on the doctrine of "dusty consciousness" (*rajas-vijñāna*). He initially questioned him using the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) perspective, to which Sengji responded by interpreting it through the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).

Huiyuan laughed and said, "The Great [Vehicle] encompasses everything that is not subsumed; however, you have lost the core tenets of the Small [Vehicle]. Later, he resided at Konghui Temple south of the prefecture.

By nature solitary and upright, he did not associate with the crowd. He was frugal regarding food and rest, devoting himself exclusively to contemplating the profound and the mysterious. He remained seated behind closed doors for twenty years.

On another day, because he had not eaten for so long, the assembly feared his life would be endangered. Using a pretext, they said, "The state is urgently searching for those with artistic and technical skills.
Since you have been fasting and staying shut in your room, the people of the world call you a sage; we pray you will cease these rumors and join the assembly at the proper time.
Fearing that this was a deceptive maneuver, the Master immediately opened the door and partook of food. From then until now, nearly thirty years have passed. One.
He lived alone and did not keep attendants. He took but one meal a day and did not accept offerings from others. Whenever there was a lecture, he would listen;

at night, he slept in his own room, sitting only upon his meditation seat. Dust accumulated on both ends of it. Aside from a single footprint on the floor of his quarters, everything else was covered in moss and green lichen.
His robes were tattered and worn, barely sufficient to ward off wind and cold; in winter he added a quilted robe, and in summer he wore plain cotton.
He wore robes made from tattered winter rags and hung them upon a beam. When someone heard the Master’s name and came to his room to pay their respects, he would go out to meet and receive them;

it was only after several days that they would actually see him. Whenever he posed profound questions, his speech was lofty and far-reaching. Those who had previously occupied the foremost seats all stood in awe of him.
He passed away at the age of ninety.
Shi Yu’s secular surname was Chen. He resided in Taizhou. His parents died early, so he supported himself through manual labor.
His physique was robust and tall, measuring eight chi and three cun. He aspired toward the principles of the Buddha, yet had no means to achieve his goal.

In the twelfth year of the Daye era, he went to Master Lun at Zhenxiang Temple in Mianzhou to receive the precepts. He practiced the dhūta of eating once a day, persevering with constant diligence. Next, he went to...
Originally registered in Lizhou, he resided at a temple there. Later, he went to Mount Xiangying in Mianzhu County, Yizhou, where he lived alone for many years.

Four monkeys provided him with sustenance. There was a lay devotee surnamed Mu who passed by the mountain; he was astonished to see that even in such a remote wilderness, incense such as *kunkuma* and *agallochum* was being burned constantly.
As he reached the midpoint of the mountain, he saw two figures of a blue-green hue, their appearance extraordinary, each carrying—
Above him were lotuses, sugarcane, and taro; he then asked where he was going. The man replied, "I am going to provide for the Dhyāna Master.
Thus he lived in the mountains for three years, consuming only a little over one *shí* of rice. He practiced the Way during the six periods of the day, taking monkeys and birds as his companions.
Initially there was but a single spring, but later three springs emerged together. In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he dreamed that four dragons entered his bosom; upon waking, he felt great...

Having realized the essential tenets of the Three Treatises (Sanlun), he subsequently went to attend the lectures of Dharma Master Lingrui. The words and principles he heard there were as if they were old acquaintances;
he immediately reviewed and recounted them. He then traveled to Mianzhou and resided at Dashisi. Later, he went to Chonglesisi and announced his intention to travel abroad.
Someone remarked, "This very place is 'all quarters' (zhufang). He returned once more to Dashisi, where a fragrant aroma filled the chamber as he sat in meditation.
Three gold coins were found where he had passed away. The Master then sat cross-legged; holding an incense burner in his hand, he passed into extinction.
The Regional Inspector Liu Dewei, delighted by what he had never heard before, constructed a shrine to enshrine him. For three years, the body did not fall over. He was sixty-three years of age.

he only regretted not taking more, as if wishing to swallow the sea itself. While traveling for trade, he reached Niutou Mountain in Xincheng Commandery, Zizhou, where he encountered the Chan Master Sengda preaching the Dharma, which said:
"Birth and death are long-lasting; there is no love that does not end in separation. Even one's own body..."
How much more so, then, regarding material wealth? When the teacher first heard this, joy and vigor arose within him, and he reflected deeply, saying:

"Throughout my life, I have been full of greed and have aspired to the accumulation of possessions. Now that I have heard the True Dharma, it is clear that this teaching is ultimate. Whether I lose what I have or am separated from it, this must inevitably happen.
It would be better to sink my treasures into the river, leave the household life to abandon attachment, and remain in a state of quietude free from disturbance. Would that not be a source of joy?"
He immediately sank one boat into the deep river. He was about to sink another as well, but the crowd collectively stopped him, urging him to cultivate meritorious deeds.

The Master said, "In the end, it will only lead to turmoil and cause hardship for both myself and others. He then sank that boat as well. He took leave of his wife and children and went to see Da-fang.
Seeing the frozen water shimmering and surging, he knew that [Da-fang] had entered meditative concentration (samādhi), and his faith grew even deeper. He then went to Zhulin Temple on Mount Guankou.
He then left the household life. On the day he first cut his hair, he made a vow before the assembly, saying: "If I do not attain the Way, I shall not leave this mountain.

He immediately withdrew from the tracks of men and built a dwelling in a mountain cleft; companions who practiced meditation gathered there one after another. Whenever he read the scriptures, he would...

When people first began to see that the Buddha was in such-and-such a place, there were none who did not choke with emotion, crying out, "Why have I not encountered him? I see only his remaining writings.
Thus he stood preeminent and beyond compare. Whenever anyone came to inquire or study with him, he would respond with skillful means, his answers resonating in profound accord with the True Dharma.

From the time he first entered meditative absorption, he would remain seated for four or five days at a stretch; this was his constant practice. At times, he would announce in advance that a guest would arrive the following day, and it always happened exactly as he said.
Prince Dan of Shixing of the Liang dynasty, who had traveled through the three regions of Shu with his curtains drawn aside, honored him with the respect due to a teacher.

He brought him to Juyu in Shanfu, and in the sixteenth year of the Tianjian era, they arrived at Qingxi Mountain, where [the Master] formed the intention to spend the remainder of his life there. Thus...

He cleared away the weeds so that only a rope bed could fit. At that time, the Daoist hermitage was spacious and open, and the practitioners in their head-cloths and coarse robes were numerous and bustling;

they frequently rebuked him, causing him great anxiety. Yet the Master remained composed and unruffled, showing not the slightest sign of agitation. One night, the Daoists suddenly saw a fire break out on the eastern ridge;
fearing that a wildfire would burn and harm the Master, they each took up water vessels to come to his rescue. When they arrived, they found the Master sitting there as usual.
A great fire broke out with fierce, blazing flames. All marveled at the divine power of the Fire God.

The Daoist Li Xuezu and others donated land to create an image, and the temple and stupa were suddenly completed. People from near and far turned to him in faith; nine out of ten households became his followers.

The Regional Inspector, Prince Huai of Poyang, personally paid homage and received his teachings. Toward the end of the Tianjian era, Prince Shixing had a mysterious spiritual response at Liangtai Temple.
He fashioned images of the Four Heavenly Kings. Every morning on the six days of the *poṣadha*, he would regularly prepare pure offerings.
Later, when the Master attended the assembly, five-colored light radiated from the crowns of the four kings' heads, and incense smoke spontaneously rose from the censer the Master held.

In the past, during his humble and lowly days, Taiwei Lu Fahe had lived in the mountains for several years serving as the Master’s attendant. When some monks rebuked him, the Master said: "This man is a member of the Three Dukes."
"Noble Lord, for what reason do you revile us? We both cannot fathom your nobility. Thereupon, Huo indeed ascended in ceremonial robes.

Whenever the Master was fatigued or ill, he saw a youth in pale-blue garments emerge from the Qingchi Stream, carrying a bowl filled with marvelous medicine, which he knelt before him to offer for his consumption.
He recovered in no time at all. He dwelt in the mountains for twenty-eight years, after which he traveled to Jingluo, where his transformative teachings spread widely.

At a time of severe drought, the common people requested prayers; the Master went directly to the dragon’s lair and struck its door with his staff, saying three times, "Why do sentient beings indulge in such excessive sleep?
Having finished speaking, he ascended into the void. Immediately, dark clouds gathered from all sides and a torrential rain poured down, upon which the people relied [for their survival].
All those who receive this grace come to offer prayers of thanksgiving, reverently regarding him as a celestial deity. Whenever they require śarīra relics, they immediately make a petition;
he arrives at the mere thought of him, providing exactly what is needed.

The Venerable Master Xiang was unfathomable in his origins. At the beginning of the Liang dynasty, he arrived at Feifu Temple on Mount Qingcheng in Yizhou, where he joyfully resolved to spend the rest of his life there.

At that time, according to local custom, people would invariably go to the mountains for excursions and picnics on the third day of the third month, often bringing wine and meat to indulge in revelry together.
The Master constantly exhorted them to change their ways, yet they remained unswayed. On the third day of the third month the following year, it was just as before.
The preceding assembly had concluded according to custom. The Master ordered his attendants to dig a pit in the square area of the seat; no one knew his intention.

He said to the people, "You patrons always eat and drink yourselves, yet you have never given anything to me. Today, for the sake of the assembly, we must take one meal. Everyone vied with one another to offer delicacies and wine;
as they were received, they were consumed until exhausted, as if filling a vast chasm. Those who understood him were struck with wonder. When [the meal was finished],...
In the evening, he said, "I am greatly intoxicated and satiated. Support me to the pit; otherwise, I shall soil the ground. When they reached the pit, he opened his mouth and vomited profusely.
As the chicken meat left his mouth, it immediately flew and cried out; as the mutton left his mouth, it immediately galloped away. The wine and food poured out in disarray, nearly filling the pit.
Fish, shrimp, geese, and ducks swam and frolicked amidst one another. Everyone was filled with wonder and sighed in amazement. He then vowed to renounce pungent flavors.
He executed [the man], and from that time on, the consumption of wine and meat was permanently discontinued upon ascending the mountain. The virtuous influence of this master still endures today.
Luo Yan, the Regional Inspector (Biejia) of Yizhou, served the Liang dynasty. When Master Zhigong said to him, "Is incense expensive or cheap in Yizhou?

he replied, "It is very cheap. At first, Yan did not realize that [Zhigong] was a supernatural person. Zhigong said, "Since it is so cheap for people, why do you linger here so long? Yan could not fathom the meaning of these words.
Someone said, "This must be the Venerable Master Xiang of Qingcheng. He then went to the mountain and related the matter in detail.

The Master said, "Since you, donor, have come from afar, it cannot be a false report. That very night, he passed away. His disciples prepared a tomb for the funeral; they found the coffin suspiciously light.
When he opened [the door], he saw only a small table and a staff.

Dhyāna Master You of Duobao Monastery in Yizhou was a man of the Dao named Lin, the son of the Yang family. He applied himself to recitation for over forty years, never ceasing from morning until night.
On the wall behind his room in the courtyard, he had painted the nine meditations on the repulsiveness of the body; he kept his rope bed exposed and covered it with a *zōng* mat.
During the day, he followed the monastic custom; at night, he slept within his cell. Throughout the entire day, he would take only one meal.

In this manner, he gradually increased the interval until he ate only once every seven days. The monks took this as their constant routine and did not find it strange. In this way, more than twenty years passed.
When a month had passed and he still had not emerged, they decided that since he kept no attendants, his failure to emerge was surely due to him having entered meditative absorption;

thus, they did not trouble themselves to look for him. Suddenly one night, during heavy wind and rain, the painted walls and corridors collapsed. When dawn broke, the assembly went to inspect the site.
He tried to pull back the coconut-fiber quilt, but saw nothing at all; only the rope bed and sitting mat remained.
As for the monk Dū, no one knew his origins; he traveled between towns and fields without any fixed residence, and people of the time called him a madman.
During the Zhou dynasty, King Zhao was in Yizhou. There was a man named Wang Hou from the city of Pi who, being on intimate terms with the king, intended to rebel.

Someone reported this to the king, but he did not yet believe it. At dawn, the troops of Pi indeed arrived; Wang Hou was leading them at the main street west of the city, sitting upon a large square couch.
At that moment, the Master (the narrator) was wearing a single leather boot; he passed through the western part of the city, dropping excrement as he fled, until he reached Pan.

"Tata! Discard your boots and turn back. The crowd found this strange and could not fathom its meaning. Furthermore, one who was about to return requested the Master to determine whether his journey would be auspicious or ominous using paper and brush.
The Master took up the brush and wrote the two characters "Zhou-du" (State-Degree). The man rejoiced, saying, "He gives me 'Zhou-du';
this is auspicious. Zhe said, "If he goes there, you will perish; if you go there, he will perish. He is certain to be overcome."
At that time, King Zhao occupied the tower at the western gate. He dispatched three thousand elite cavalrymen;

as soon as they engaged the enemy, they retreated, whereupon [the Master] followed and slew them. Reaching Bāndha, he decapitated more than a thousand soldiers. The place where the stūpa is particularly high to the east is this very spot.

Later, it was verified that the Master wore a hide; "hide" (*pí*) and "Bāndha" (*bān-tuó*) share the same phonetic component. [The soldiers] dropped their excrement and fled, scattering it across the ground of the stūpa. This is what was said.

Zhoudu (pronounced with the *tu* and *ge* initials) immediately decapitated him, providing immediate proof. Later, when others reported this to the King, he dispatched men to search in all directions, but they ultimately lost his whereabouts.
Wei Yuansong was a native of Chengdu in Yizhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth and became a disciple of the Dharma Master Wuming.

He was exceptionally intelligent and did not conform to worldly ways. Once, while attending to him at night during a time of stillness, he said, "The world is in a state of turmoil; people value what they hear and despise what they see. How can one truly know right from wrong? What virtue could there be in that?
Wuming replied, "If you desire fame and reputation, yet do not feign madness, you will find no virtue in it. Thus spoke the Master.
His mind was thus resolved. He then feigned madness and wandered aimlessly. People pursued him in great crowds, yet he composed verses upon whatever he encountered.

After traveling for more than twenty years, he entered the Guanzhong region under an assumed name and moved to reside at Yian. There he fashioned his own lute music, titled "The Lament of a Celestial Maiden Stirred by the Wind.
Those who heard its sound once said to his elder brother, "The land of Shu is narrow and small; it is insufficient to fulfill one's aspirations. I wish to travel further."

"I am going to the capital to compete with the scholars of that land. What do you think, elder brother? The elder brother said, "In these times, Wang Bao and Yu Xin have their fame resound through the four seas.
What do you know? You will only bring upon yourself humiliation. He replied, "They have read many books and composed their own literary works;
however, as for natural genius and grand strategy, it is not within their domain. Elder brother, simply listen and watch. He then set out for the pass with light-hearted ease.
Fearing that he might be held accountable for a crime, he donned lay clothing and turned back at Guanzhong.

The guards seized him, but the Master feigned innocence, saying, "I am a member of the household of Yu Changgong of Chang’an; I merely wished to flee to Shu. The Yu family escorted him in turn to the capital.
Yu Gong had previously traveled to Shu and was acquainted with the Master; their sudden meeting filled him with boundless joy. His noble reputation was thus established.
There was no one to whom Shi would not go. He urged the Emperor to abolish Buddhism, whereupon he himself returned to lay life. The founder of the Zhou dynasty accepted his words;
furthermore, together with the Daoist Zhang Bin, he secretly spread delusions. The Emperor believed him and did not suspect him, so he proceeded to suppress and eliminate [Buddhism].

The Master composed a poem of a thousand characters, which roughly stated: "Dragon-head, green smoke rises; Chang'an becomes a mound of earth for a generation. These lines accorded with the prophecies.
Wei later informed him of the matter. In the eighth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Du Qi of Jingzhao died and revived after three days, saying that he had seen King Yama.
The King asked, "What office did your father once hold? He replied, "My father served as an Upper Officer of the Office of Destiny (Siming Shangshi) during the Zhou dynasty.
The King said, "If that is so, you have been summoned in error; you may be released at once. He then asked, "Do you recognize Emperor Wu of the Zhou? He answered—
He replied, "I formerly served as a judicial officer of the Left Imperial Guard and was constantly on the palace steps; I know him very well. The King said, "Go and see your Emperor Wu.
An official led him to a certain place where the doors, windows, rafters, and tiles were all made of iron.
Through an iron window, he saw a man who was extremely emaciated, his body the color of iron, wearing an iron cangue and shackles. He cried out in prayer to be seen, saying, "My Lord!"
"For what reason are you so distressed? He replied, "I have encountered great suffering and distress; you simply did not see it.
Now that I have reached this place, it is truly a source of great joy. Qi asked, "What sinful karma did you commit to undergo such suffering and distress? He replied, "Do you not know?
Because I believed the words of Wei Yuansong, I defiled and abolished the Buddha-dharma; for this reason, I am undergoing this suffering. Qi said, "Great Master..."
"Why have you not cited Wei Yuansong in your commentary? The Emperor said, "I have indeed looked for him in my commentary.

However, officials have searched everywhere throughout the three realms, yet they report that he is nowhere to be found. Had he come this morning, I would have been released by evening; what more is there to discuss?
Return to the people of the world and tell them to perform meritorious deeds on behalf of Yuansong so that he may come quickly to save me. If he does not arrive, [there is nothing more to be done]."
