There was no prospect of liberation. [The author] prayed for his resurrection and did not forget the affairs of the netherworld. He exhorted others to raise the merit that would assist him, saying:
"Shangyuan, surnamed Chen, was a native of Luo in Guanghan. He left the household life and used incantations to save sentient beings.

When Prince Xiao Ji of the Liang dynasty’s Wuling commandery encountered ghosts and monsters within his palace who possessed the court ladies—some singing and some wailing, creating a chaotic and disorderly scene—the Prince then ordered..."

The skilled archer drew his bowstring and aimed; the ghosts then manifested their forms. He immediately released arrows to shoot at them, but they would catch them from afar and hurl them back at him.
This continued for a long time without ceasing. Hearing that the Master was reciting mantras, they invited him into the palace.

There, the various ghosts vied with one another to manifest transformations—dragons, snakes, and a hundred beasts, appearing and vanishing in an instant before and behind him, in the air and on the ground, displaying many strange and wondrous changes. The Master...
Sitting calmly, he addressed them, saying: "You are ghosts from humble households. For what reason did you dare enter the royal palace?
Though you can transform my body in ten thousand ways, you are merely small ghosts. All of you, stay and listen to these words of mine. The ghosts joined their palms and stood still.
The Master began by uttering "Namo Buddhāya," whereupon the ghosts lost their bearings. From that time on, all was peaceful. When Emperor Wu heard of this, he summoned him. Great...

Having received imperial favor and patronage, he encountered the turmoil caused by the Liang dynasty’s collapse. When the Master traveled to Shu, all his ailments and afflictions were thereby relieved through protection.
At the age of eighty-one, he passed away at his residence in Zhicheng.
The Chan Master Wuxiang of Xiangsi Temple in Fuzhou was of unknown origin. He suddenly arrived at a mountain temple appearing no different from an ordinary person.
This temple was situated on the northern cliffside of the Great River, upstream from Fuzhou; there was an inscription there measuring approximately five feet square.
The characters were as large as palms, yet none could be deciphered. Below was a footprint of the Buddha, nine feet apart [from another], measuring about three feet in length;

it had pressed into the stone as if it were mud. Monastics and laypeople alike held it in deep reverence. Once, when they were crossing a river at the same time and there were no boats, he placed his alms bowl in the water and said, "Why must you always carry me?
You may cross by yourself. He then took a plantain leaf and stood upon it, bridging the water.

As he crossed to the upper bank, his almsbowl followed behind him. In a short while, they reached the shore. At that time, some woodcutters saw this and spoke among themselves. The Master became aware of them and took his leave;
though his disciples earnestly tried to detain him, they could not stop him. Upon reaching the water’s edge, he boarded the boat.

When the people bowed and entreated him to stay, he gave them neither oar nor paddle, but instead grasped the gunwale and crossed straight across. He departed without looking back, and no one could fathom where he had gone.
Tongjin was the son of the Li family of Mianzhou. After he left the household life, he did not observe conventional etiquette and took pleasure only in drinking wine.

He would say to others, "Fill a jar to the brim with my body; even then, the Master is still not drunk. On one occasion, while singing wildly in a state of intoxication, he urinated, creating a foul stench.

The multitude all censured him, but those with discernment remarked, "The distinction between the ordinary and the sage is difficult to fathom. This occurred during the time of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty’s eastern expedition.
It was said that a potent poison was required. An edict was issued to the Luzhou Prefecture to construct a workshop and assign officials and laborers to collect medicinal herbs from the *lao* tribes.

Over several dozen varieties were gathered, including the head of a viper, the root of the *tie-xing*, the root of the great bee, wild *ge* (*Aconitum*), and the feathers of a *zhen* (*Cassida*). These were fermented in iron cauldrons.

Once the medicine was prepared, one had to wear leather garments and blindfold oneself with glass before approaching it; otherwise, the vapors would strike the skin, causing sores that led to death. When the medicine was applied...

If humans or livestock were to have meat pierced [by a thorn], they would die immediately. When the Master heard of this, he went to that prison. An official teased him, saying, "If you can drink a cup, are you not a man of wine?
The Master replied, "I need one *sheng* to relieve my hangover. The official said, "Drink as much as you wish; why limit yourself to one *sheng*?
He then took an iron ladle from a vat of medicinal liquor, scooped up a ladleful, and drank it. His speech and demeanor remained composed and natural throughout. All...
It caused them no distress. When the Daoist practitioners heard this, they all came to look; the Master again raised a ladle to offer it to them, whereupon they all fled far away to avoid him.
Someone said, "This man intentionally kills people; how can he be without guilt? The Master replied, "There is no suffering involved. He took the medicine himself; who was there to urge him?
He then let out a yawn and said, "Today I have obtained a drunken sleep," and lay down upon a flat stone. A short while later—

He suffered from urinary incontinence; the stones upon which he urinated were all shattered. After a long while, he woke from sleep, his spirit and vigor restored to normal. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he passed away without illness.
When his disciples inspected his clothing, bedding, and mats, they found them all to be exceptionally fragrant and pure.
No one could discern the origins of this wealthy man. He habitually stayed overnight at Jingde Temple in Yizhou and buried a large bamboo hat on the road.
During the day, he sat upright and read the sutras; although people passed by, he did not call out to them to solicit alms. If anyone happened to toss money his way, he would accept it.
He did not offer prayers for blessings. He always frequented quiet paths and avoided bustling crowds, appearing as though he were about fifty years old.
Although he had lived there for many years, no one could discern his age. A person of faith remarked, "To the west and north of the city, the population is dense and alms are plentiful;

why do you remain here? He replied, "One or two coins are sufficient to sustain my life; what further use would I have for more? (The text ends with the mention of) Zhao, the Regional Inspector of Lingzhou.

Zhongshu was a cruel official of the Three Dynasties. He was utterly devoid of faith and respect. Hearing of [the Master’s] reputation, he went to test him. Riding his horse straight past, Zhongshu feigned the dropping of a string of coins.
The Master merely continued reading his scriptures; his eyes never glanced back. When they had gone some distance, Zhongshu ordered the coins to be picked up, yet the Master still did not look.
Zhongshu then turned back and said, "Did you see my money fall to the ground? The Master replied, "I saw it. Zhongshu asked again: [The Master replied,] "I saw it. Zhongshu asked:
"Where is the money now? [The monk] replied, "I saw a man pick it up and take it away. Shu said, "You spend all day on the road begging for a single coin;
how could you not have taken a string of coins when they were lying on the ground? When you saw someone taking them, why did you not stop them?"
The Master replied, "This is not my property. Why do you falsely claim it? Zhongshu said, "I wish to have the *kāṣāya* from your person.

The Master said, "If you can take it away, there will be another to give it to you. He then folded the robe and handed it over. Zhongshu dismounted, bowed in thanks, and said, "I, your disciple, am a man of the Zhou dynasty.
My official career has spanned three reigns. I have frequently associated with the great assembly of monks; there are few who do not [know me]."
Tán heard his name and went to visit him; originally, he had no ill intent. He requested to go to Língzhōu, to which the Master replied, "Very well.

However, I, this poor monk, wish to establish many karmic connections. I hope you will assist the state in bringing peace and stability; in doing so, you will be able to receive offerings for a long time.
Shū took his leave and sighed, saying, "There are truly men among the monks; they must not be treated with contempt. After that, he was never seen again. This was Jì Xiāng of Yìzhōu.
Later, when [the author] returned from Yangzhou, he saw him; the monk had likewise buried his hat by the roadside, and his physical appearance remained as it was before.
De Shan was unknown to anyone as to where he came from. One day, weary of the world, he abandoned his wife and children to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way.

He had no time to shave his beard and hair, nor did he have leisure to provide for his food and clothing; he sought only to cease all external conditions and dwell in stillness of mind in order to awaken to his own nature. No one knew him.

Regarding his contemplative practice, he observed its manifestations as if he had attained meditative concentration. At that time, he traveled to teach and transform beings at the Bamboo Grove and the Dragon Pond, awakening both monastics and laypeople.
He took purity and simplicity as his fundamental principle, often saying: "The afflictions of turmoil are a common failing among both monastics and laity;

thus, when administration is burdensome, the state falls into chaos, and when the mind is troubled, the will becomes disordered. When the water is clear, fish and stones can be seen; when the spirit is pure, inverted perceptions are overturned."

It can be understood that even those who study purity and simplicity still find themselves amidst clamor and distraction; how much more so for one in the midst of chaotic affairs—how could such a person speak of the Way?
Huilin was the son of the Xue family from Shenquan in Mianzhou. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he lived in seclusion at Jianming Temple.

He maintained a state of pure emptiness and tranquility, remaining apart from the worldly crowd. There was a clay statue in the temple to which he constantly and diligently made offerings; the statue grew thirty-six whiskers.

Stem. At the end of the Daye era, he cleared away an ancient tomb and erected two bamboo poles, claiming they were "heavenly eyes. Later, he suddenly pulled out one of them, saying, "Yang of Hongnong has been pulled out by Māra.
Not long after, the Yining era succeeded the calendar. At times he wore double-layered robes and sat atop a tomb during the summer;
though the sun was scorching, his body showed no signs of heat. Although his mouth engaged in the Way, his physical appearance remained [as it was].
In the course of their conversation, the Master always prioritized reason. There was already a stūpa of King Aśoka in Luòxiàn;
one day, the Master suddenly traveled through the villages and borrowed three hundred carts, saying, "I wish to go to Luòxiàn to welcome the stūpa and install it here."
Before even ten days had passed, he was consumed by fire. During the Wude era, he lived in hiding among the grasses and wilds, unknown to anyone.
There was a master named Yang Hu, whose origins were unfathomable; he went directly into the thicket to meet him. Although they had never met before, it was as if they were old friends.
Each said, "It has been eight hundred years since we last parted. [Yang Hu] once used incantations for a person’s illness and cured them; the patient...
He instructed a woman to bring a skirt as an offering. The woman then left her garment and sent the payment instead. Seeing this from afar, the Master said, "Just bring the skirt;
I have no need for money. The woman was struck with wonder at his saintliness. In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, he displayed his personal belongings and passed away.
*Jinjiang Chandelu*, Scroll 18; *Jinjiang Chandelu*, Scroll 19.
Huicong’s secular surname was Wang.
After he left the household life, he traveled about to attend vegetarian feasts and lectures, never letting go of his scrolls from his hands as he sought out the essential meanings of the sutras.
His heart leaped with joy. He disciplined his body, restricted his food, and practiced the conduct of contentment, saying to himself:

"In the Lotus Sūtra, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging did not exclusively recite the scriptures; he merely performed prostrations before the fourfold assembly and yet still attained the purification of the six sense faculties."

"Why should I not pay homage to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones? Thinking thus, he immediately closed the door in a separate wing of the monastery and constantly paid homage to fifteen thousand Buddhas.
Following the sutras, he recited them aloud himself and prostrated to each one. The monks of the temple marveled at his actions and watched him through a crack in the wall.
When he was seen bowing his head in prostration, the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, also bowed their heads; this occurred repeatedly, not just once.
Anyone who came to his monastery would invariably depart with a trembling heart. A pervasive and extraordinary fragrance was constantly perceived.
After his passing, during the Zhenguan era, no one went to the monastery; yet every night, the sounds of snapping fingers, prostrations, and circumambulation were regularly heard.
Zhìyǐn was the son of the Li family of Beizhou and was a disciple of Master Huayan Zang. After receiving the tonsure and entering the monastic order, he devoted himself to propagating the Dharma.
His wisdom and understanding were such that he never required instruction twice; his spirit was noble and outstanding, and he held a refined preference for purity and detachment.
He discoursed on the Buddha Vehicle (Buddhayāna) such that his listeners forgot their weariness. In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, Master Zang was summoned;

the Master accompanied him to the capital and resided at Daxingshan Temple. There he thoroughly mastered the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

He clarified their doctrinal points and mastered both the principles and their applications. The assembly unanimously proposed him to succeed [his predecessor] in propagating the Dharma, and an imperial edict was issued to appoint him to lecture and debate at Jingzang Temple, where he continued to propagate the teachings of his predecessor.
He passed away from a slight illness; by imperial decree, his śarīra were sent to Fayu Temple in Yizhou, which had been built by Prince Xiu of the Shu kingdom.
His Way permeated Western Shu, and his transformative teachings flourished extensively, drawing forth all its golden resources.

The shell [relic] was enshrined, and all followed in joyful accord. Before even ten days had passed, the stupa was completed. As it was about to be lowered for interment, the heavens rained silver flowers and emitted white light;

such occurrences were not limited to these alone. At the very moment of its entry into the stupa, five-colored clouds were moved to cover the reliquary casket, forming a perfect circle like a parasol.
Six large birds circled amidst the clouds, and once the lid was closed, they all dispersed together. People spoke of this event.
Upon hearing this, the King of Shu was greatly delighted.

Fanneng was a native of the province; his surname was Pang. Initially, Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty had dreamed of traveling to Mount Qi, but he did not know in which prefecture or county it was located.

He issued a proclamation throughout the empire to search for it. At that time, the elders of the Master’s fatherland submitted a memorial stating that it was seven *li* north of the city of the province.
In the village there was Mount Chenren, formerly known as Mount Qi. Emperor Wu dispatched [officials] to establish a vihāra there, ordaining monks and granting them land and estates.
The Master had received ordination while still a youth; he focused his mind on upholding the precepts, and his virtue and realization improved daily.

Furthermore, he devoted himself to the study of the mind, reciting the sūtras at times and later practicing dhyāna-concentration. Sometimes he emerged from samādhi after three days, and sometimes after seven days. The assembly...
He went to the window and peered inside; it appeared that [the monk] might be in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Thus he remained for a month without emerging, still not consuming food or drink.
When the assembly went to exhort him, although he did take food, he gradually took only a small portion. When he reached the age of seventy, he placed a seat before a Buddha image and sat down.
First, he burned off one finger, remaining motionless day and night. As the fire then reached his arm, his disciples wished to go [to him].
He tried to extinguish it, but the Master forbade him, refusing to allow it. Flames burst forth from his arm and grew increasingly fierce until they reached his limbs.

For seven days and seven nights, the multitude prostrated themselves and offered praise. When his body had been consumed by the fire until nothing remained but a heap of ashes, the assembly together erected a stupa over them;
the vihāra still stands today.

Sengya was the son of the Mou family of Fuling. In the ninth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, when Zhu Lingshi campaigned against Shu, three hundred households of the Qiang people of Fuling followed the army to assist in the pacification.
They subsequently settled in the Jinyuan Valley of Guanghan. Sengya was a descendant of those people.
From his childhood, he spoke little; whenever he went to mountain springs, he would invariably pay obeisance before drinking, or else he would gaze at them with deep contemplation.
Shun would sit for the entire day. When people asked him the reason, he replied, "This body is loathsome; I am merely contemplating it. In the end, it must be burned.
Later, when he grew older, he entered military service. He was resolute and upright.

Once, while accompanying others to fish, he threw his own share back into the water and said to his companions, "Killing is not a wholesome occupation. Now my entire body is the same as that of other living beings."

He subsequently abandoned his home to leave the household life and practiced meditative contemplation. At that time, several hundred Qiang chieftains were jointly constructing a dam across a pond to provide for fish farming.
The Master went there to observe, when suddenly a strange snake about a foot long appeared, its head and tail both being red.
In an instant, it grew large, reaching over ten feet in length and five or six feet in circumference. The herd of *mi* fled in all directions, and the snake then headed toward the water.

Raising its tail, it entered the clouds; a crimson light spread across the fields before finally vanishing after a long while. Immediately thereafter, the crowd gathered again and discussed the preceding events in detail.

The Master said, "This is no cause for sorrow. Simply cease the act of killing, and the snake will not harm people. He further advised them to dismantle the dammed pool, but the assembly did not grant permission.
Shortly thereafter, the embankment burst and collapsed. At that time, there was the Chan Master Yixi, who provided service and support with diligent effort;

though he performed all manner of menial tasks, his speech was stammering and his movements appeared dull-witted. Yet, every response and every word of his accorded perfectly with the Great Principle.
He remained there for several years, yet nothing extraordinary occurred.

Dharma Master Shao was the son of the Pu family of Wuxuan in Zizhou. Before he had left the household life, while walking in the mountains, he saw a large, very emaciated tiger that was carrying a cub;
it was catching shrimp in a mountain stream to eat. The Master sighed and said, "This beast must surely be..."

In the deep mountains, he was overcome by extreme hunger. Thinking, "Since death is inevitable for both, it would be better to satisfy this hunger," he stripped off his clothes and lay down before the insects.
The insects then moved away. Only after this did he leave the household life; he devoted himself solely to reciting the sutras and practicing the Way, performing no other extraordinary deeds.
At the beginning of the Daye era, insects swarmed uncontrollably within the borders of Ruzhou. Groups of three, five, or ten people would travel about carrying staves, inflicting injury upon many.
The Master went to that place and sat within a thatched hut he had erected; the insects all fled far away, and the roads became clear and peaceful.
At the age of one hundred and nine, he manifested illness and passed away. His disciples collected his *śarīra* relics and erected a stupa to enshrine them at A-yuan.
Fa-jian was the son of the Zhu family from Luoxian in Guanghan; he had recited a thousand scrolls of sutras and spent his leisure time traveling about, having no worldly attachments.

Cè remained in seclusion for several days, neither leaving his room nor taking any food. He was heard only reciting scriptures, yet he chanted in such a low voice that the sound did not penetrate beyond the walls.
Someone leaning against the wall to eavesdrop on the resonance heard only a continuous, flowing murmur, like the waves emerging from a hidden current;
at times it would emerge once, but upon following its source, nothing could be heard. When Prince Wuling traveled eastward, he ordered his younger brother—

Senggui was defending Yizhou when the Wei dynasty dispatched General Wei Zhireng to invade Shu. Having already surrendered, Senggui found that the many renowned monks within the city were all under arrest.
At night, a brilliant light suddenly appeared. Wei Zhireng sent men to investigate the light;

they found that while all the other monks were asleep, only Senggui sat upright reciting sutras, with the light emanating from his mouth. Upon hearing this, Wei Zhireng went in person to the master’s seat.
He paid his respects and sat to listen. When dawn arrived, Senghui asked, "What sutra did the Dharma Master recite last night?
He replied, "The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, ten fascicles from the lower volume. Senghui said, "Why do you not recite it from the beginning? He replied, "I have reached this point in my recitation.
Senghui asked, "How much of the sutra has the Dharma Master been able to recite? He replied, "I resolved my mind with the desire to recite one [fascicle]."
Zang remarked, "My mind has long been full of indolence; it is only now that I have obtained these one thousand scrolls. I am struck with such great astonishment and doubt that I cannot believe them.

I wish to test you: please recite them all from memory in a single pass. Will this not cause you some fatigue? The Master replied, "The reading and recitation of the scriptures is the constant duty of a śramaṇa."
Undaunted by the toil and hardship, he prepared a high seat and ordered the assembly of monks to hold their respective texts and listen.

As the Dharma Master ascended the seat and recited, it was like a torrential stream gushing down a steep ravine; his modulation of syllables and phrases, and his regulation of breath and inhalation, were at times like a pure breeze entering a lofty pine forest.
As the assembly heard the lingering resonance of his voice, their hearts grew detached from worldly concerns and their spirits soared, as they gazed vacantly toward his departing dust.

For seven days and seven nights, the count reached a full thousand, yet [the rain] still did not cease. Huijing arose and took his leave, saying, "Your disciple’s military commanders cannot remain stationed here for long;
I beg to take my leave from this point. Consequently, all the monks were released.

As Huijing departed, he sighed and said, "Since the Tathāgata declared his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda has been renowned as the 'Upholder' (Dhāraṇīdhara). How could anyone surpass him? Yet here in Shu, there is one such as..."
This monk was thus constantly protected by peace and joy. How marvelous, how marvelous! When the Master reached the age of eighty, he passed away.
Huigong was the son of the Zhou family in Chengdu. Before Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou suppressed Buddhism, he [Huigong] and Huiyuan of the same monastery—
Having made a solemn vow to apply himself diligently to study, he traveled far to Chang’an to listen to and gather teachings. Meanwhile, his teacher went to Jingzhou and Yangzhou to seek the Way.

[The master] wandered through the capital, where he listened to and mastered the *Abhidharma* treatises: the *Kātyāyanīputra*, the *Kuśalāśaya*, the *Dharmaskandha*, the *Tattvasiddhi*, the *Vibhāṣā*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Upon returning to Yizhou, he lectured and taught with such outstanding brilliance that he stood apart from all others; both monastics and laypeople held him in profound esteem and offered him alms.
Huiyuan’s provisions were abundant. When Master [Daoan] returned from Jiangzuo, the two met and rejoiced.
They recounted their parting over more than thirty years and stayed together for one night. Their conversation flowed as freely as a spring, yet Huiyuan said nothing at all.
Huiyuan asked the Master, "We have been parted for a long time; now that we have met, I rejoice in this happy reunion. What is there to discuss? However—"
"Does the Venerable One realize that there is nothing to be said and nothing to be attained? The Master replied, "Because my nature is dull and inferior, I have no understanding at all.
Huìyuǎn said, "If you have no great understanding, why not recite a single scripture?
The Master answered, "I can only recite one scroll of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra. Huìyuǎn said with a stern expression, "The Avalokiteśvara Sūtra even children can recite. Moreover—"
"Virtuous youth, you left the household life and made a vow at a great distance to realize the fruits of the Path.

How could it have been more than thirty years since then that you have recited nothing but a single scroll of scripture, no larger than a finger? This is not the act of one who is dull-witted or indolent; I pray we sever our ties.
I hope the Dharma Master will depart soon, so as not to increase my affliction at this distance. The Master said, "Though the scroll of scripture is small, the Buddha..."
Regarding what is spoken from the mouth: those who revere it obtain immeasurable merit; those who treat it with contempt incur immeasurable sin.
I pray that you will temporarily set aside your anger and recite [this] once for the sake of the Dharma Master; then we shall part forever. Yuan laughed loudly and said:
"The *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* is the 'Universal Gate' chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*. I have already lectured upon it more than a hundred times. How could this possibly be the case?"
"Is this merely to disturb people's ears? The Master said, "A secular text states: 'It is man who can propagate the Way; it is not the Way that propagates man.
You must simply listen to the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart; how can you discard the Dharma because of a person?

Thereupon, he established an altar in the courtyard, set up a high seat, and circumambulated the altar several times before prostrating himself and ascending the seat. Yuan was left with no choice but to sit upon a folding chair beneath the eaves to listen.
When the Master first raised his voice to chant the title of the sutra, a wondrous fragrance billowed forth, pervading the entire chamber.

As he entered into the text, celestial music resounded from the air and the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers. The music was so resonant it shook the void, and the flowers fell in profusion, covering the ground.

When the recitation was finished and he descended from his seat, the music and flowers finally ceased. Huiyuan prostrated himself at the Master’s feet in worship, his tears flowing freely as he expressed his gratitude, saying: "Hui..."
"The scale of Yuan was but a single lamp. How could he dare to travel under the light of heaven and sun? I beg you to stay for a moment and grant me your instruction.
The Master said, "This is not due to my own merit, but through the power of the Buddhas' protection.
That very day, he shook out his robes, offered a long bow, and followed the current away. Thereafter, despite inquiries, no one ever knew where he had gone.
Fatai was the son of the Lü family from Longshan County in Meizhou.

Initially, he served as a Daoist for over ten years, but one day he suddenly realized his error and turned his mind toward true awakening. He immediately shaved his head and began reciting the Lotus Sūtra; he soon mastered it.
Thereupon, he diligently transcribed a copy of the Lotus Sūtra, during which several miraculous omens occurred. He then intended to take it to Yizhou to have it bound.
Huang ordered one man to carry [the relics]. When they reached Zuo Bridge, the bridge suddenly collapsed. The Master was behind, and both he and the carrier fell into the water.
The man floated out, but the carrying pole sank and could not be seen. On the bank, the Master beat his breast and wailed, saying:
"The rest are all trivial matters; how can I bear to let the sutra sink? He then cried out in a loud voice, "If anyone can fish it up, I shall reward them with two strings of cash.
At that time, a man who heard this took off his clothes and entered the water, searching several times, but he obtained only the money and his own robe-bag, while failing to recover the sutra.
The Master wept even more bitterly as he walked up and down the bank, gazing toward a small island.
Above was a bundle; he ordered someone to retrieve it, and it was a scripture. The grasses and trees had supported it, so that not a single spot was damp.

The Master was overcome with joy and immediately paid three thousand coins to the person who had filtered [the water], saying: "The Dharma Master wailed as if mourning the death of his own parents, which is why I sought this on his behalf;
it was not out of greed for money. Though I am but a common man, my disciple also understands the retribution of merit."
"Please use this money to pay for the cost of its adornment. Having spoken these words, he vanished. The Master wished to speak further, but did not know where he had gone.

Upon arriving at Chengdu, the Master commissioned the binding, including the sandalwood rollers, the silk covers, the cloth bindings, and the case. He intended to return them to his home temple to install them in a separate location. One night, a supernatural fragrance arose.
The Master applied himself diligently to the recitation and maintenance of the text, without ceasing day or night. At that time, [Biao]...

The Dharma Master was his neighbor. At night, when he wished to read and recite, he constantly resented the Master for disturbing his mind. He went secretly to request that the Master lower his voice;
however, he saw a great multitude of people before the Master, all kneeling with palms joined. Frightened, Xiu retreated and broke into a sweat, whereupon he immediately moved his residence.
The Master passed away at the age of eighty.

Baojing was the son of the Ma family in Mianzhu, Yizhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth. Pure, upright, frugal, and simple, he made the recitation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* his constant practice.
He traveled through villages and hamlets, exhorting all to revere the Buddha-dharma. Later, he moved to the provincial seat and resided at Fushou Temple.

He took it as his priority to encourage and lead the lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) of the city wards and districts; whenever he formed a group for a district, there were invariably thirty people. Together—

He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, with each person assigned one fascicle. He organized monthly vegetarian assemblies where they would recite in succession. In this manner, the community of practitioners eventually numbered in the thousands.

Those who heard of him from afar all came to pay their respects; the Master seized these opportunities to bestow his transformative teachings, and people submitted to his influence as soon as they heard of his reputation.

He maintained a humble and modest demeanor, prioritizing benevolence over personal virtue. When walking along the paths, he yielded the way to others; when conversing and responding to questions, his voice was pleasant and his manner humble and respectful.
He did not curry favor with the times. In his native district and the neighboring counties of Changfeng, the people were all followers of the Way (Daoists) and particularly did not revere the Buddha.
Consequently, there were no donors available to provide support for those monks who sought refuge there, leaving the elderly and young among them...
The appearance of a śramaṇa was such that many did not recognize him. Although the Master was from their own hometown, local customs were difficult to change;
though he sought to enlighten them, none were able to accept his teaching. When the various clans of the Li family were holding a Daoist assembly, they invited the Master to attend.

He sat there without performing the customary salutations. Everyone remarked, "To fail to pay homage to the Celestial Honored One is contrary to the Dharma. The Master said, "The heterodox and the orthodox differ in their paths, and what each serves is distinct. Even Heaven..."
He did not prostrate. How much less would he have done so for the Old Lord (Laojun)? The assembly’s discussions were tumultuous, and they largely treated him with contempt and derision.

The Master said, "I do not prostrate to that which is unworthy of prostration; I fear it would bring me disgrace. He then performed a single prostration. The Daoist image and its pedestal shook and became unstable.

Upon another prostration, the image and its pedestal overturned together, collapsing and being crushed upon the ground. The Daoists looked at one another, claiming it was caused by a gust of wind, and vied with one another to come around [the image].

"Correct," the Master said. "This is what I have done; do not harbor groundless resentment. At first they did not believe him, but once they were settled, they again paid their respects. Yet, as before, the hall collapsed.

The entire assembly was struck with alarm and fear, and they prostrated themselves before the Master as a whole. In an instant, they turned to faith and received the precepts for returning to the path.

The people of the surrounding districts and villages came together in wonder and admiration; they all returned to honoring the Dharma and dared not again transgress it. All of them received the Bodhisattva precepts.
The District Magistrate Gao Da had long possessed sincere devotion; having received the Dharma wind, he propagated the Way even further at the state temple, summoning monks to lecture extensively.
The entire region listened with rapt attention, and from that time on, the community flourished. He passed away in his residence in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era.
Mingda was the son of the Kang clan of Kangju. He left home to become a monk while still a child and strictly observed the precepts.

After receiving full ordination, he guarded his five sense faculties; as he reached the age of maturity, his practice became even more rigorous. His side never touched the mat, and he did not eat a second meal each day.

While his external conduct followed the formal rules, he cultivated the causes of the Path within. With universal salvation as his aspiration, he made constant wandering his primary task. At the beginning of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty...
They came from the Western Rong tribes and reached Yibu. At that time, the barbarians of the Ba and Gorges regions were plundering as they marched forth.

The provincial and commandery governments conscripted troops, setting a date for their punitive expedition. Master Shi took pity on those about to suffer and resolved to rescue them; he traveled alone to the rebels, climbed their fortifications, and offered words of consolation to entice them.
Before they had yet become familiar with his intentions, a storm suddenly broke out, and the heavens grew dark and gloomy as thunder and lightning struck.
The bandits were struck with terror; moved by compassion, they sought his mercy. The Master then prepared a thousand lamps and offered sincere prayers to the Triple Gem.

As soon as the preparations were complete, the gloomy mists instantly cleared, and the mountains and marshes breathed in harmony as heaven and earth opened to bright clarity. Consequently, the entire nation looked toward him in expectation, all submitting to the King’s transformative influence.

Carrying their infants in swaddling clothes, they flocked from the thickets; even otters and wild beasts ran forward before him, until his followers filled the marshlands. Thus, the river routes were rendered secure and clear.
Traveling back and forth was unimpeded; no military force was deployed, yet ten thousand *li* were as level as a palm. This was due to the power of the Master.
Later, while traveling on official business, he encountered on the road a person who had tied a pig to the ground. The pig spoke in human voice, saying: "I pray that the Supreme Sage will save me."
The Master immediately took off his own garment to ransom it and set it free. Once, in the middle of the night, he asked for water to wash his feet.

His disciple did as instructed, but the mud would not come off at all. He washed them again with hot water, yet it remained as before. Finally, the Master poured water over them himself, and his feet became clean.
The Master said, "This is fish oil; one cannot fathom its origin. Later, he traveled to Niutou in Zizhou.
Mount [Name]. He wished to construct a stupa, yet instead of seeking timber and stone, he went directly to look for craftsmen.

Both monastics and laypeople found his words strange. At that time, in the third month, the waters had receded; he went down to seek water and found therein a long beam of wood, which was perfectly suited for the central pillar of the spire.
Its length and dimensions were exactly as required, so everyone was delighted. They then drew it up and erected it. By the fourth month, the Fu River...
There was a great flood; the waters overflowed and covered the rivers, coming to rest against the village banks without a single drop flowing away.

The Master led the assembly of both monastics and laypeople to collect the materials, which were piled up like mountains from all sides. With everyone from far and near exerting their strength, the construction was completed simultaneously;
the work did not exceed a short time, yet it was suddenly finished. As for his own attire, he wore the three robes, all of which were made of coarse cloth.

Neither cold nor heat could alter his state. At times, while he sat in meditative concentration upon a rope-bench, a great fire suddenly erupted; when the multitude rushed forward to extinguish it, they perceived only a refreshing coolness.
There was a śramaṇa named Sengjiu who suffered from a disease that left him withered and crippled; he came to the Master to beg for a cure. The Master immediately gave him a staff and had him walk;
before the sun had even shifted its shadow, he returned, walking with rapid strides. Such was the manifestation of his hidden virtue and saving grace—its merit cannot be fully known.
Such instances were numerous. Furthermore, during the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, he would sit ahead of the assembly. Once, there was a thief who broke through a wall and carried off goods;

having gone outside, he became disoriented regarding his location and returned to seek refuge at the monastery. [The Master] instructed him and sent him away. Thus his transformative influence spread throughout the regions of Chu and Shu.

His virtue subdued all like the wind; thus, among the commoners of the three Shu regions, some held incense burners to offer worship, some scattered flowers and spread their robes, some renounced secular life to seek repentance, and some shaved their heads to follow the Dharma.
Day by day they accumulated and year by year they increased, beyond all reckoning.
Senghuang was the son of the Feng family of Nanchang in Fucheng, Mianzhou. He stood eight chi tall; his countenance was magnificent and imposing, and his dignified bearing was strictly orderly.

His movements accorded with every rule of propriety, yet he possessed the eyes of a hawk and the body of a tiger, with the gait of a swan and the stride of an elephant. His voice was powerful and resonant.

His ambitions and strategies were grand and far-reaching. At the age when one first applies himself to learning, his literary talent was already broad and profound, and he shared a reputation for excellence with his contemporaries.

He once dreamed that he held the sun and moon in his hands while sitting in the midst of the vast void; immediately, he felt a brilliant weariness with the mundane world and took joy in aspiring to leave the household life.

He privately established for himself the name Senghuang (Monk-Splendor), but his parents did not grant permission. He bound his two feet with shackles and tied them to a pillar in the house, vowing to end his life if his resolve was not fulfilled. He made a solemn oath: [text continues]
His mind remained unshaken; the lock opened of its own accord. He then sighed and said:

"As for the reach of one's will, by it mountains and peaks are moved, rivers and streams are cut off, city towers are brought down, and the vast oceans are exhausted; even the sun and moon are made to hide."
When his light shone forth, Mount Sumeru crumbled for him; the constellations shifted their courses for him; and noble trees were broken and withered for him.

How much more so, then, could mere metal and wood, or shackles and fetters, suffice to bind his mind? His parents, observing his resolute determination, finally allowed him to follow Dharma Master Tuan to leave the household life.
He mastered the teachings and attained thorough understanding, assuming the leadership of the Dharma and becoming a preeminent leader in the regions of Min and Ba.
He was universally esteemed and looked up to by all.
Zhitong was the son of the Chen family of Zizhou; he left home to become a monk at the age of eight as a disciple of Dharma Master Zhengdao.

Later, he recited the Lotus Sūtra and practiced the study of its exegesis. He was adept in maintaining dignified deportment and was steadfast and austere in observing the precepts. It was said that two geese would always appear at the appointed times to attend him.
While he was giving lectures, he emitted light twice every day. During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he ascended the seat and addressed the assembly, saying, "I now bid you farewell forever.
Having finished speaking, he passed away at the age of ninety-seven.

Wuquan’s style name was Juehai. He possessed a nature of wisdom. In Xiazhou, there was a wealthy man named Cheng Yibo who, at the age of twenty-nine, dreamed one night that his father said to him, "You are destined to die this year;
you should consult Juehai. Cheng was utterly bewildered and did not understand.
One day, a monk was interpreting physiognomy and happened to bear the character "Jue" (覺) in his name. Cheng requested a reading of his own physiognomy and asked, "What is my lifespan?"
"How many [people]? Juehai replied, "The old monk has no requests at all; I simply seek one cup of water.

He blew his breath into the water and had Cheng drink it, saying, "Tonight you shall have an auspicious dream, which you may report to me. That very night, Cheng dreamed that he arrived at a government office.

The men and women in the left corridor were dressed with solemn dignity and all appeared joyful; the men and women in the right corridor were all bound in shackles and fetters, wailing and weeping profusely.
A person nearby said, "Those in the left corridor are people who have built bridges; those in the right corridor are people who have destroyed bridges.
If you desire merit and longevity, you may choose for yourself. Cheng immediately awoke from his dream and resolved his mind [to cultivate virtue].
Within a radius of one hundred li, he had every bridge and road repaired and maintained.
When the work was completed, Juehai came again and said, "By performing this deed, you may extend your life by ten years. From then on, Cheng worked tirelessly upon the roads;
he lived to the age of ninety-two, and his lineage flourished for five generations.
Sengchou’s surname was Sun; his ancestors originally hailed from Changli, and later he resided in Yingtao, Julu. His character and disposition were pure and noble.

Upon reading Buddhist scriptures once, he attained a profound spiritual understanding. Having shaved his head as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) at a young age, his peers would often engage in wrestling matches during their leisure time.
Sengchou was frequently bullied for being physically weak, which filled him with shame. He subsequently entered the hall and shut himself inside the door.
He clasped the feet of Vajrapāṇi and made this vow: "I am weak and have been treated with contempt by my peers; you are renowned for your strength, so you must assist me.
I shall hold your feet for seven days, and you must grant me your power. If you do not, I shall surely die and never return.
When the sixth day was approaching dawn, the form of Vajrapāṇi appeared, holding a bowl of sinews in his hand, and said to the Master: "Little..."
The Master wished to gain strength and intended to eat this sinew, but he declined on the grounds that it was against his monastic precepts (*śīla*) and did not wish to eat it.

The spirit then threatened him with a pestle; terrified, the Master finally ate it. The spirit said, "You now possess great strength. However, uphold the Teaching well and exert yourself. With these words, the spirit departed. At dawn, the Master returned.
His colleagues again mocked and ridiculed him, but the Master said, "I have gained strength; I fear you will not be able to withstand me. The assembly then tested him.
He extended his arm; its tendons and bones were so strong and resilient that it was almost beyond the ordinary. As the assembly looked on in wonder and doubt, the Master said, "I shall test you.
Thereupon, he entered the hall and walked sideways along the wall from west to east for several hundred paces.
He also leaped his head up to the rafters four or five times and lifted a weight of a thousand *qun*. His agility and prowess were such that everyone was struck with awe and admiration. Once...

He resided at Songyue Temple, where there were a hundred monks. The spring water was barely sufficient for their needs when, suddenly, a woman in tattered clothes appeared, holding a broom and sitting on the steps, listening to the monks recite the sutras.
The assembly did not realize she was a divine being and immediately rebuked her and drove her away.

The woman showed a look of indignation and, kicking the spring with her foot, caused the water to dry up instantly; her body then vanished. The assembly reported this to the Master, who then called out to her.
The upāsikā called out three times before emerging. She then addressed the deity, saying, "The assembly of monks is practicing the Way; you should provide them with protection.
The woman then used her foot to nudge an old spring, and water immediately surged upward. The multitude marveled at this wonder.

Later, she went to Mount Wangwu to the west of Huai Prefecture to cultivate the aforementioned practices. Hearing two tigers fighting, their roars shaking the cliffs, she [struck] with her *khakkhara* staff.
They dispersed and departed. Suddenly, at that moment, two scrolls of a *xiánjīng* (immortal scripture) appeared upon the bed. The Master said, "I originally cultivate the Way of the Buddha;
how could I be constrained by those who seek longevity within the mundane realm? Having spoken these words, they vanished in an instant. Later, he moved his residence to Mount Qingluo.
Whenever he entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), he invariably set a period of seven days as his limit. He heard of an imperial summons, but [refused it].
He did not accept the command. After being earnestly exhorted with great persistence, he finally granted his request.

On that very day, as he was about to leave, brushing aside his robes, two mountain peaks suddenly shook with a start, their echoes mournful and piercing, causing alarm and agitation among both humans and animals. Birds and beasts fled for three days. The Master looked back and said:

"Those who admire the Way and cherish benevolence are found everywhere among all classes of beings. Is it not because human affection is easy to guard against, while self-indulgence is difficult to restrain?"
Indeed, he did not remain bound by worldly affairs, but instead took up his staff and traveled to the Chang and Fu rivers.
The monk Qun was pure and poor, maintaining his integrity; he lived on vegetarian food and recited the sutras. He dwelt at Mount Huo in Lujiang County, where he constructed a thatched hut.

This mountain stood isolated in the midst of the sea; upon its peak was a stone basin, six feet deep with water, which always contained clear, flowing streams. Thus it has been passed down by the ancients.
The tradition holds that this was the dwelling place of various immortals. Because the Master had ceased eating grain, his hermitage and a stone basin were separated by a small stream;
he would always use a wooden beam as a bridge to draw water from it. When he reached the age of one hundred and thirty, he suddenly saw a duck with a broken wing blocking the head of the beam.
As the Master raised his staff to push it aside, fearing he might further injure it, he turned back and subsequently ceased all activity.
He died after several days of illness. As he was about to pass away, he said to those around him, "In my youth, I once broke the wing of a duck;
I take this as evidence of the retribution for that act.

The śramaṇa Shao Shuo was a native of Kangju and was on the closest terms with Master Zhi. He entered and left [the Master's presence] and walked with him constantly, regardless of whether it was night or day.

In the morning, he later traveled to Yizhou. With his humorous and witty speech, he was able to provoke laughter from people; he would then use this to exhort them toward goodness, and every household delighted in this.
If he slept on the floor at someone’s house, someone would inevitably die; if he asked for a fine mat from someone, a young child would surely perish. At that time, everyone took these as omens.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, while the procession of the Buddha’s birthday was being held in Chengdu, he was among the crowd.
He assumed the form of a lion. On that very day, [the people of] Pí County also reported seeing the Master manifesting as a lion; they then realized he was a manifestation of his own body.
The Regional Inspector Xiao Huikai and Liu Mengming both paid him reverent homage.
Mengming gave two robes for men to his two concubines to wear and tested the Master, saying, "I shall provide these two women to serve you as attendants; would this be acceptable? The Master—
He was fond of elegant verse. He then said to Ming, "I would rather beg for my own food to enjoy pure banquets than spend the remainder of my years with Afu.
Later, he suddenly appeared wearing a cloth cap and visited Ming; a short while later, Ming passed away.

Previously, Shen Zhongyu, the Chief Secretary of Mengming, had revised the regulations for the use of the whip and staff, making them more severe than the standard rules. The Master said to Yu, "Heaven and earth are crying out in distress..."

This was the beginning. If one were to exclude Zhongyu from the position of Regional Inspector (Cishi), it would be like removing a jade ornament. When Zhongyu died the following morning, he indeed carried out the affairs of the province.
In the ninth month of that year, as he was about to pass away, he said to the śramaṇa Fajin, "I wish for my remains to be exposed beneath the pines;
however, my feet must be shod with sandals. Fajin consented. Shortly thereafter, he passed away. They placed his corpse there exposed. When they went to look at it the next day, it had vanished.
Shortly thereafter, someone arriving from Pei County said, "Yesterday I saw Master Shuo walking through the marketplace wearing a single sandal.
He said, 'Tell Master Jin for me that the boy has deceived me; he only gave me one sandal. Jin was startled and questioned the śrāmaṇera."
The answer was: "When the corpse was being carried out, one sandal fell to the ground; because they were walking in haste, he did not have time to tie it.
Master Hui was the son of the Jia family from Yonggui County in Shu. He entered the monastic order at the age of six and became a disciple of Dharma Master Bin.
He established seven monasteries in Huang’an County, ten monasteries in Zizhong County, and three monasteries in Wulian County.

When he reached the age of twenty in his first year [of ordination], wishing to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), there was no one qualified in his own region; he therefore entered the capital to receive the precepts at Gānlù Monastery.

He listened only to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, while other meanings were understood through collateral study. He dreamed that for three days and three nights, heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness and sentient beings were blind;

after this period, it suddenly became bright, and his eyes regained their clarity and purity. Upon waking, he broke out in a sweat. One hundred days later, Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou destroyed the Buddhist teachings;

only then did he realize the significance of the omen. He immediately returned to his hometown and hid himself in the Southern Mountains, subsisting solely on pine needles. Various species [of animals]...
Birds and beasts gathered together in silence. Sometimes mountain spirits would present him with *fuling* (hericium erinaceum) and *gansongxiang* (cedrus deodara), which he accepted as offerings.
As he practiced the Way during the six periods of the day, the birds and beasts followed him; they prostrated before the Buddha and recited the scriptures as if listening with reverence.

He further conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon those in both the hidden and manifest realms. Later, a troop of monkeys assisted him in repairing the path. The Master said, "Your nature is restless and agitated. Why do you do this?"

"Why is this? he asked. [The response was: "The contemporary ruler is exceptional; the Buddha-Sun is all-pervasive. I found these words deeply strange. Soon thereafter, there were further extraordinary omens:
dragons soared and beasts gathered, and fragrant incense filled the mountains in great numbers.
Huixuan’s secular surname was Dong. He left home to become a monk at an early age while residing in Xiangzhou.

After Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou suppressed the Dharma, he traveled south to the Chen territory and entered Maoshan, where he studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) under a renowned master. He subsequently went to Xiqia Mountain, where he studied the *Sijun* (Four Treatises), the *Dapin* (Large Perfection of Wisdom Sutra), the *Nirvana Sutra*, and other texts under Master Xuanbu.
Later, he went to Dalinsi in Anzhou, where he studied the commentaries on the *Śāstra* under Master Yuan. In all that he...
Moving with ease and mastery, he simultaneously realized the profound ultimate truth. Later, returning to his native village, he resided at Guangfu Temple on a mountain ridge.

Finding the labor of drawing water for irrigation too great, he was about to move to another temple when he saw a divine being in a dream at night. The being was one zhang in height and wore a purple robe;
bowing his head in prostration, he said to the Master, "We entreat you to reside here and preach the Mahāyāna. Do not speak of the Hīnayāna. As for those of the Hīnayāna..."
Just as a high mountain without water cannot benefit others, so too is the Mahāyāna like the great ocean. Many Buddhas appear in this mountain;

if even a single person reads, recites, and expounds the Mahāyāna, it can cause the precious jewels where they dwell to radiate light, their retinues to flourish and excel, and their food and drink to be abundant.
I pray that you will uphold and propagate it widely, lest our hopes be in vain. The Dharma Master requires water; here—

"It will be easy to obtain. On the eighth day of next month, there will certainly be water. I shall go myself as a minor deity to the Great Spring on Mount Cimuzi in Jiannan to invite the Dragon King.
Having spoken these words, he vanished from sight. Precisely at the beginning of the first watch on the seventh day of the following month, a great wind suddenly arose from the southwest;
thunder shook the earth and rain poured down behind the Buddha hall below the Han Gao Temple to the north of the monastery.
For about a hundred paces, the sound continued throughout the night until dawn, when it finally ceased. Only pure, fragrant, and delicious water was seen, bringing joy to the entire assembly.
Daozhao, the son of the Kang family from Jianzhou, had fallen ill in his youth and did not recover consciousness; he said that he reached the Office of the Netherworld and saw a good...
Regarding matters of evil retribution, he subsequently left the household life. He resided on Mount Taihang for forty years, his observance of the precepts being refined and austere.

He frequently spoke of people's future affairs; at first these seemed obscure, but later they were all clearly verified. Once, two guests came: one was named Yao Miao, who had passed the examination on the Classics;
the other was a member of the Zhang family, who held office by virtue of hereditary privilege. The Master said to the Zhangs, "You shall be granted an official post."
Fourthly, he cautioned that one must never accept a salary from Fanyang. On the eighth day of the fourth month, he fell ill and was not expected to recover.
He then said to Yao Miao, "It will not be advantageous for you to wear the official hairpin and tablet. If you can serve in the military, you shall likewise remain free from want for thirty years.

Furthermore, if you fall ill, do not allow a foreigner (Hu) to treat you. That year, Zhang established an office in the region between Xiangyang and Dengcheng. Subsequently, he was repeatedly recommended for office and once sought [an appointment] in the south.
He was also appointed to the prefecture. Later, he was selected again and was indeed granted the post of Magistrate of Lushi County in Guozhou.
Upon arriving at his post, he died two days later; it was precisely the eighth day of the fourth month. Only then did he realize that Fanyang was the ancestral seat of the Lu clan.
Miao failed the examinations and served as the acting military governor of Yongzhou for thirty years. He was successively promoted to right-hand offices. Later...
Because he had taken another wife, he sought out an attendant. He subsequently fell ill and died after taking the medicine of the old woman Huang Shi.
Later, when they investigated Huang Shi’s background, it was discovered that she was a maidservant released by the Cave Lord and was a Hu (foreign) woman.
The monk Changluohan of Jiazhou frequently exhorted people to establish vegetarian feasts for arhats; thus he acquired his name.

A lady of the Yang family was fond of eating chicken, and the number she had killed throughout her life was beyond counting. After she died, her family performed rites for her posthumous merit, and a Daoist priest was just beginning to offer incense petitions when the Master suddenly arrived.
He told the son, "I shall perform repentance on your behalf. The Yang family was greatly delighted.
A seat was prepared and he was invited inside. The Master looked at his servant and said, "Go to the [X]th house east of the street and buy a hen with flowers on its head.
Following these instructions, they obtained one. He ordered it to be killed to prepare a meal. Yang Xi wept and pleaded, saying, "Venerable Sir, you have deigned to visit me."

It was not that he had anything for which he felt attachment; rather, it was because today was the opening of a ritual feast (*qianyan*), and his entire household, both inside and out, had long abstained from meat and strong flavors.

He requested that [the meat] be given to a neighbor. The Master said, "That will not do. If he insisted on cooking the food, once it was ready, he sat down cross-legged in the hall, sliced the meat until the dishes were full, and distributed it among the nine seats of the High Truths (*shangzhen*).
Only then did he eat what remained. When the fast-breaking meal was finished, he departed without bowing. That evening—
The poultry seller and the Yang family both dreamed that the old woman arrived and thanked them, saying: "In my lifetime, due to my sinful karma, I was reborn as a chicken.

It was by the grace of the Arhat’s repentance and apology that I have now been liberated. From then on, whenever the people of the commandery performed Buddhist rites to dedicate merit for the deceased, they would pray for her arrival so that she might receive assistance in the netherworld.
She passed away at the end of the Shaoxing era; her physical body remained for a long time without decaying.
Huài-dào was the son of Pán of Cháng-lè. In his youth, he followed his uncle to the capital. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order under Master Yuǎn of Lú-shān.
He thoroughly studied the sutras and the vinaya, and was particularly proficient in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. He practiced the Way for over several decades. Once, he traveled through Liáng Prefecture.
The Master was surrounded by Qiang rebels and was on the verge of losing his robes and alms bowl. Together with several disciples, he made a solemn vow to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara in unison.
After a short while, he felt as if clouds and mist were covering his body; the bandits searched for him but could not find him. Thus, he escaped with his life.
Later, hearing that Dharma Master Xuangao of Hejian was profound and vast in both meditation and wisdom, he wished to go and follow him as a disciple.

However, on the way, he encountered the disturbances caused by the Tuyuhun and consequently could not proceed. Thereupon, he returned to Chengdu. The Retired Scholar Fei Wenyuan had previously studied under him;

[Huiyuan] then established a monastery to the northwest of the provincial capital, naming it Qihuan (Jetavana), where his transformative influence spread throughout Ba and Shu, and his reputation grew.
This reached both the court and the commonalty. Shen Tan, the Regional Inspector of Liangzhou, had been an old acquaintance of the Master.
Later, when Tan fell ill, the Master intended to go visit him and planned to remain there. Fei Wenyuan then submitted a memorial to the Regional Inspector Zhang Yue, stating:

"The Dharma Master Daowang is pure in both knowledge and conduct; his integrity grows ever more rigorous through the trials of wind and frost. He stands solitary and peerless, firm and unshakable. Recently, I have heard..."

The Liangzhou authorities dispatched an envoy to welcome him back. Although he accepted the imperial decree and permitted his departure, public opinion throughout the entire region unanimously declared it inappropriate.

They argued that their remote and frontier province had ten thousand monks and nuns, who relied entirely upon him for their training in meditation and precepts. "How can we allow the waters to lose their pearl, or the mountains to forfeit their jade? they pleaded.

"We pray you will consider the sincerity of both the clergy and the laity, so that the fourfold assembly may have someone to rely upon. Huiyue then earnestly detained him, and thus the departure did not take place.

Huiyue returned to the capital and related the Master’s virtuous conduct in detail to Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty. The Emperor immediately issued an edict to welcome him and appoint him as the abbot of Zhongxing Temple.

The Master, however, declined the offer through Huiyue on the grounds of illness and was thus spared from the appointment. Thereupon, he excused himself from official duties and withdrew behind closed curtains, severing all ties with the world of men.
Later, when Liu Sikao governed the province, he established a grand Dharma assembly and invited the Master to lecture on the sutras. It was then that...
He should have been invited. Someone asked the Dharma Master, "You have always vowed to maintain stillness; why do you now violate this discipline?
He replied, "Lord Liu is a man of profound faith, and it is upon him that the Great Dharma now relies. How can I decline such a minor labor?"
Dharma Master Huizhi was traveling to Mount Emei when he entered meditative absorption within a great tree by the roadside in Jiazhou.
In the fourth month of the third year of the Zhenghe era, a violent storm arose and the tree was broken down. A magistrate out on patrol encountered him;

seeing that his hair and beard covered his body and his fingernails and toenails encircled his frame, he found it quite extraordinary. He subsequently reported this to the imperial court, and an edict was issued ordering [the remains] to be carried...

The carriage arrived at the capital. At that time, the Master from Western Heaven (Xitian Zongchi) used a golden gong to rouse him from his meditative absorption. He then asked, "In what era’s reign do you serve as a monk?
The Dharma Master replied, "I am the younger brother of Dhyāna Master Huiyuan of Donglin. Because I have been traveling to Mount Emei, I no longer remember how many eras have passed."
He asked again, "Is Dharma Master Yuan still alive? Zongchi replied, "Since we last inquired about his succession, approximately seven hundred years have passed.
How could he still be here? Thereupon, he ceased speaking. He asked once more, "Where do you intend to go? The Master said, "To Chenliu County," and then entered meditative absorption again.
Huiyì was a native of Jizhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth and maintained a character of austere integrity. He frequently traveled to various regions to study the sutras.
While traveling through the western borders of Shu, he was abducted by someone and forced to herd sheep. A merchant who was a man of faith and reverence saw him and found him extraordinary;

suspecting he was a śramaṇa, the merchant questioned him on the meaning of the scriptures. Huiyì was thoroughly proficient in all matters and reached a complete understanding of them. The merchant then ransomed him with gold.
Having returned, he resumed his saffron robes and applied himself to study with even greater devotion. He traveled through various kingdoms as far as the borders of South India;
regarding phonetic translations, glosses, and commentaries, as well as the diverse doctrines of different regions, there was nothing he did not thoroughly understand.
The poem by Master Luo Guanshan of Luzhou (the Emperor Jianwen) says: Wandering through rivers and lakes for several decades, I return to find snow already filling my hair.
Heaven and earth harbor resentment; where is my home? The Yangtze and Han rivers are heartless; the waters flow on their own.
The clouds within the Changle Palace have vanished; beyond the Chaoyang Pavilion, the sound of rain stirs sorrow. The new rushes and slender willows turn green year after year;
the village elder swallows his laughter, yet cannot cease. Inscription on the Wall: Having finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I strike the bell with weary hands.

I laugh as I gaze upon thatched cottages and round watchtowers. To the south, the Zhanghai Sea stretches out in a thousand layers; to the north, the Heavenly Gate lies ten thousand miles away. With a golden hoe...
The azure silk hair is shorn away; the *kāṣāya* robe replaces the dragon-embroidered *gǔnpáo*. As for where the hundred officials have returned, none can say;
only the flocks of crows come to pay their morning and evening court.
Master Chen Xiyi, whose courtesy name was Bo, was a native of Chongkan Township in Puzhou. While traveling for his studies, he arrived at Mount Hua;
seeing the mountain ridges were steep and perilous, he lay down upon a precipice where it was difficult for a person to set foot, remaining there for several decades.

Emperor Taizu of the Song dynasty, admiring his lofty character, issued three imperial edicts summoning him to leave the mountains, yet he did not emerge. In the Jiawu year of the eleventh year of the Dading era, there was a monk named Che...
Kō served under the Venerable Master Setsu at Kyokutei. He composed this poem in praise of him: The man’s strides have no known origin;
Day after day he takes Mount Hua as his pillow. He has lain there for five hundred years now; The game remains unfinished, yet it feels like many millennia.
Fire returns with wind and rain, and heaven becomes his roof; He feeds on clouds and mists, his breath like that of an ox. Through the twelve hours...
Presented for the Master’s use. [The author] does not know who his fellow practitioner is.

On the day of the Winter Solstice in the Wuli (戊子) year of the Wanli era, Da’guan Dharma Master of Lengyan Monastery in Jiaxing Prefecture, while residing at Taiping Monastery in Langzhong, composed this eulogy for the image of Mahākaruṇā Bodhisattva.
Prostrating before the Honored One of Perfect Fulfillment and Sovereign Freedom, throughout the dust-motes and lands...
The wheel of unimpeded flight soars eternally, crushing all forms of extreme suffering. It causes all sentient beings universally to attain compassion and wisdom:
wisdom discerns objects as devoid of self-nature; compassion rescues and delivers all, whether in adversity or prosperity. This wisdom resides in the eyes, penetrating the ten directions.

This compassion resides in the mind, benefiting the three periods of time. The measure of the three periods and the ten directions is immeasurable; hands and eyes are required in thousands of myriad forms.
Such wondrous functions are like the moon reflected in water—clearly visible yet ungraspable. Dividing the body and dispersing shadows, they are originally without permanence.
Viewing all things with loving-kindness, one sees them all as straw dogs. If a person perceives the Bodhisattva in this way, that person is indeed [the Bodhisattva].
O sons of the Bodhisattvas: to seek extraordinary matters apart from this is to allow demons and spirits to destroy the True Dharma.
Desheng, whose style name was Wanan, was the son of the He family of Hanzhou. In his youth, he was immersed in the filth of worldly dust; as he grew older, he awakened from his dream.

At twenty, he received the full precepts and devoted his mind to the lecture halls. The fourfold assembly ranked him as a "Tiger of Meaning. Suddenly, he set aside his intellectual understanding and became humble. He then...
However, he changed his course, changed his clothes, donned a bamboo hat, and went to visit Master Wenshu Dao to earnestly inquire about the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
Dao spoke a verse, saying: "The Khitans have broken down the Persian camp; They seized the precious jewel and sell it in the village.
A destitute beggar at the crossroads Has a fashionable pouch hanging from his waist. As the Master was about to offer a reply, Dao rebuked him, saying:
"Do not err. Thereupon, he withdrew for three years of contemplation before finally grasping the previous instruction. He went to Mount Gu in Min Province to pay his respects to Zhuan-an.
He asked about the Master’s statement regarding "not crossing the stone gate": "What is the meaning of this? Zhuan-an replied instantly, "Idle words."
He attained sudden enlightenment upon hearing these words. Later, a monk asked, "What is the true person of no station? The Master said, "Wealthy when heard;
impoverished when seen."
A Verse by Chan Master Chen of Jianwei for Layman Zhao: When one has eaten their fill, there is neither sorrow nor joy;
how wonderful! This scene of springtime dreams—when will it ever return? If you wish to awaken, awaken at once; Do not wait until the vines wither and the trees fall.

With staff and sandals, seeking the secluded, the mountain path slants away. The celestial wind carries me into the mists and clouds. The clouds tower over the Dharma-realm for three thousand *zhang*; Spring...

The *pāramitā* of giving was fulfilled across a hundred thousand households; the patriarchs and Buddhas transmitted the secret seal to one another, and the enlightened monks successively bestowed the *kāṣāya*.
The great intent of the West’s arrival manifests at every turn: where birds cry and monkeys howl, they turn the *Dharmapada*.
On Mount Waguan, there had never been tigers or leopards. The monk Shou'an said to Yang Shen’an: "Now there is a beast whose name we do not know;
it resembles the *krodana* (角端) depicted in illustrated maps. It devours tigers and leopards but does not harm humans.
This monk protects it to guard this mountain. Shen’an said: "I have heard that the *krodana* brings an end to killing; now I hear it has also come to eliminate [the beasts]."
Its auspiciousness surpasses even that of the qilin.
At Kaiyuan Temple in Kuizhou, Zhang Sanfeng—of the early Ming dynasty—took leave of the monk Guanghai and once presented him with a poem, which said:
"Deeply entering the Buddha-dharma, he severs worldly attachments; The practice of *śamatha* is perfectly in accord. Heaven..."
The flowers subtly manifest a faint auspiciousness; the wind-blown leaves chime in rhythmic praise of the Mahāyāna. In the secluded chamber, the day is leisurely with clouds forming a canopy;
in the empty pavilion, the night is still with the moon serving as a lamp. Spirit dissolved and form dispersed, there is nothing at all—reaching this state, who could see this old monk?
At his departure, he left behind a pair of straw sandals and three pieces of fragrant incense. Later, Hai composed a poem concerning these two [items].
He presented these offerings. Emperor Wen replied by bestowing upon him a single jade ring and a set of the "Thousand Buddhas" *kāṣāya*.
During the Zhengde era, Mount Lingyun in Jia Prefecture was a battlefield. At that time, there was a monk named Qianfeng who had once served as a jailer;
the prisoners were very numerous. Feng said, "The world is in chaos and punishments are manifold; many are not guilty of their crimes. Out of compassion for you, I shall release you."
"I, too, shall depart from here. He subsequently shaved his head to become a monk and built a thatched hut on Mount Jiufeng.

His meritorious achievements in construction were numerous, though they are not recorded here in detail. His incorruptible body remains at Thousand Peaks, currently enshrined before the Śākyamuni Relic Stūpa by the Śarīra Spring.
Examining the inscription on the stele, he was the eleventh-generation descendant of Chan Master Qing-su of Jiuding. Qing-shou’s dharma name was Dao-hui.
Fu Gong dreamed of a divine response and had a stupa and quarters newly constructed with gilded garments. The stupa master Xintong invited Chan Master Shengke to dwell there in retreat.
He once inscribed a eulogy on the wall, saying: "Stones may crumble and iron may wear away; How much more enduring is this physical form?
Do you know that the Dharmakāya possesses a visible sign? This boat enters the eye from across the Bridge of Ten Thousand Li."

There was one who tested his authenticity by scraping his chest; he immediately developed an abscess, which healed after he offered a repentance and apology. Consequently, no one dared to treat him with contempt.
At the ancient temple, Master Wukong Hongren, the head of the Yang family, was a native of the Yang clan of Mianzhu. He built a thatched hut on Mount Qingcheng.
When the Prince of Shu heard of his reputation while crossing the river, he opened the state treasury to provide for him, establishing the Dragon Pavilion and the Jewel Hall.
Yan said: "The Guangyan Temple houses the scripture collection from Jingyin Temple, featuring Sichuan woodblocks, Song dynasty paper, ivory bookends, and brocade covers—none can rival it.
It is situated in the center as a place for the fourfold assembly to behold together. Though the eons may turn crimson with destruction, these precious models still remain.
The physical body of the Master [Wuzu] and his golden stūpa are unharmed. In the spring of the Wuchen year, Zhaojue [Temple] reached its eightieth anniversary."
The elder Zhao Xuezui Lao Ren led the assembly in transcribing and collating [the scriptures]; this was the fulfillment of the Master’s ocean-like vow.

To the left stood Cuo’e Temple, where at that same time there were also Sichuan woodblocks for the Tripitaka. Amidst the calamities of the fires at the end of the kalpa and the upheavals of the Qi dynasty, these were damaged by wind and rain.
The woodblocks for the scriptures preserved at the great monastery of Jingyin were likewise reduced to ashes. Now, at Wanfu Temple outside the West Gate of Jinguang...
This was a temple.
A practitioner from Mount Emei, a native of Shu, was exceptionally strict in his observance of the precepts and had not descended from the mountain for twenty years.

One day, a person dressed in plain clothes and a blue fur cloak, a remarkably imposing figure, arrived. After conversing with him for a long time, he made an appointment for that same day the following year.
They met again and agreed to wait for that same day the following year. On that day, the practitioner bathed, sat upright, and passed away. As evening fell, the eminent man indeed arrived.
He asked, "Where is the practitioner? and was told, "He has passed away. The eminent man sighed deeply for a long time, wrote several words upon the wall, and said:
"The setting sun slants; the western wind is cold. Will the recluse come tonight or not? It makes one stand until the night is spent."
The calligraphy of "Tung-t'ung-ying" (Pine and Crape Myrtle Shadows) is soaring and dynamic, like a phoenix in flight or a peacock dancing;
it is no brushwork of this world (some say it was by Lü Dongbin).
*Jinjiang Chandeliers*, Scroll Nineteen; *Jinjiang Chandeliers*, Scroll Twenty.

Xianhu was the son of the Sun family from Liangzhou. He came to reside at Yanxing Monastery in Guanghan, where he constantly practiced meditative concentration as his primary vocation, while also strictly observing the monastic precepts without violating even the slightest detail.
