He passed away in the fifth year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty. At the moment of his death, five-colored light issued from his mouth, illuminating the entire interior of the monastery.
He left instructions that his body be cremated; subsequently, when his limbs and joints were completely consumed, only his hands remained.
One finger [of this record] is not so.

Faxu was a native of Gaochang. His conduct was pure and prudent, and he resolved his will upon the practice of dhyāna. Later, he entered Shu and practiced as a dhūta ascetic among the mountains and valleys near the tomb of Master Liu;
tigers and rhinoceroses did not harm him. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, constantly dwelling among the rocks.
Within his chamber, he habitually maintained this practice. During the height of summer, he passed away in his room;

for seven days there was no odor, and a wondrous fragrance arose that did not dissipate for ten days. Every evening, he emitted light that illuminated several li. The villagers immediately erected a stupa beside the chamber.

Facheng was a native of Liangzhou. He left home to become a monk at the age of sixteen; his studies encompassed both the Sūtras and the Vinaya. He abstained from the five grains, consuming only the resin of pine and cypress trees.
Dwelling alone in mountain caves, he devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna. During the Yuanjia era, Wang Huaisu, the Prince of Donghai, was serving as the governor of Baxi;

having heard of Facheng’s reputation, he sent for him. They met at Fucheng, where Facheng presided over the summer retreat and lectured on the Vinaya. When the session concluded, he took his leave to return, but subsequently remained there.
Guanghan further propagated the methods of dhyāna. Later, while suffering from a slight illness, he addressed the assembly, saying, "Facheng constantly recites the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*;
let us now recite it together by our own strength. He then began to recite it himself, but after reaching only half a fascicle, his breath failed him and he was unable to continue.

He then had someone read it aloud; only when one full recitation was completed did he pass away with palms joined. More than ten people who were attending to his illness all saw a dark-blue horse in the air, its back...
He carried the golden coffin upon his shoulders and ascended into the sky, departing.
During the period of the funeral rites, Xiang, a son of the Xiang family from Pei County, had lost both parents early in life and served his elder brother as if he were a father.

At the age of fourteen, he left home to become a monk and sought instruction in the practice of dhyāna from Zhimeng. Together with Falin of Lingqi Temple, he practiced meditative contemplation; whatever Zhimeng was familiar with and knew, [he mastered].
He had already realized all of these. Later, he met Xuanchang and further pursued his studies under him. When Xuanchang went down to Jiangling, the Master followed him as well.

Regarding the *Ten Stages Meditation* (*Shizhu guanmen*), he had already attained nine of them; there was only the "Lion’s Seizing the Swift" (*Sīṃhavijṛmbhita*) samādhi that he had not yet fully mastered.

Chang sighed in admiration and said, "Since I traveled west across the shifting sands, trod north through the dark deserts, explored eastward the Cave of Yu, and reached the southern limits of Mount Heng and Luofu, I have seen only this one disciple who possesses a special affinity for dhyāna.
He later passed away at Changsha Temple at the age of sixty-two;
a divine light shone forth for several li, and his body became fragrant and pure.
Daofa was the son of the Cao family of Dunhuang. He left his home to enter the religious life and specialized in the practice of Chan meditation.
At times he also performed divine incantations. Later, he traveled to Chengdu and served as the abbot of both Xingle and Xiangji Monasteries at the request of Wang Xiuzhi and Fei Keng.
He had a method for instructing the assembly: he constantly practiced almsround (*piṇḍapāta*) and did not accept individual invitations.

When the Sangha went on almsround, he would always set aside a portion of what he received to give to insects and birds. Every evening, he would strip off his clothes and sit in the open air to feed the mosquitoes and gadflies. Afterwards, he would enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

He beheld Maitreya emitting light from his navel, which illuminated the retributions of the three miserable realms. Thereupon, he redoubled his diligent efforts, remaining constantly seated without lying down.
In the second year of the Yuanhui era, he passed away while in meditative absorption, sitting upright on a rope bed with an appearance as serene as ever.
Puheng was the son of Lady Cheng. During his childhood, he once saw a holy monk preaching the Dharma in the midst of the sunlight while suspended in the air.
When he described this to his family members, no one believed him. Later, he earnestly sought to leave the household life and took refuge at Anle Temple.

He dwelt alone in a single room, did not establish a circle of followers, and practiced the meditation of stillness, becoming skilled in the meditative states of entering, abiding, and emerging. Together with...

The Vinaya Master Shutao of Shu agreed with this view. He himself claimed to have entered the Fire-Light Samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), wherein light descended straight from his brow down to the *vajra*-limit (*vajrakoṭi*).
Within that light, he beheld various forms and images, including the karmic retributions of his previous lives, which he perceived with considerable clarity.
He passed away in the third year of the Shengming era of the Song dynasty at the age of seventy-eight.
Falin was the son of the Le family from Linqiang in Jinyuan. He left home to become a monk in his youth and resided at Pei Temple in Shu Commandery.

He specialized in the study of the precepts and devoted his mind to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong). He often lamented that there were no excellent masters in the Shu region. Shortly thereafter, Master Yin arrived in Shu;
Falin then disciplined himself, even piercing his own flesh with a stylus, practicing day and night as usual. When Yin returned to Shaanxi, Falin followed him for several years.

He thoroughly mastered the Vinaya of all the various schools and understood their nuances to the depths of his heart. Later, he returned to Shu and resided at Lingjian Temple. Among the monks and nuns of Yizhou, there were none who did not revere him.
He constantly prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) and would regularly recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.

Each time he did so, he would see a śramaṇa of exceptionally handsome and imposing stature who was always present before him. In the second year of the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, he fell ill and his condition did not improve.
He focused his mindfulness on the Western Quarter and performed rites of repentance without ceasing.

He saw various worthies and sages all gathering before him, and he described what he had seen to his disciples, instructing them to cremate his body after his death. Having finished speaking, he joined his palms and passed away.

Immediately at the crossroads of Xinfan, wood was piled up and his corpse burned; the smoke and flames rose to the heavens and lasted for three days before subsiding. His remains were then collected and interred right there.
A stupa was erected at that site. Sengqing was a native of Xi'an Han from the Chen family;
his ancestors had followed the scholarly tradition of Confucianism for generations. At birth, Sengqing was accompanied by extraordinary auspicious signs.

At the age of thirteen, he left the household life and relied upon Jingxiu of Yixing Temple to cultivate the pure conduct of a *brahmacārin*. He vowed to seek a vision of the Buddha and first sacrificed three of his fingers as an offering. Finally, he made a solemn oath.
He set fire to his body and gradually ceased consuming grain, subsisting only on fragrant oil.
On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Daming era, he performed the offering of self-immolation before the Vimalakīrti image he had commissioned, west of Wuduan Temple in Shu.

The Regional Inspector Zhang Yue personally came out to witness it; monks, laypeople, and both local and foreign residents flocked from the entire city to observe. Clouds formed into canopies overhead, and bitter rain fell in sorrowful sympathy.
At midnight, the sky suddenly cleared and brightened; the atmosphere became pure and serene. A creature resembling a dragon was seen ascending to heaven from the [卄/積] mound.
At that time, he was twenty-three years old. Pei Fangming, the Governor of Tianshui, erected a stupa for the collection of the śarīra.

Sengsheng was a son of the Yuan family from Pei County. He left home to become a monk at a young age and gained renown for his ascetic practices. Song Feng and others from Chengdu invited him to reside at Sanxian Monastery;
he made the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* his primary vocation.

Once, while reciting the sūtra in the mountains, a tiger came and crouched before him, departing only after he had finished. Later, whenever he engaged in chanting, he would invariably see four people standing by his side.
The attendant, though advanced in years, remained exceptionally diligent in his devotion. Later, when he was slightly ill, he spoke to his attendant monk, saying, "I am about to depart.
Thereupon, he met his end with a serene countenance.

Xian Song was the son of the Li family of Tóngliáng in Chóngqìng, Western Shǔ. Having thoroughly studied under many masters and grown weary of wandering, he emerged from the monastic life to reside at Xuānmì Monastery in Bāchuān.
For thirty years, his footsteps never crossed the threshold of the monastery gate. During the Xiàngshī era, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:
"For eighty years I have wandered in vast expanse, Grandly opening a marketplace for mani-jewels; Yet there has not been a single person with whom to deliberate."

"It is not that this mountain monk has closed his shop early," he said, and having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. When his body was cremated, the *śarīra* relics were beyond counting.
At that time there was the Venerable Jingye, whose secular surname was Wen; he was the son of Shizhao. In his youth, he had worked as a butcher. He once had a ewe that was nursing two lambs.

He was about to kill them when two lambs took hold of his knife and knelt prostrate at the gate as if begging for their mother’s life. The Master was moved with deep emotion and left home to become a monk.
He applied himself diligently to study under a patriarchal master until he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "Yesterday was the heart of a rākṣasa;
today is the face of a bodhisattva. Between the rākṣasa and the bodhisattva, there is not even a single thread of separation."

Chanhui was a man of mountainous renown whose family had pursued the Confucian arts for generations. Having failed the imperial examinations several times, during the Yuánfú era, the prefect Lǚ Yóuchéng mocked him by presenting him with a monastic certificate;
he consequently abandoned Confucianism to follow the Buddhist path, diligently investigating the ancestral Way until he attained great enlightenment.
At first, he resided at Tianning Temple in his native district. Whenever he went out or returned, he invariably rode a horse or traveled in a carriage.
Several senior monks remarked, "In the Buddha-dharma, ascetic practice is held in high esteem; it is certainly not appropriate to travel in carriages or horses or wear fine silks and brocades.
The Master replied with a verse: "Mañjuśrī rides a lion; Samantabhadra mounts the Elephant King. A newly arrived Buddha—riding a horse does him no harm. Thus it was.
The Dharma he taught was characterized by sharp and agile wit; his recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulate in the world. Baoyue was a native of Fuling.

From childhood, he spoke little and took no pleasure in play. He left home to become a monk and wrapped his five fingers in cloth to burn them, saying, "If one’s faith in the Buddha is such as this, it is sufficient.
People considered him mad and asked, "Why do you not treat this? He replied, "The body..."
Since [the body] is but emptiness and sound, how could the four great elements and five limbs possibly exist? He threw himself into fire to extinguish his body, yet his mind was not destroyed.

Shiyan Kun was a native of Jiangling who resided at Fangguang Monastery in Fuzhou. His family had pursued the Confucian arts for generations, but after failing the imperial examinations several times, he abandoned them to enter the Buddhist gate.
He strictly observed the precepts and clarified his mind through meditative contemplation; although he delved into the mysteries of the Mahāyāna, [he remained steadfast].
The various members of the assembly remained solemnly silent. Knowing in advance that the time of his death had arrived, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse:

"This illusory body moves due to delusion; I have expounded the treasury of the Dharma for your sake. Where there is thought, there is form and transition; Where there is no mind, there is no defilement.

In every dust mote is the Dharmakāya; In every world-system is the divine eye. Coming and going are like flowers in the sky— Who, then, revolves through birth and death? Having finished speaking, he passed away.
He passed away while sitting upright. His worldly age was sixty-nine, and his monastic seniority was twenty-eight summer retreats.
Venerable Āśvaghosa of the Tang dynasty was a native of India who entered China during the Tang period and resided at Mount Lingya in Guankou.
He constantly sent his white ox down the mountain to gather provisions and fetch water. His divine transformations and miracles were exceedingly numerous;
a stone-carved image of him still exists today on Lingya Cliff.
Daohui was a native of Zixian who met with Fan Ding, the Magistrate of Deyang, and became a "square external friend" (a spiritual associate). This occurred in the Gui-chou year of the Wanli era.
In the summer, Fan’s illness became severe. During a period of extreme heat, he dreamed that the Emperor commanded him to become the deity of Mount Tongbai.
He sent a letter to inquire about this. The Master said to him, "All karmic actions are created by the mind; all fruits are realized by the mind; even the Emperor’s command is altered by the mind.
When you perceive the ground of reality as you do in your daily life, how do you apply your attention here? Fan asked again, "The pain and illness are so severe; what should I do? The Master said:
The Master brought up the central theme. Fan asked, "Who is the master? The Master said, "It is that which perceives the pain.
Fan said, "When the four elements disperse, one does not even know pain; who then is the perceiver? The Master said, "Awareness is originally without pain, and pain is likewise not knowing."
"Perception is without pain; when pain arises, it is immediately detached. Why wait for the dissolution of the four elements?

If they must necessarily dissolve, how could there be a ghost crying out in pain and seeking a needle? The essence of perception is boundless; the four elements are but floating bubbles. At these words, Fan Da attained great realization.
Mingcai was a native of Chongqing Prefecture. He entered the monastic order in his youth, and upon reaching maturity, he specialized in the teachings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
He did not rely on written texts. In the forty-fifth year of the Wanli era, he passed away. That night, some one hundred monks beheld a purple vapor heading toward the southwest as it departed.
A verse states: "When thought ceases, cessation itself also ceases; what more remains that does not cease? The original nature..."
Originally there was no explanation. Jiaoyue Dangkongche. Mingben was a native of Hanzhou.

In his youth, he relied upon his maternal uncle Gao Sheng’s household. He would gather firewood and tend the hearth. One day, while returning from the mountains carrying wood, the donkey would not move forward.
In a fit of anger, he hacked at its ears until blood flowed across the ground. His heart immediately felt remorse and he attained awakening. Thereupon—
Having shaved his head to become a monk, he entered Changfeng Gaoshan Temple for many years. His meritorious practice was extremely arduous.
On the day of his death through meditation, someone arriving at Chaoying Huashan saw Ben’s single sandal entering the mountain. He said, "I lost one sandal beneath my meditation couch;
you may have my disciple send it back. When the messenger arrived, he learned that Ben had already passed away.
Kongan Chang was a monk of Xiangshui Temple in Zhangming County who attained enlightenment in the Chan school. Every year, he purchased medicine to relieve the sick and fed grain to birds;

when he reached a thousand or a hundred birds, they would gather around his shoulders and back to eat from his hands. He was skilled at composing poetry, and his recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulated in the world.
He lived for over one hundred years before passing away while seated in meditation.
De’ai (德愛), styled Yinxin (印心), was a native of Huayang. He lost his parents at birth; his wet nurse abstained from wine and meat whenever she nursed him.
At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order. Intelligent and wise, he was fond of the Way, mastering both Confucianism and Buddhism, while also possessing knowledge of medicine.

He traveled extensively through mountains and rivers, providing medicine to rescue those who fell ill whenever he encountered them. In the year of Renzi, during a famine, he provided meals for the sangha and displaced persons, thereby bringing relief to many.
In his later years, he returned to Chashi to practice *zhi-guan* (calm abiding and insight) and meditate. On the twelfth month of the year Yimao, he suddenly addressed his disciples, saying:
"On the fourteenth day, I shall return once more to the realm of creation. When the appointed time arrived, he faced west, recited a verse, and passed away.

Two pearls, each over a chi in length, emerged from beneath his nostrils; his facial complexion remained as if alive. During the night of the cremation, a crimson light ascended toward the west and did not dissipate until the end of the night. His disciple Ke... [text ends].
Following the tradition of his predecessor, the Grand Censor (Dazhongcheng) Lord Wu inscribed the title "Lotus Pure Realm" (*Padma-viśuddha-kṣetra*).

The Dharma Master Wan-zhu was named Shao-qian and styled Yi-qing. By nature he was serene and dedicated to study; he once repaired a thatched hut on Mount E-ling at Xue-yuan, which could barely accommodate his knees.
For three years he subsisted on vegetables alone, yet his spirit remained harmonious and vigorous. Upon returning to Chengdu, he associated with the Way...
The friend Xiquan built a hermitage atop the Hundred Flowers Pond and investigated the essence of the Mind School with direct penetration. He further took the name Wanzhu (Ten Thousand Bamboos).

One day, he was suddenly awakened as if from a dream and applied himself to the Way with great vigor. He subsequently entered the lecture halls of the Southern Capital, where those who came to hear the Dharma gathered like a marketplace.

Later, he set sail for Mount Wutai, where he drew blood and ground gold to transcribe the *Lotus Sūtra* over a period of nine years. Thereafter, he traveled to the capital of Yanjing, where he resided at Puxian Monastery.

He published the *Annotated Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra* and lectured daily on various sūtras. The two Holy Mothers, Chen and Li, bestowed upon him the purple robe from afar and paid him their respects.
At that time, there was a sandalwood image at Juefeng Temple whose origins were unknown to anyone;

as soon as the Master saw it, he recognized it, saying, "This is the image carved by King Udayana when he longed for the World-Honored One while the Buddha was preaching the Dharma to his mother in the heavenly palace."

Once it was completed, it ascended into the void. The Buddha then touched its head and prophesied: "A thousand years hence, you shall go to Zhendan (China) to benefit those with whom you have a karmic connection.
Thus, after this millennium, the image appeared spontaneously. Later, it returned to Shu, where it planted its staff at Huankua.

The gentry and scholars of the capital gate presented poems as parting gifts; both the Grand Historian Huang Gong and the Grand Historian Liu Gong composed poems to see him off, as recorded in the *Xubuyi*.
The Master returned to his native village. There, officials such as He, the Provincial Inspector, and various scholars and gentlemen daily discussed matters concerning the Chan school with him.
The Prince of Shu provided timber to construct a lecture hall beside the Huantua Creek. One day, he ascended the hall and assembled the congregation.

He passed away while sitting upright. Miaochin, whose style name was Wuxian, was a native of Huayang. His mother, née Gao, had seen strange portents whenever she became pregnant. From birth, his appearance was extraordinary and ancient;

he could recite from memory any internal or external classic upon merely glancing at it. He was skilled in poetry and proficient in calligraphy and painting; occasionally, one might obtain a composition of his.

The term "chapter" (zhang) signifies something precious and treasured like a jewel. Later, he entered the state of Chu and became renowned for his paintings of oxen; the common people called him "Master Ox" (Niuheshang). Upon returning to Shu, he resided at the Caotang Hermitage.

He constructed a chamber to the east of the *xi* trees, where there were a thousand stalks of plum blossoms. His paintings of plum flowers reached a state of sublime mastery, and he styled himself the "Elder of the Plum Hut.
When the Provincial Education Commissioner, Lord Chen Wuyue, admired and held him in high esteem, he subsequently engaged him in playing the *qin* lute and composing poetic exchanges. Wan...
In the ninth year of the [Wanli] reign, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away while reciting a verse on the Way.
Chan Master Xue’an Lèjìng was the son of the Tán family of Ān County. In the *rénchén* year of the Jiājìng era, he shaved his head and traveled south to study;

upon returning to Shǔ, he succeeded Hǎizàng as his dharma heir. He resided at Dàofēng Yuàn, where through quiet cultivation he attained realization of the Truth. On the first day of the New Year in the eleventh year of the Wàn’lì era, he requested...
He wrote a verse with his brush, saying: "This mere bubble and illusory reflection has accompanied me for over sixty years.

Lying horizontally through the three realms in an instant, there is nowhere in the human world where it is not inverted. Now, like a bright flower in the sky, its shadow is severed; seeing and hearing are silent, still, and empty."
He asked for the true face of Xue’an. Having finished writing, "Everywhere green waters and blue mountains," he sat in *kaḍa* (cross-legged) meditation and passed away.
No one knows who Wu Xia was; he lived in ascetic practice at the summit of Mount Jiufeng.
He would occasionally travel through the villages, where he saw the daughter of Ma Zhong, who was about one year old and ill. He gave her a piece of torn cloth to eat, and she was immediately cured.
It was further said, "This girl shall be noble; later she will marry Zhao Zhixin, a student of the Xiang Academy, and will indeed be enfeoffed as a Gongren.
She often went to the county seat to visit the Bian family. One of her companions envied their opulence and splendor, saying, "You are from the Lüan clan;

why do you not come here yourself? Three days later, that companion died. Bian gave birth to a son who would not nurse and wept incessantly. The Master went to visit him and rubbed the top of his head, saying, "Since..."
"Why must you weep at my coming? The disciple then ceased his crying. One day he said to his disciples, "I am about to pass away.

You may prepare a vegetarian feast for me and invite the monks from all the mountains for a final farewell. When the monks arrived and were seated, the meal concluded; with a single smile, he passed away.
Zhenrong was the son of Lady Xü of Róngchāng. From childhood, he went to Guānyīn Temple to pay homage to the Buddha and observe the tonsure ceremony;
after receiving the precepts, he passed away. He was then reborn into the family of Wèi Bólù at Bìshān. At the age of seventeen, he was unable to speak.
One day, he said to his family, "In my previous life, I was a monk at Guānyīn Temple; I must now return to that temple. He then departed, and the monks there came forward to greet him.

Upon seeing it, he immediately knew its name. He then directed them to retrieve the original collection of śarīra relics and ancient paintings, and they visited the graves of his ancestors in succession.

When they discussed events from his life, everything was found to be accurate without exception. Whenever people went to visit him, he would always know beforehand whether their intentions were sincere or not.
County Magistrate Zhou Jun secretly sent someone to observe him; that night, the Master ordered one of his disciples to prepare tea.

When he went to wait upon others along the road, everyone marveled at him and called him a divine monk (*shénsēng*). Later, passing away without ailment while sitting in the full lotus posture, he was truly realized.

Shíxiàng was a native of Yúzhāng. In the *rénchén* year of the Wànlì era, he planted his staff at Xuefēng in Guǎngyuán. He mastered written characters and, in his leisure time, engaged in poetry and painting.
Regarding various canonical scriptures, he re-engraved seven hundred *gōng'àn* (public cases) and authored several volumes of commentaries and songs.

Many high-ranking officials and scholars collected and preserved [his writings]. At the time of his death, various extraordinary omens appeared. The Grand Astrologer Huang Hui composed a stupa inscription for him.
Master Xiaozong traveled south for over thirty years to propagate the teachings; in the *bingshen* year of the Wanli era, he returned to reside at Fanyun Temple in the county.
In the Heavenly Courtyard, he knelt and recited the Lotus Sutra, remaining within for five years without venturing outside. Later, he built a hut at the foot of Mount Ren-tou.

In the autumn of the Wu-wu year, he gathered the monastics and the laity to inform them that he was about to depart. The assembly, thinking he was going elsewhere, earnestly entreated him to stay. He replied, "Not yet; I shall soon take my leave.
At that time, wolves and tigers roamed across this mountain, such that no one dared to step out of their doors. That night, the people...

In his dreams and while asleep, he repeatedly heard the sound of knocking at the door followed by voices of gratitude. When he went to investigate at dawn, [the monk] was already deceased, sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
A stream of tears flowed from his nose down to his knees. The assembly constructed a stupa to enshrine him.
The Bodhisattva Zhìhuì was the daughter of Teacher Zhōuxiáo of Gǔchéng. From birth, she abstained from pungent foods and delighted in reciting the scriptures.
At the age of nineteen, when someone came to inquire about her name, Huì would simply face the wall for ten days without rising. She had frequently fasted from grain and subsisted on cypress leaves.
In the fifth year of the Chénghuà era, she took leave of her parents and traveled to the Bai-ma Temple at Jiānglìkǒu, where she went up onto the scripture pavilion. From there—

He burned incense, sat in the full lotus posture, and entered extinction. Even during the height of the scorching summer heat, his body remained odorless and incorruptible, manifesting divine and miraculous wonders.
The people of that capital subsequently built a sand mound over his remains and fashioned it into a sculpted image, naming him the Bodhisattva Jñānaketu (Wisdom Banner).
The masses vied with one another to serve him, and miraculous responses followed in succession.
Chan Master Guzhou was a man of unknown origins. During the early Wanli era, he arrived at Banxi Temple in Zhen’an and sat facing a wall for several years.
One day, he said to the abbot, "I shall pass away tomorrow. Outside the temple, there are two trees that are about to break.
The one that breaks with a sound will be the abbot, the elder; the one that breaks without a sound will be I. The next day, the two trees indeed broke.

He passed away. He spoke a verse, saying: "Having thoroughly realized that the world is neither existent nor non-existent, what thing remains clearly manifest in the heart? Self-nature has already returned to perfect stillness;
the pure breeze and bright moon are spontaneous. He sat upright and passed away.
Fuzhan, whose style name was Tianyuan, was a native of Chu. He resided at Zhilin on Pengxi Mountain, where he practiced with diligent austerity and attained realization of emptiness and stillness.
During his time, he was a prominent figure in the Chan school. His writings include the *Tianyuan Lu* (Record of Tianyuan) in two fascicles.

Upon his death, he left behind a verse which says: "Seventy-seven years end with a single laugh; Riding backward on a wooden horse, I roar into the western wind. I now cast off my shell and fly away; The bright moon..."
He was like a pure breeze;

his name was Liaoyong, and his style name was Xueji. A son of the Zhang family of Suining, he was skilled from a young age in responding to others' needs. One day, upon hearing of matters that transcend the ordinary, he attained realization.
He sat in meditation for several years until he had gained profound insight. He sought certification from Master Tianyuan, who once composed a mountain [poem] for him.

A Poem on Dwelling: Beside the trees, a long hermitage leans against the emerald peaks; Mist and clouds wind around, as white vapors nestle in the crags. Foolish as I am, it is fitting that I dwell by springs and ravines;
In my failing years, what hinders me from discoursing on past and present? At the edge of the stream, strange rocks erase the traces of my path;

Amidst drifting mists beneath the cliffs, no marks remain of those who come. It was only because I entered the Way that I hid in this secluded valley; I have severed all climbing and clinging—seek no further.
He passed away at the age of seventy-two. On that day, colored clouds covered the temple; everyone marveled at this.
Xuanchang was the son of the Zhao family of Jincheng in Hexi. In his youth, his clan was destroyed by the Hu barbarians.
When disaster was about to befall the Master, the barbarian commander, seeing that his appearance was ancient, pure, and extraordinary, stopped him, saying: "This boy’s gaze shoots outward."
He was no ordinary youth, and thus he escaped [the peril]. Later, he went to Liangzhou to enter the monastic life.

His original name was Huizhi; having encountered Xuangao, he became his disciple. Xuangao always marveled at him and consequently changed his name to Xuanchang to signify the intent of his entrustment.
Subsequently, when the cruel invaders annihilated the Buddha-dharma and harmed various śramaṇas, only the Master managed to escape. In the twenty-second year of the Yuanjia era...

In the intercalary fifth month of that year, he set out from Pingcheng. His route passed through Dai Commandery and Shanggu, crossing the Taihang Mountains to the east, traversing Youzhou and Jizhou to the north, and turning southward toward Mengjin.
He carried nothing but a bundle of willow twigs in his hand and a pinch of scallion leaves.
The barbarian cavalry pursued him, nearly overtaking him. He then struck the sand with a willow branch, whereupon it suddenly became dark as night;
men and horses could not advance. After a short while, the sand subsided and the cavalry arrived once more.
Thereupon, he threw himself into the river and crossed the water by drawing air through the nostrils using scallion leaves. In the eighth month, he reached Yangzhou, having mastered the sutras.

He was well-versed in the Vinaya and had deeply penetrated the essentials of dhyāna. His prognostications regarding auspicious and inauspicious matters were invariably verified. He had extensively studied the *Feng* and *Suo* (the Classics and Histories) as well as the works of the various masters of the schools (*zǐshì*).
As for worldly arts and miscellaneous skills, there were few he did not master. Initially, the great compendium of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was vast and profound in both its phrasing and its meaning.

From antiquity until now, there had never been one who could explain and interpret [these teachings]. The Master then exhausted his thoughts in profound inquiry, analyzing chapters and comparing phrases;

his lectures were peerless. Furthermore, he was skilled in the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and became a patriarch for students. Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty held him in deep esteem and requested that he serve as the tutor to the Crown Prince.
The Master declined three times with firm resolve. His disciples said to him, "The Dharma Master is now about to propagate the Way and save all beings."
He widely proclaimed the teachings of the Name and Instruction. Now the Emperor has humbled himself to extend an invitation, and the Crown Prince has accumulated rites with thoughts of reverence.

If the Way were propagated by Your Holiness’s own person, then the four seas would all turn toward your virtue. Yet now you resolutely decline with lofty humility; is this not the conduct of a Śrāvaka? The Master said:

"This can be discussed with those who possess wisdom; it is difficult to speak of it with worldly people. It was only through the events of the Taichu era that [the Emperor] finally came to recognize his prior enlightenment.

From that time on, he moved his residence to Jingzhou and stayed at Changsha Temple. At that time, the śramaṇa Guǒdézhí was translating the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha) and other texts;

the Master edited and corrected the wording, making the phrasing elegant and the meaning profound. Furthermore, he could extend his hand to emit fragrance and draw water from his palm, such that no one could fathom these wonders.
Reaching the final years of the Song dynasty, he set sail upon a distant journey and arrived in Chengdu. Initially...
He stayed at Dashi Temple and personally painted images of the sixteen deities, including Vajrapāṇi and Guhyapada.

In the third year of the Shengming era, he traveled again to the western frontier and gazed upon the Min Mountains. There, on Mount Qihou within the borders of Guangyang County in northern Minshan Commandery, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.
Consequently, leaning against a cliff and beside a valley, he tied together grass to construct a hermitage for himself and his disciples.
During his final period of practice, he saw a divine being riding a horse, dressed in green robes, who circled the mountain once and then pointed out the location for building the stupa.
He passed away on the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the first year of the Jianyuan era of the Qi dynasty.
Puan was the son of the Cai family of Handong. Having received the Dharma from Baizhang, he addressed the assembly during the Tahe era, saying:
"I am not yet weary of traveling through mountains and waters; let none of you detain me. Tiantai’s Chicheng is where Daoyou once resided.

At the Flower-Crested Stone Beam (Huading Shiliang), where Zhizhe had subdued the māras, he was about to travel there. Starting from Xiangyang, he proceeded by stages through Wozhou and Tianmu, entering the western gate of Tiantai. There, in the midst of a level valley, he found a great peak named Pingtian and settled in a thatched hut upon it. Not long after, he saw a tigress nursing her cubs; they stared at the Master with fixed eyes. Postscript:
In the past, when the Tathāgata was in the world, he entrusted the coming age of the Dharma-ending period (*mappō*) to Śakra and the various kings of nations.

This was because the power of the heavens can subdue ten thousand evils, while the majesty of the king can lead the myriad subjects. As for the intent behind this entrustment of the bequeathed Dharma, it lies in relying upon these two.

It protects and promotes the circulation [of the Dharma]. Fearing that the Three Jewels might decline due to the weakness of the fourfold assembly, it relies upon the sovereign power of the king to cause those who are unworthy to cease their errors and disorder.
It assists the Great Way to bring about renewal and fans the Imperial Wind so that it spreads far and wide.

Thus, throughout successive dynasties, from lords of the land to dukes, ministers, scholars, and commoners, there has been none who, upon hearing of the alms-round (*piṇḍapāta*), has not bowed their hearts in devotion.

[The Buddha] also exhorted [his disciples] to protect [the Dharma]. Thus, sentient beings cannot save themselves without the Buddha-dharma; the Buddha-dharma cannot be propagated without sentient beings.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself recorded his own testament, entrusting it for its circulation. There was a profound reason for this earnestness:

one knows that the World-Honored One’s compassionate gift of the Dharma is such that, even if there were a single person in immeasurable lands who did not hear this Dharma, it would mean the Tathāgata’s original vow had not been fulfilled.
